papers.abstract: Long-term agents accumulate large external memory stores as interactions unfold, increasing the costs of storage, retrieval, and response generation. Efficiency is constrained by two coupled factors: a growing record count increases retrieval overhead, while longer retrieved contexts increase prefill computation and decoding-time attention costs. Existing methods prune or consolidate records, but pruning can discard useful evidence, whereas consolidation may produce fewer yet longer retrieval units. We introduce MemFolder, a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces record count and context length. The framework comprises two core components that share memory groups, using cross-record structure to guide both evidence consolidation and compact representation. RecordFolder grounds entity mentions, progressively selects representative yet complementary anchors, and combines semantic and entity affinity with temporal chaining to consolidate compatible records into fewer retrieval units. ContextFolder encodes the original records within these groups into compact text and uses verification feedback to revise encodings when key facts cannot be recovered. Experiments on the three text-based memory benchmarks LoCoMo, PersonaMem, and LongMemEval and the two multimodal benchmarks M3-Bench-web and M3-Bench-robot demonstrate the strong performance of our methods. Notably, on Mem0, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of the original average performance across the three text-based benchmarks with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in performance retention. Combined with ContextFolder, existing record compression methods further shorten their output records while retaining most of their performance.
authors: Xuyang Liu, Chenwen Lu, Junxi Wang, Siyu Ren, Xinying Lin, Siteng Huang, Hongli Sun, Linfeng Zhang, Honggang Chen
bullets: Targets rising storage, retrieval, and context-processing costs in long-term agents.
RecordFolder uses entity, semantic, temporal, and complementary-structure signals to merge compatible records.
ContextFolder creates compact text representations and revises them when key facts cannot be recovered.
Evaluated on three text-based and two multimodal memory benchmarks.
On Mem0, RecordFolder retained 99.0% of average performance with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in retention.

papers.selection_reason: Structure-guided memory folding reduces agent memory storage, retrieval, and context costs.
papers.title: MemFolder: Structure-Guided Memory Folding for Efficient Agent Memory Management
papers.tldr: MemFolder efficiently compresses agent memories by structurally grouping, consolidating, and shortening records while preserving most of their useful information.

papers.abstract: Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-N (BoN), improve language model outputs by generating multiple candidates per prompt and selecting among them using a reward model. Much of this cost is wasted: a fixed budget is applied to every prompt, although the computation required by prompts varies widely. Adaptive methods halt once sampled answers appear settled, but their thresholds are tuned heuristics with no statistical control over early-stopping errors. We instead seek an anytime-valid stopping rule that takes an error tolerance $\alpha$ as input and halts only once an answer is certified to hold a majority ($\theta_a > 1/2$) under the generator's distribution. We aggregate candidates by final answer with a reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) score and treat stopping as a sequential test over the resulting clusters. Applying Wald's sequential probability ratio test to these clusters yields SPRT-RWSC, which performs well empirically, but its guarantee fails because the leading answer shifts during sampling, and the run is continuously monitored. Our main contribution, e-RWSC, replaces Wald's test with a betting supermartingale (an e-process) for every answer the policy produces, bounding the probability of ever certifying a non-dominant answer by $\alpha$, uniformly over time and across all answers. The RWSC scores drive the bets, so they affect only how quickly a dominant answer $a^\star$ is certified, not validity; certification takes $O(\log(1/\alpha)/d_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta_{a^\star}\|1/2))$ samples. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward models confirm the predicted $1/d_{\mathrm{KL}}$ scaling of cost and show that accuracy improves over baselines at substantially lower token cost.
authors: Vishesh Kumar Singh, Sayak Ray Chowdhury
bullets: Fixed-budget Best-of-N wastes computation because prompts require different numbers of samples.
The method clusters sampled answers using reward-weighted self-consistency and applies anytime-valid betting tests.
Its e-process guarantee controls the probability of ever certifying a non-dominant answer at tolerance α, despite changing leaders and continuous monitoring.
Certification requires O(log(1/α)/d_KL(θₐ*‖1/2)) samples for a dominant answer.
Experiments across models, datasets, and reward models support the predicted cost scaling and show higher accuracy at substantially lower token cost.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an anytime-valid stopping rule (e-RWSC) for inference-time alignment in LLMs using betting supermartingales, directly addressing efficiency and validity in inference-time optimization.
papers.title: Sequential Anytime Valid Tests for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment
papers.tldr: e-RWSC enables statistically valid, adaptive inference-time alignment by stopping once a reward-weighted answer is certified as dominant, reducing token cost while improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.
authors: K. R. Jayaram, Vatche Isahagian, Aswath Vaithinathan Aravindan, Vinod Muthusamy, Punleuk Oum, Gaodan Fang, Michal Ulewicz, Gegi Thomas, Evelyn Duesterwald
bullets: The pipeline mines 1–3 lessons per trajectory, consolidates them into weighted guidelines, and supplies either all or a selected subset at inference.
On AppWorld, stronger models benefited from adding more guidelines, while weaker models often performed better with a smaller selected subset.
DeepSeek-V3.2 improved with its full 191-guideline memory; gpt-oss-120b performed better with about 29 selected guidelines than with all 199.
Deployment uncovered risks including misleading high-support guidelines, lost provenance, swallowed API errors, and baseline-comparison confounds.
The system is available in altk-evolve and deployed in IBM’s CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies how much memory LLM agents should retain, mining and consolidating lessons into guidelines, fitting the LLM Memory subtopic.
papers.title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Self-distilled memory improves long-horizon LLM agents, but the optimal number of stored guidelines depends on the model’s strength and requires careful deployment practices.

papers.abstract: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router-ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges - collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct, a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, while ClonAct's routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.
authors: Xufei Tian, Han Hu, Wenli Du
bullets: Shared linear contexts cause cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line delays; router hierarchies add lossy handoffs and routing overhead.
ClonAct uses a routerless, single-pass Context MMU with Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus, an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk.
The trial merge gate raises true-conflict merge success from 33.3% to 63.3% across three-run means.
ClonAct achieves this merge ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and avoids compact-model router collapse.
Under continuous surges, it reaches 95.0% completion with the lowest median wait and no timed-out status checks.

papers.abstract: Lifelong model editing requires continuously incorporating new facts into deployed large language models (LLMs) without expensive retraining or compromising existing capabilities. Memory-based editors offer an appealing solution by keeping the base parameters untouched, yet their practical use is hindered by linearly growing storage requirements and deteriorating retrieval performance as edits accumulate. To tackle these problems, we introduce BiSpace, a lifelong model editing framework that decouples memory retrieval from knowledge injection across two distinct representation spaces. BiSpace routes queries and identifies relevant edits in an external semantic space, while injecting the corresponding knowledge into the internal representation space of the LLM through sparse and storage-efficient updates. Extensive experiments show that BiSpace shrinks each entry's storage to only about 10.2% of the original and shows strong resilience to long edit sequences of up to 16K edits. On a more challenging benchmark, BiSpace further improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods. These results advance memory-based editing toward reliable long-term model maintenance at scale.
authors: Yue Che, Jingze Wang, Chen Guoyi, Yujie Wu, Xuming Ran, Mingkun Xu
bullets: Addresses growing storage costs and declining retrieval quality as lifelong edits accumulate.
Retrieves relevant edits in an external semantic space while injecting knowledge into the LLM’s internal representation space.
Uses sparse, storage-efficient updates while leaving base model parameters untouched.
Reduces per-entry storage to about 10.2% of the original and remains resilient through up to 16K edits.
Improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods on a challenging benchmark.

papers.abstract: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.
authors: Yifan Lu, Gaoyang Guo, Wen Chen, Ziyun Zou, Jian Wu, Han Zhu, Imran Razzak
bullets: Addresses outdated or misapplied preferences caused by storing interaction content without tracking currentness or scope.
Models the user as a latent preference state updated and revealed by every interaction, including the current request.
Stores relevant beliefs with supporting evidence, scope, and status rather than raw history alone.
Uses a trained writer to produce belief records for a frozen agent.
Achieves the best results among evaluated memory systems across two agent families and two benchmarks; request conditioning improves answering, while auxiliary tasks improve tool use.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HabitusMem. It then projects only the beliefs that bear on the user query to the agent, which answers or acts on the user query. Here, the bland diet and the late-shift hospital address shape the dinner order, whereas the partner-specific vegetarian preference and the one-off oat-milk instruction are kept but not projected. A single writer learns these steps from four tasks: direct writing, state update, request projection, and action projection.

papers.abstract: Revising every answer from a long-term memory can consume substantial inference budget and damage facts that were already correct. We introduce MemMend, a modular selective revision framework that routes potentially incomplete answers to an editor, represents corrections as bounded exact-text replacements, and accepts only edits with resolvable source coordinates and valid edit operations. The editor preserves the current answer when no legal repair is proposed; accepted edits require no additional semantic-verification call. On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, MemMend achieves 67.17 conversation-macro F1 and 88.35 mean Judge score, improving over a verified revision chain by 0.82 and 1.24 points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls. Routing uses 54.15% fewer revision calls than ungated local review, with similar F1 but a 0.67-point lower Judge score. Applied directly to native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, the editing interface raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points. It outperforms same-gate rewriting and saves 49.85-83.72% of editing calls relative to ungated editing, which retains higher F1 in this adaptation. A source-by-editing factorial supports local editing for F1 but leaves an independent quality benefit from source obligations unresolved. Transfer to 451 LongMemEval-V2 Small questions also favors revision efficiency, while an external PerLTQA dialogue subset reveals a completeness gap. These results support selective editing as a reusable quality-cost operating point.
bullets: Targets the cost and risk of revising every answer, which can damage already-correct facts.
Routes uncertain answers to an editor that performs bounded exact-text replacements with valid source coordinates and legal edit operations.
On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, it improves over a verified revision chain by 0.82 F1 and 1.24 Judge points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls.
Direct editing improves native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, with gains of 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 F1 points, respectively.
Results support selective editing as an efficient quality–cost tradeoff, but show a completeness gap on an external PerLTQA subset and unresolved source-obligation effects.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.
authors: Aryan Jain, Abhishek Jha, Anish Nediyanchath, Promod Yenigalla
bullets: Addresses the limitation of memories that record what happened but not how experiences shape user behavior.
Maintains an Episodic Graph linking interactions temporally, causally, and semantically, plus an Insight Graph of LLM-extracted behavioral signals.
Retrieves behavioral knowledge directly from insight nodes grounded in supporting events, avoiding repeated episodic traversal.
Projects event-as-edge knowledge into relational embeddings to transfer insights across users and infer missing knowledge for cold-start users.
Reports gains on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, and LongLaMP, including cross-user improvements at 5% graph sparsity.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on persistent memory to plan tool calls and complete multi-step tasks, which exposes them to memory drift: an adversarial or misleading memory alters the execution path and final outcome. In this work, we investigate online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. We identify two fundamental challenges. (1) Content-level features are insufficient for causal memory-drift attribution, as perplexity or retrieval relevance alone cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized; (2) Counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, as it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory, exceeding real-time serving budgets. To address these challenges, we propose DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. Specifically, DriftGuard first constructs causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score (MDS) that captures action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. Guided by this supervision, DriftGuard then learns an online risk model that estimates MDS from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories via its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DriftGuard-7F0B.
authors: Licheng Pan, Yuzhou Chen, Zhixuan Chu, Yichen Sun, Han Zheng, Zhiyu Wang, Hao Wang, Yan Wang, Bingyu Zhu, Haiwen Hong, Longtao Huang, Kui Ren
bullets: Persistent agent memory can drift and redirect tool use or task outcomes when memories are misleading or adversarial.
Content signals such as perplexity and retrieval relevance do not reliably identify causally influential memories.
Offline, paired counterfactual replays compare original and single-memory-neutralized trajectories to build component-wise memory drift scores.
An online risk model estimates these scores from pre-action information and flags memories using their maximum component risk.
Experiments show accurate identification of drift-inducing memories and efficient online defense, without serving-time counterfactual rollouts.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.
authors: Hang Zhang, Yuzhi Pan, Ziyao Zhong, Chaokun Wang, Shuo Cao, Zeyu Huang, Yue Xue, Fang Niu, Bofan Xie, Guanchen Ge, Zecheng Li, Leqi Zheng, Ziyang Liu, Wei Wang, Miao Gu

GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest reported average score of 56.1, compared with 44.4 for the composite Human-SOTA baseline.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents rely on stored records to recover a person's state as facts change. Reliable answers depend on how facts are recorded, retrieved, and presented to the reader. We treat a long-form persona dossier as a memory representation of a known latent state, an invariant identity plus a timeline of facts, routines, and decision rules tied to life phases. We present ChronoDossier, a benchmark of 311 synthetic dossiers of 1k-10k words written by seven generators from dated timelines. Intrinsic metrics evaluate the records against their intended states; extrinsic metrics test recovery by five readers on a seeded 32-persona GPT-5.1 panel balanced across lengths (520 rated turns per condition). The linked states, records, evidence packets, and answers support tests of construction and evidence delivery. In a contextual-stress control, tag-scoped writer inputs remove detected out-of-scope anchor copying. Frozen questions authored on staged dossiers transfer less reliably to one-pass dossiers of the same states. In matched evidence controls, whole sections repair 29 of 32 GPT-5.1 and 25 of 30 Sonnet 4.6 failures labeled as packaging, compared with 2 of 8 and 1 of 8 answer-formation failures. Attribution uses separate key-based and key-free support measures, with model disagreements retained. Length remains confounded with persona and question composition; the observed between-bucket widening depends on excerpt construction. The benchmark supports offline evaluation against known facts. Memory acquisition from interaction and validation against real users remain outside its scope.
bullets: Models personas as an invariant identity plus time-linked facts, routines, and decision rules across life phases.
Introduces 311 synthetic, 1k–10k-word dossiers from dated timelines, evaluated with intrinsic state-matching and extrinsic reader-recovery metrics.
Matched evidence experiments found whole-section packaging repaired many packaging failures, but rarely corrected answer-formation failures.
Frozen questions transferred less reliably from staged dossiers to one-pass dossiers representing the same states.
Length effects are confounded by persona, question composition, and excerpt construction; interaction-based memory acquisition and real-user validation are out of scope.

papers.abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of continual-learning-style memory systems that retain information indefinitely.
Uses a fixed-capacity LoRA substrate with k-hot rank combinations to reduce interference and independently control temporal decay.
Trains a lightweight controller to decide what to store, how deeply, and for how long based on incoming user events.
Evaluates long-horizon user trajectories with queries testing recall while facts are valid and abstention after expiration.
Achieves 86% of oracle performance, balancing recall and abstention better than continual-learning and RAG baselines.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.
authors: Ziyan Yang, Taiwei Shi, Jieyu Zhao
bullets: Addresses context-window limits and the information loss caused by summarization, masking, and structured memory.
Uses only an append-only text log plus on-demand grep-style regex search—no embeddings, indexes, memory extraction, or extra models.
Trains Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning across five context-management strategies and evaluates multiple long-context memory tasks.
Achieves 95–97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and beats SUPO summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi.
Remains effective as input streams grow and stays on the accuracy–token-cost Pareto frontier across the evaluated tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: GREPMEM Overview. (a) The basic agent loop generates responses and tool calls from its active context, while GREPMEM additionally appends these interactions and tool results to a persistent history log. (b) Context compaction generates a summary when the working context reaches the compaction limit, allowing the agent to resume execution with a compacted context. GREPMEM builds on SUPO’s summarization loop. Extending this framework, GREPMEM enables (c) on-demand retrieval through grep_history and (d) a lossless, append-only full history log containing user messages, tool calls, tool results, summaries, and agent responses. By combining context summarization with a log preserving every message and tool output verbatim, GREPMEM enables grep_history to retrieve matching log lines after the first compaction without embeddings, a retrieval index, or an additional model.

Figure 1: Mean Accuracy vs. Token Cost After RL. We compare four context management strategies by their mean accuracy and token usage across five evaluation tasks. SUPO compresses context through summarization, while Masking discards older tool outputs to free context space. Our method, GREPMEM, combines summarization with a lossless, searchable history log, enabling on-demand retrieval through grep without a retrieval index. papers.abstract: Developing effective forecasting models for diverse time-series domains requires substantial expert knowledge, evidence from scientific literature on the web, and iterative experimentation. However, translating this knowledge and research experience into model designs requires preserving source context and testing applicability under task-specific assumptions. In this paper, we propose NeoResearch, a literature- and experience-guided autonomous research framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) as researchers to discover lightweight, domain-specific forecasting models. Specifically, NeoResearch establishes an expert-inspired dual-loop research workflow, coupling hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with iterative training and hyperparameter optimization through experimental feedback. To enable knowledge-grounded discovery, the agent autonomously mines scientific literature from the Web, extracting modeling mechanisms, empirical evidence, and applicability conditions to formulate task-grounded, testable architecture hypotheses. Furthermore, a hierarchical experience memory links literature findings to experimental outcomes and consolidates conditional lessons, guiding architecture discovery and training optimization while supporting reuse across forecasting tasks. Experiments on ten datasets show competitive performance and support dual loops, literature extraction, and memory reuse. Our code is available.
bullets: Targets the expert knowledge and iterative experimentation typically required for forecasting model design.
Uses a dual-loop workflow combining hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with training and hyperparameter optimization.
Mines scientific literature for mechanisms, evidence, and applicability conditions to create testable architecture hypotheses.
Maintains hierarchical experience memory linking literature insights with experimental outcomes for reuse across tasks.
Experiments on ten datasets show competitive performance and support the framework’s dual loops, literature extraction, and memory reuse.

papers.abstract: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/KnowledgeClaw.
authors: Haoran Luo, Jiapu Wang, Linhao Luo, Luu Anh Tuan

KnowledgeClaw constructs an omnimodal typed hypergraph, maintains it through a closed-loop lifecycle agent, and routes queries to the needed granularity.
It ranks first among 30 baselines across all six tasks, achieving an overall OKE score of 55.9, 14.6 points above the strongest baseline.
The benchmark and system are publicly available.

papers.title: KnowledgeClaw: Towards Agentic Knowledge Engineering via Omnimodal Hypergraphs
papers.tldr: KnowledgeClaw introduces an agentic framework and benchmark for building, updating, and querying live knowledge bases across multiple modalities and granularities.

papers.abstract: Kernel Ridge Attention (KRA) is a recurrent sequence mixer that combines learned nonlinear features with covariance-guided memory updates. It stores associations through recursive ridge regression, using correlations among past keys to determine how new observations modify memory. A content-dependent Ornstein--Uhlenbeck transition controls retention and restores uncertainty for future writes. This construction admits an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and maintains an inference state whose size is independent of context length. Associative block maps and explicit adjoints support parallel training while preserving the recursive update. In controlled language-modeling experiments, KRA improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines, strengthens natural associative recall over the evaluated recurrent models, and achieves practical distributed training throughput. These properties provide a principled foundation for nonlinear, adaptive sequence memory.
authors: Haowei Chen, Yichen Wang, Congfu Xu
bullets: Uses learned nonlinear features and covariance-guided recursive ridge-regression updates to store associations.
Applies a content-dependent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck transition to control retention and restore uncertainty for future writes.
Has an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and an inference state whose size does not grow with context length.
Associative block maps and explicit adjoints enable parallel training while preserving the recursive update.
Controlled language-modeling experiments report better prediction quality than attention and recurrent baselines, plus stronger associative recall than evaluated recurrent models.

papers.tldr: KRA is a recurrent sequence mixer that provides nonlinear, context-length-independent memory with content-dependent forgetting and parallelizable training.

papers.abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.
authors: Zeman Li, Ali Behrouz, Yuan Deng, Praneeth Kacham, Rami Al-Rfou, Meisam Razaviyayn, Vahab Mirrokni
bullets: Builds a two-layer nonlinear memory by placing an activation between two delta-rule linear memories.
Uses chunk-level target propagation to provide hidden-layer targets while retaining efficient unmodified delta-rule kernels.
At matched sizes and training budgets, outperforms KDA across five model sizes on C4 and PG19; C4 perplexity matches or slightly improves on attention.
Its attention hybrid achieves the best perplexity among four tested hybrids, and its largest model reaches 51.84% mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks.
Maintains lower loss than KDA through 20K-token contexts and is substantially faster than tested Titans configurations at 32K context.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a nonlinear memory architecture for LLMs using cascaded linear memories and target propagation, directly fitting LLM Memory.
papers.title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
papers.tldr: Toaster creates a fast nonlinear recurrent memory by cascading two linear memories with target propagation, achieving stronger language-modeling and long-context results than comparable linear and deep-memory baselines.

papers.abstract: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.
bullets: Uses timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes across 3,629 questions and six models.
The Verify prompt increases adoption of false answers on pre-cutoff events in all five tested models, often displacing previously correct answers.
On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini shows increased false-answer adoption; passage priority alone raises adoption, while adding checking lowers it.
Adversarial-Aware restores 82.5–98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with less than one percentage point change in true-passage accuracy.
The framework supports reproducible evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.

papers.abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).
authors: Jiangyun Zhang, Zhou Tang, Kristen Surrao, Zhiyu Chen, Albert Guan, Tor Nitayanont, Yupei Zhang, Roopali Singh, Yunkai Xiao, Shreya Pandit, Julia Huang, Shayan Ali Akbar, Erwin Cornejo, Yuan Li, Yi Zhang
bullets: Targets dynamic enterprise environments where models, workflows, and cost requirements change over time.
Uses self- or teacher-model failure attribution to create corrective micro-memories, consolidate them into macro rules, and retain updates only when held-out accuracy improves.
Evaluated across 14 SOP-Bench and τ²-Bench workflow domains with 5 models.
ARISE-Teacher improves baseline accuracy by 10.9 percentage points on SOP-Bench and 5.8 points on τ²-Bench; ARISE-Self gains 10.0 points on SOP-Bench.
ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost.

papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving memory architecture for LLM agents, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
papers.tldr: ARISE improves enterprise-agent accuracy and efficiency by turning failures into validated, retrievable memory and rules without changing model weights, tools, or workflows.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
authors: Shobhita Sundaram, Cansu Sancaktar, Phillip Isola
bullets: Studies whether agents need explicit instructions for how to self-improve.
Agents receive basic tools, resources, a goal, and a compute budget, but no prescribed learning loop or real-world data.
In gameplay, agents construct their own context-based self-learning algorithms and update text artifacts from collected experience.
Their strategies resemble self-regulated learning and self-generated curricula from prior cognitive and machine-learning research.
Learned artifacts improve performance across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Do capable models specify their own self-improvement? We give a frozen LLM (here, Claude Opus-5) the general goal of improving itself at gameplay, and place it in a constrained workspace. We do not provide real games to practice on, or prescribe a particular self-improvement loop. We instead provide a toolset {Read, Write, Bash, Gameplay}, and allow the teacher to generate its own games and organize its own learning procedure. At the start (t = 0) the teacher uses its tools to build a test game, spawn a player session to play that game, analyze the result, and then update the player context (e.g., skill files). Later (t = 60), the teacher decides to write an adversarial game and observe the player attempt it with and without the optimized context. The teacher then uses the observed failure mode to make another context update.

Figure 7: Self-improving agents use learnability-seeking task selection. (left) Across models, most generated games are easy. (right) Newer model generations spend the most effort (# replays) on games with low to medium win rates. Observed win rates are computed over the first k plays for each game (k ∈ [2, 6]). This can lead to an inverted-U resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play and UED.

Figure 6: Self-improving models display human-recognizable learning strategies. Alignment scores to 13 subprocesses of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning cycle, annotated by an LLM judge and averaged over 3 teacher sessions per model. Models that self-improve score higher across most subprocesses. Average over seeds; individual seeds in Appendix D.2.

Figure 8: Excerpts from a Claude Opus-5 teacher session with high alignment to self-regulated learning subprocesses. In the first example (task-strategies) the teacher writes a random level generator and BFS solver to filter generated games for difficulty and employs A/B testing to identify where its optimized text artifacts are useful. In the second (learning goal orientation) the teacher designs an adversarial game to test its advice and runs validation tests across earlier games to identify regressions.

Figure 11: Generalization with respect to progressively richer information, via context and toolsets. (Left) We run teacher sessions using Python Gameplay with increasingly detailed descriptions of PuzzleScript-Narrow games. Performance initially improves both on the same games, and ARC-AGI-3 transfer, however at higher levels of detail transfer plateaus. (Right) We ablate the teacher’s toolset and Gameplay constraints; performance initially improves on both PuzzleScript-t20 and PuzzleScript-t30 with richer toolsets, however declines on PuzzleScript-t30 after adding t20-specific token and turn budgets. Error bars show ±1 SD over three independent teacher seeds.

Figure 5: Algorithmically measured behaviors. (Left: Game play and design) Newer models more often use A/B Testing (generated games played with and without teacher-written artifacts) and produce fewer games that have low complexity and low difficulty (optimal solution length < 5 and 100% teacher-observed win rate). (Right: Updates) For GPT and GLM, newer generations exhibit more updates that improve the observed win rate on at least one self-generated game. For Opus and GLM, newer models prefer smaller context updates.

Figure 9: Improvements from self-organized learning transfer across benchmarks. Player performance is evaluated at intermediate context updates along the self-learning trajectory on PuzzleScript-t20, PuzzleScript-t30, ARCAGI-L1 and MazeBench. The context optimized under our canonical setting, Gameplay (PS-t20), improves over the unoptimized baseline (dashed line) on PuzzleScript games with both 20- and 30-turn horizons. These gains transfer to different game engines and representations in ARC-AGI-L1 and MazeBench. We also compare progressively richer teacher toolsets, starting from Read/Write, adding Bash, and then PuzzleScript-Gameplay tools. Error bars show ±1 SD over three independent teacher seeds.

Figure 4: Recent models self-improve. Results on PuzzleScript-t20 for two models in each family. Newer generations self-improve over the baseline while older generations fail to do so. Error bars are ±1 SD over 3 seeds.

papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.
bullets: Recasts traditional NLP: language is not only analyzed or generated but also used to structure reasoning and orchestrate workflows.
Defines Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical extension centered on prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts.
Introduces Dialogic Working Memory, where prompts and conversational states temporarily externalize goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and reasoning states.
Relates memory architectures such as BTMA, SKGE, and RMR to episodic, semantic, and metacognitive support for long-horizon dialogue.
Argues for a post-symbolic, post-interface view of AI systems in which natural language combines communication, specification, cognitive scaffolding, and distributed memory.

papers.abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.
authors: Deokhyung Kang, Minjae Gwon, Sangdon Park
bullets: ExploitBench agents frequently stop with execution budget remaining, leaving their ultimate exploitation capability unclear.
Continuing after the first stop yields additional verified gains, but progress diminishes over longer runs.
Less productive continuation is linked to repeated stop responses and summaries that preserve unproven impossibility judgments.
SCoRe compacts context during stop bursts and marks such judgments as unproven, improving verified capability over evaluated continuation baselines.
With SCoRe, MiMo reaches 67.0% capability coverage at 2,000 turns, versus 32.4% under the original stopping policy and 58.6% for GPT-5.5’s 300-turn reference results.

papers.abstract: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.
bullets: Evaluates 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains while varying only how the assistant’s memory is created: stated, inferred, or planted in a summarized webpage.
In two tested models, a planted preference for very short answers and no warnings led to critical omissions in 93% and 84% of later answers, usually without disclosure.
With neutral memory, neither model made value-dependent choices; with the preference, they chose for users in 80% and 95% of such cases.
A one-line instruction reduced but did not eliminate silent gaps; listing must-know points before applying the profile restored more content in four of five models.
The scenarios, evaluation harness, and logs are released.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how stored user preferences in assistant memory silently remove decision-critical information, directly relevant to persistent/agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
papers.tldr: An Inspect benchmark shows that AI assistants can silently omit decision-critical information and make value-dependent choices when stored user preferences conflict with safety-relevant content.

papers.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.
authors: \"Omer Faruk Akg\"ul, Shuli Jiang, Yuting Zhang, Yi Zhang, Xiaohan Fei, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
bullets: Previously useful skills may lower task performance by over 10 percentage points or raise execution cost by nearly 40% after changes.
The impact depends on which environment details become outdated and whether current observations let the agent compensate.
Selective maintenance replays checks from successful executions to detect conflicts, repair affected state, validate updates, or rebuild when needed.
Across four task settings and two models, maintenance improves accuracy by up to 67 percentage points and reduces execution steps by up to 37% versus stale-state reuse.
Scope: results cover the evaluated task settings, models, and environment changes; no change description is provided to the agent.

papers.selection_reason: Selective maintenance of agent skill state in evolving environments; relevant to test-time/continual adaptation and agent memory.
papers.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
papers.tldr: Stale agent skills can harm accuracy and efficiency after environment changes, while selective maintenance restores much of their value without extra model calls.

papers.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.
authors: Wei Hou, Jingxin Geng, Xin Chen, Zheqing Jiang
bullets: Uses calibrated lineage metadata to attribute output sentences to input spans across multi-source, multi-turn contexts.
Detects concept drift and compacts only no-longer-referenced documents while preserving user instructions verbatim.
Window-level embedding similarity better captures paraphrased support than whole-document or lexical matching.
A greedy-window method is faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line matching; attribution remains stable through 40 turns and completes in about 1 second per turn on one GPU.
Drift compaction is conservative, reporting 0% false compaction, with recall limited by attribution accuracy.

Right ribs: inflow this turn (user prompt above, tool calls/results/web below). Expanding a beat reveals per-sentence cards with (type, value, confidence) triplets. papers.tldr: LMLineage traces each agent output sentence to supporting context without model internals or extra inference, then safely compacts context that has drifted out of use.

papers.abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.
authors: Hejia Zhang, Zhongming Yu, Yimin Ding, Wei-Ting Chen, Hengjia Yu, Wentao Ni, Yijun Liu, Cong Xu, Xin Chen, Matrix Yao, Fan Zhao, Jishen Zhao
bullets: Problem: Separate worker contexts can prevent the lead agent from accessing all evidence needed to identify factual conflicts.

Delegation raised retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7%, but lowered conflict detection from 16.2% to 13.2% across three models.
Workers reported both claims in only 35.2% of retrieved conflict pairs; detection was better when one worker saw both claims than when claims were split across workers.
Scope: Results concern the evaluated models and Harvey LAB document-review setting.

papers.abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.
authors: Jingyu Liu, Zongze Li, Zach Xu, Zhanhui Zhou, Tahseen Rabbani, Dawn Song, Ce Zhang
bullets: BRIDGE uses chained observation notes, hybrid BM25–cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering with one LLM call per ingestion or query.
It matches prior state of the art on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and outperforms the best matched-reader baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7–6.3 points.
BRIDGE operates at roughly 5–7K reader-prompt tokens per query, suggesting many advanced memory primitives may not justify their cost on standard benchmarks.
Five adversarial probes show no architecture wins universally: atomic-fact extraction favors rule application, while block summaries favor pattern induction.
Retrieval benchmarks miss failures in how agents use memories: fact extractors lose demonstrated patterns, while block summaries may retrieve rules without prompting action.

papers.abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval update streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
authors: Qingcan Kang, Mingyang Liu, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan
bullets: Addresses stale long-term memories and delayed feedback when memory validity is hidden.
Maintains Local and Global Advisors, using comparisons with a no-memory answer as evidence.
A Meta Governor defaults to local updates and switches to global sharing only after positive pooled utility accumulates.
Provides a finite-time switching guarantee under delayed feedback.
Outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2–7.3 points across reported disagreement episodes and held-out settings; removing modules lowers accuracy by 2–7 points.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Kaichao Liang, Xiaojin Fu, Tao Zhong, Linqi Song
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed memory-update operators and schedules in evolving LLM-agent memory.
Uses a policy conditioned on memory state and recent task history to select and instantiate Abstract, Refine, Bridge, or Reframe operators.
Trains the policy with bi-level fitness: transformation-level retrieval gains regularized by memory complexity, and strategy-level historical efficacy, prediction accuracy, and diversity.
Evaluated under one-pass online plus frozen-transfer settings on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB).
Reports improvements over MemP and MemRL, with the largest ALFWorld gains; ablations support the importance of both fitness levels and the operator library.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of EvoDisco. A frozen language model interacts with a one-pass task stream, retrieves a subgraph, and writes new memories after each episode. A strategy policy reads the memory-graph state and selects one of four operators—ABSTRACT, REFINE, BRIDGE, and REFRAME—which the operator executor applies to the graph. Immediate utility scores each edit by the change in retrieval quality regularized by graph complexity. Every N events, strategic efficacy combines operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity, and updates the policy. Evolution runs only before the cutoff; afterward the agent continues to write memories. Held-out evaluation freezes the accumulated memory.

papers.tldr: EvoDisco enables agents to learn which memory-evolution strategy to apply, when, and how, improving online and frozen-transfer performance across several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
bullets: Three frontier LLMs were given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox to generate weights or design architectures.
On mainly multiple-choice tasks, LLM-designed sparse tables reached up to 54.4% test accuracy.
One designed model outperformed the best released Transformer written by the same LLM while using about 1,800× fewer parameters.
The table structure makes facts interpretable and locally editable: each row corresponds to an answer and errors identify rows to revise.
The proposed associative-memory model was up to 17× faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer; pretrained LLMs remained more accurate.
