papers.selection_reason: Proposes an associative memory-based model for LLMs, challenging the Transformer architecture.
papers.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
papers.tldr: When LLMs write model weights without gradient training, they favor sparse associative tables over Transformers, achieving competitive accuracy with far fewer parameters and potentially faster inference.

papers.abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra derivation between stored conversations and assistant queries.
Restores cached sessions and appends the question, while retaining raw text as the authoritative fallback.
Defines budget-based retention, append-only reads, bounded aggregation, and a cost model for storage and querying.
Estimates substantially higher cache storage than text, with costs varying by model architecture and retention scenario.
Introduces logical QA evaluation via session prefill plus a separate real-cache replay test for numerical equivalence and runtime cost.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Published system-level comparisons under two different benchmarks and source evaluation protocols: (a) LongMemEval’s 97-question subset with 3–6-session histories [1, Fig. 4a]; (b) LoCoMo J scores from Mem0’s vendor-authored evaluation [2]. Full-history reading scores highest among the selected systems shown in each panel, not across all evidence. Zep’s separate vendor-reported LongMemEval-S comparison favours its retrieval system over a full-context baseline averaging about 115K tokens and is not plotted here (§3.2, §8.1). These comparisons do not isolate a memory mechanism, and scores depend on evaluation labels and judges (§9.1). L1–L4 are our descriptive memory modes; KV-LTM has no measured accuracy bar (§8). Costs are modelled separately (§7).

Figure 2: KV-LTM write flow (once per session): canonical per-session prefill creates the stored state at session end; session text, metadata with integrity digests, and native reader state are retained under the §4.8 storage and latency policy, which may evict or invalidate state — the text is always kept. Boxes denote logical steps or stored objects, not software components.

Figure 4: BF16 state bytes per token, logarithmic scale, for six pinned configurations and one representative DeepSeek-V3-class assumption (marked †, not a pinned checkpoint). MLA values assume compressed-latent storage. Kimi-Linear shows only its MLA-layer component (bMLA = 8,064 B/token); its per-session recurrent state is symbolic and not drawn. The plotted per-token spread is ∼40× (the hybrid’s bMLA part at the low end); among the non-hybrid configs the spread is ≈10.5× (31,104 → 327,680).

Figure 3: KV-LTM read flow (per question): each retained session’s text is verified against its stored digest first — a known-good copy is recovered and re-verified on failure, and an unrecoverable session counts as unavailable (out of coverage), never as evidence. Valid state is read from a request-local working copy; when policy allows, invalid or evicted state is rebuilt from the verified text (§4.3), otherwise the session is counted as not cached and delegated to the §4.8 text fallback, outside the depicted cache-read path. Per-session outputs supply bounded evidence to the aggregator (§4.6); optional hybrid, verifier/reranker and joint-evidence lanes (§4.5, §4.7) complement the reference read. Boxes denote logical steps or stored objects, not software components.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes persistent per-session KV caches as long-term memory for LLM assistants, directly addressing LLM memory and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
papers.tldr: KV-LTM proposes storing each conversation session’s raw text and model KV cache to preserve long-term memory while accelerating future question answering without recomputation.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.
authors: Xin Guo, Qiang Zhang, Xiang Zhou, Arushi Rai, Siyu Lin, Yifan Wu, Xiang Shen, Lei Huang, Qunshu Zhang, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: Repeated profile-text prefills dominate ranking inference because profiles appear after varying prompt prefixes, preventing effective prefix caching.
Lightweight LoRA writers, trained by self-distillation, generate reusable profile KV caches during profile updates.
A KV scheduler overlaps host-to-GPU cache transfers with computation for the next batch.
On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, ranking quality shows no statistically significant difference from full prefill across memory updates.
Under saturated load, throughput improves 4.0–4.5× for scoring and 1.4–1.9× for profile updates.

papers.selection_reason: Reusable KV caches as persistent user memory for LLM recommenders; fits KV cache efficiency and LLM memory.
papers.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
papers.tldr: KVUse accelerates LLM recommendation serving by storing user profiles as reusable KV caches instead of repeatedly prefilling their text.

papers.abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.
bullets: Tests Hoel’s overfitted-brain hypothesis: dream-like distortion may prevent overfitting to recent experiences.
An LLM agent rewrote text memory nightly after simulated conversations, with controlled detail or random-text corruption and memory limits.
Across 30 runs, corruption did not improve transfer of earlier learning to new tasks.
Replacing details in 40% of turns reduced recall from 76% to 60%; the agent answered corrupted-detail questions correctly 40% of the time versus 75% without corruption.
Random text had little consistent effect because the model recognized and excluded it as corrupted; future tests may need a learner less able to detect corruption.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method. Each simulated day adds about 130,000 tokens of conversation. In the corrupted conditions, 5 to 40 percent of the day’s turns are corrupted before the model rewrites its memory under a size limit. This repeats for 10 nights, and day 11 holds the final tests. The ticks under the boxes show which steps each condition runs. With no rewrite, memory holds the most recent turns that fit under the limit.

Figure 1. An illustration of the overfitted brain hypothesis, not our data. Ten training points (filled circles) come from a smooth function with a small amount of noise. The left panel fits a flexible curve to only these points, and the curve passes through every point and swings between them. The right panel fits the same curve to many noisy copies of the points, and the curve is smoother and closer to the held-out points (open triangles). Our corrupted conditions apply the same idea to the text the model rewrites into memory each night.

The dotted line marks the clean rewrite and the dashed line marks the no-rewrite baseline. Bars show one standard deviation over the three histories. Differences of 2 points or less are smaller than the standard deviation across the three histories, which is 5 points for the clean rewrite.

Figure 4. Percent of the 12 facts about the user acted on per condition, on similar tasks (filled) and different tasks (hollow). The grey square is No rewrite, where both values are 8 percent. Values are means over the three histories.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies persistent text memory, nightly rewriting, and forgetting in an LLM agent, fitting LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory
papers.tldr: Corrupting an LLM agent’s nightly memory replay did not improve learning and often caused it to store false details as facts.

papers.abstract: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.
bullets: Introduces “Experience Rot,” where prior memories, histories, notes, and skills become liabilities after tool changes.
Tests agents using tools defined under the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
After silent changes, experienced agents fail on most tasks while task-new agents mostly succeed.
The failure occurs across all tested memory types and worsens with more experience; agents often incorrectly report success.
Simple fixes—announcing updates or referring agents to documentation—are insufficient, especially when documentation is incomplete.

papers.selection_reason: Shows experience can hurt agents when tools change; relevant to continual learning and agent memory.
papers.title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
papers.tldr: Agents with accumulated experience can fail more than novices when tools change silently, because they repeat past calls instead of checking the current interface.

papers.abstract: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
bullets: Frames memory systems as custodians of users’ persistent information with explicit behavioral responsibilities.
Introduces an open-source benchmark suite covering performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty, while identifying remaining gaps.
Provides MilaMem and a governance layer for controlled study of memory-system design choices.
Finds that no system dominates all performance benchmarks, and strong task performance can coexist with weak privacy, sovereignty, and security.
Shows that recall and retention policies can improve privacy and poisoning resistance, though recall may reduce helpfulness.

papers.abstract: A useful memory need not resemble the question it helps answer. Jetriever ranks each stored memory by Jev's decision score for its usefulness to the current question, replacing similarity search with full-pool utility scoring. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, it places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases; matched BM25 and MiniLM controls reach 1.6% and 0.0% when indexing user turns. A 20-question comparison separates finding evidence from ranking it: Jev and Qwen3.5 9B each find 90% of gold exchanges by rank 50, while Laya finds 30%; at rank one, Jev reaches 85% and Qwen3.5 9B 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever's four-dimension score is 55.4%, against 44.3% for ReFind on the same questions. Jev retrieval costs USD 0.00834 per InMind question and USD 0.03103 per MAB question on average. These results show the value of world knowledge, scores that rank decisive memories first, and affordable full-pool scoring.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now assist users across sessions of images and text, carried by an external memory of what was said and shown. When such an assistant answers wrongly, the failure usually began earlier, in how a record was written, updated or retrieved, and the answer alone does not say where. We formalize multimodal memory as four stages, Write, Update, Retrieve and Answer, and define nine error types across them. A stage-resolved analysis on Mem-Gallery traces most failures to a source stage, and most of those lie before the answer. Injecting known errors against fact-preserving control edits, we then follow each tainted record downstream. Early errors survive to the answer as apparent evidence, and hurt most when no other record holds the fact. A diagnosis that trusts the quoted evidence therefore blames the stage where the error surfaces, not the one where it began. We propose MemDoctor, in which the MLLM that built the memory diagnoses its own failures. It traces each needed fact backward through the four stages, accepts a diagnosis only when the cited evidence is found in memory, and repairs that stage before answering again. On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on both Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.
authors: Ruiyang Jiang, Xinyang Liao, Weikai Huang, Yuqi Niu, Junjie Zhou, Yubin Zheng
bullets: Frames multimodal memory failures as nine error types across four stages: Write, Update, Retrieve, and Answer.
Finds that most failures originate before the final answer, with early errors propagating as misleading evidence.
Shows that evidence-based diagnosis alone can misattribute an error to the stage where it becomes visible.
Uses backward fact tracing and memory-grounded diagnosis to repair the responsible stage before re-answering.
Improves accuracy on Mem-Gallery and MemLens, and also benefits MuRAG and A-Mem, using a 4B backbone.

papers.title: MemDoctor: Stage-wise Error Attribution and Repair for MLLM Agent Memory

papers.abstract: Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.
bullets: Addresses growing costs, extraction errors, and missed cross-session patterns in text-based memory systems.
Uses a recurrent hypernetwork and gated latent state to consolidate session knowledge into a fixed-size adapter.
Combines consolidated parametric memory with verbatim episodic retrieval for complementary recall and detail.
Outperforms reported agentic and gradient-based baselines on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three 2–7B open models.
Builds memory 3–151× faster than extraction systems and improves accuracy by 12–15 points when episodic retrieval misses evidence, and 4–5 points with an oracle buffer.

papers.abstract: An agent that carries memory across tasks is only as good as the entries it keeps. We begin from an observation that is easy to reproduce and uncomfortable for the field: naively accumulating cross-task experience can make an agent \emph{worse} than one with no memory at all. On AgentBoard, a workflow-induction memory solves fewer tasks than a memoryless ReAct agent in seven of eight domains, and a per-step procedural store with no surrounding structure loses half of ReAct's completions on Jericho. We argue that the missing ingredients are per-action credit assignment and an explicit life cycle for stored entries, and present AdMem, which supplies both. Before each action the actor commits to an expected outcome; a concurrently running critic scores the realized outcome against that expectation and writes a procedural entry carrying a binary reward and a reflection, so credit lands on the action that earned it and no environment reward is required. Each entry then carries a scalar utility, updated online under a noisy-OR reward model, that ranks retrieval jointly with context similarity and drives eviction and merging, giving the store a forgetting and consolidation policy instead of unbounded growth. Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains AdMem solves 441 against 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline --- a pooled gain significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test, concentrated in the domains that supply transferable cross-task structure. All memory stays human-readable text, which is what makes the failures above diagnosable --- and, as we discuss, also makes the store an auditable but attackable surface.
authors: Runzhe Wang, Huilin Lu, Shengjie Liu, Li Dong, Zhihuai Zhu
bullets: Naively accumulating cross-task memory can hurt performance, sometimes performing worse than a memoryless ReAct agent.
Before each action, the agent predicts an expected outcome; a concurrent critic compares the result with that expectation and records a binary reward plus reflection.
Each procedural memory entry receives an online-updated utility score under a noisy-OR model, guiding retrieval, eviction, and merging.
Across 707 AgentBoard tasks in eight domains, AdMem solved 441 tasks versus 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline.
The human-readable memory is auditable and diagnosable, but also presents an attackable surface; gains concentrate where cross-task structure transfers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Information flow between the environment, the actor, the critic, and the long-term memory store. The three modules run in separate threads: the actor never blocks on the critic, so memory writing and evaluation overlap with acting. The actor’s short-term memory (STM) holds the task instructions, the task and memory tool specifications, and the current task’s short-term trace, with environment facts surfaced through a priority-ranked semantic heap and event summaries through a scope-ordered episodic stack (Section 2.3); retrieved long-term memory (LTM) enters the same context. Every action the actor sends to the critic carries the expectation the actor committed to before acting, which is what the critic scores the realized outcome against; the resulting per-action reward travels to the store alongside the new procedural entry and updates the utilities of the entries that were retrieved for that action (Section 2.4).

Table 1: Task completeness (C, the fraction of tasks solved) and average progress (P, the mean of the per-task progress score pi ∈ [0, 1]) on the eight AgentBoard domains, using Claude Haiku 4.5 as the backbone for every method. Bold marks the best value in each column. Each domain is a fixed task set of the size given in the second row, so completion counts are recoverable exactly from C (e.g. 63.4% of 134 is 85 tasks); we use those counts for the Fisher exact tests reported in the text. Each configuration is streamed once over the task set in a single lifelong episode. On the three 20-task domains a single task is worth 5.0 points of C, which is why we base per-domain conclusions on the tests rather than on the point differences alone.

Table 2: Aggregate view of Table 1 over all 707 tasks. Intervals are Wilson 95% binomial intervals on the pooled completion rate. Macro-avg. C weights the eight domains equally rather than by task count; we report both because WebShop and ScienceWorld together hold 48% of the tasks. Against ReAct, the pooled difference is significant for AdMem (+53 tasks, two-sided Fisher exact p = 5× 10−3) and significant in the negative direction for AWM (−76 tasks, p = 7 × 10−5). Because all three methods are run over the same 707 tasks, both comparisons are paired; both remain significant under the least favorable exact McNemar test consistent with these margins (p = 0.03 and p = 5× 10−3 respectively, Appendix C).

Table 3: Component ablation on Jericho (20 tasks), Claude Haiku 4.5. STP: short-term planning and context management only, with all long-term recall removed. LTP: the long-term procedural store only — per-step retrieval with critic-generated reflections and the reward-based utility retained — with short-term planning and context management removed. AdMem: all components. STP and ReAct are single-epoch by construction, since neither carries anything across tasks. For LTP and AdMem the task set is streamed again each epoch without resetting the long-term store, so the epoch axis measures accumulation rather than repetition of a fixed store; entry utilities carry over with the store, so an entry that proved unhelpful in an earlier epoch enters the next one already down-weighted.

papers.selection_reason: Procedural memory with credit assignment, retrieval, and eviction for task-solving agents directly fits LLM/agent memory.
papers.title: AdMem: Expectation-Grounded Procedural Memory for Long-Horizon Task-Solving Agents
papers.tldr: AdMem improves long-horizon agents by assigning credit to individual actions and managing procedural memories through utility-based retrieval, merging, and forgetting.

papers.abstract: Cost-aware LLM routing often selects the cheapest policy meeting empirical risk and coverage constraints. Yet a router that passes an audit can violate its fixed service contract on new requests, even when candidate policies are constructed independently. We study this deployment-commitment decision with disjoint construction, audit, and test samples. Across 19 RouterBench task families, the cheapest audit-feasible router deploys in 91.82% of opportunities but violates the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments. We introduce Menu-Aware Routing Commitment (MARC), which qualifies policies using audit evidence and a serving-cost tolerance to retain the apparent winner, deploy a supported alternative, or defer. Its practical policywise variant (MARC-P) reduces observed conditional failure to 0.73% at 85.79% deployment, with higher serving cost; fixed-margin and formal risk-control procedures provide competitive alternatives. Nested audits show how added evidence changes deployable policy sets, and learned semantic routing exhibits the same commitment failure. These results establish deployment commitment as a distinct operational decision connecting router evaluation, service reliability, and inference cost.
authors: Minxuan Hu, Qishi Zhan, Ziheng Chen, Zhengtao Yao, Zihan Dong, Jiayu Yi, Wenxi Sun
bullets: Across 19 RouterBench task families, the cheapest audit-feasible router violated the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments.
The study separates router construction, auditing, and testing using disjoint samples to examine deployment commitments.
MARC uses audit evidence and serving-cost tolerance to retain the apparent winner, choose an alternative, or defer deployment.
MARC-P reduced observed conditional failure to 0.73% at 85.79% deployment, with higher serving cost.
Nested audits and semantic routing show that commitment failures persist as evidence and routing approaches change.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates deployment commitment failures in cost-aware LLM routing, introducing a mechanism to audit and qualify policies based on serving cost and reliability.
papers.title: When the Cheapest Feasible Router Fails: Auditing Deployment Commitments in Cost-Aware LLM Routing
papers.tldr: The cheapest LLM router that passes an audit can still violate its service contract after deployment, while MARC reduces failures by allowing supported alternatives or deferral.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.
bullets: Study 1 found that retaining prior replies reduced success on sharded math tasks for GPT-4o-mini and Mistral-7B; Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction without significance.
Study 2 introduced CDR-Stream, a 100-turn state-tracking benchmark with matched per-turn difficulty and exact answers.
Full-history accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within 20 turns, whereas solver-verified state summaries preserved substantially higher accuracy.
Consistency, logical coherence, stability, and tested drift monitors provided no robust, model-general early warning; single streams detected only very large drops.
The findings support storing task state outside the transcript and monitoring performance across sessions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The monitoring framework. A context policy decides what the model sees at turn t. Responses are scored into a per-turn quality vector, smoothed over a window and passed to drift detectors whose thresholds are calibrated on stationary dialogues. Exact gold is needed for CQ, RS and ES and for evaluating alarms; CS, LS and SS do not use it.

Figure 2: Study 1 primary endpoint (n = 48 paired tasks per model). Left: final-turn success with 95% Wilson intervals (Wilson, 1927). Right: paired difference, fresh prefix minus dialogue history, with 95% task-bootstrap intervals and Holm-adjusted McNemar p-values.

Figure 3: Study 2 accuracy over 100 turns in 5-turn bins: (a) all 30 dialogues per model; (b)–(f) the five scenarios, six dialogues per model each. Solid: dialogue history; dashed: verified state summary; dotted vertical lines: scheduled difficulty changes.

Figure 4: Quality metrics do not track accuracy. (a) Study 2, GPT-4o-mini, dialogue history, 5-turn means over 30 dialogues (descriptive); dashed: accuracy under the verified state summary; CS is supported by 2976 of 3,000 turns. (b) Post-hoc replay of Study 1: median and 10–90% band over 1,000 orderings of window means (W = 20) when the regime switches from fresh prefix to dialogue history at session 49.

Figure 5: Simulated detection within 33 turns versus the accuracy drop from 0.80 and the number of dialogues pooled per turn (W = 20, thresholds from 12 null streams, 5% false-alarm target). Left: change at turn 34; right: at turn 51. Dotted line: 80% detection.

Table 2: The two benchmarks at a glance. K/L: same-context repeats / reworded instructions per turn. Metric coverage lists which of the six dimensions were computed where; CQ, RS and ES always need a final answer and the gold (Section 3).
Table 1: Positioning against the closest prior work.
Table 3: Study 1 paired final-turn success over 48 tasks per model. F/D: tasks in which only the fresh prefix, or only the dialogue history, succeeded; p: exact McNemar test.

A unit is one (task, model) pair (up to 3 × 48); turns are the pre-final turns of those units pooled together, the level at which the metric is observed; tasks are the distinct source tasks contributing at least one turn, the level at which the permutation test clusters observations. rpartial: task-clustered partial correlation; p: one-sided task-clustered permutation test.

papers.selection_reason: Study of conversation history effects and state summaries in LLM reasoning is relevant to LLM memory and state management.
papers.title: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Accumulating an LLM’s conversation history can sharply degrade reasoning accuracy, while common process metrics do not reliably warn of the decline.

papers.abstract: An agent that stores facts over time eventually stores several versions of the same fact. Asked a value-agnostic question - "which team does X play for now?" - a similarity retriever cannot prefer the current version, because every version matches the entity the query names. StaleBench isolates this stale-retrieval failure on 892 real updating facts, with currency labels from the source (Wikidata validity years via TempLAMA), never from a retrieval score. Our central result is that retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards: a retention policy and its retain-everything control return the identical statement at rank 1 for every test query, yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy on two readers when no date is shown. Contamination@5, the metric we add, ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 do not. Withdrawing the lexical anchor that statements carry costs deployed keying mechanisms tens of points of freshness; entity resolution on both the write path and the query recovers most of the loss. Three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) and a reimplemented ERASE each handle supersession differently, and no single scoring convention describes all four. We release the data, a frozen evaluator, and reference baselines.
bullets: Evaluates stale retrieval on 892 real-world updating facts with source-derived validity labels.
Shows retrieval rankings can look identical even when reader accuracy differs by up to 65.6 points without dates.
Introduces Contamination@5, which identifies stale-memory failures that current@1/current@5 miss.
Finds removing lexical anchors severely harms freshness, while entity resolution on writing and querying recovers most of the loss.
Compares supersession handling in Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem, and ERASE, and releases data, evaluation tools, and baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The keying ladder as the lexical anchor is withdrawn. The inventory-based keying rungs are indistinguishable at a=0, and at a=1 the gazetteer falls 65.8 points below the oracle; the entity linker (handed the alias inventory) tracks the oracle, while the two mechanisms deployed memory systems use do not. The oracle keys perfectly but still retrieves by similarity, so the two rungs that resolve the query as well are not bounded by it — and the upper one, which resolves symmetrically with a complete alias table, is close to flat across the whole axis (0.994 to 0.912). Withdrawing the anchor costs almost nothing to a system that resolves entities on both paths.

Figure 1: StaleBench in one picture. (a) Real updating facts become a chronological stream with one value-agnostic query per fact and a source-defined current label; two knobs set how hard same-fact detection is. (b) A policy is store-all retrieval, optionally time-aware, or retention = a keyer (is this a fact already stored?) × a mechanism (overwrite, or invalidate and keep), run on the write path, the read path, or both. (c) Each top-k is scored by retrieval metrics, by what its text says, and by what a reader answers.

Figure 3: Left: retrieval current@1 against reader accuracy for the primary reader; the dashed line is what a retrieval metric would predict. The arrow is the controlled pair — two keyers that return the same statement at rank 1 on every query of this configuration, so they share an x exactly and the vertical distance is what contamination of ranks 2–5 costs. Right: constructed contexts, where contamination is manipulated rather than observed.

Table 5: Three deployed systems and ERASE, reimplemented, under the rungs’ harness, streams and encoder (test subsample, n=150 facts, p=0.5). cur@1 attributes the top memory to its source statement, by text scores what it says, cont.@5 is contamination@5 by text, and reader is qwen2.5:14b answering from the system’s own top-5. The Mem0 and Graphiti rows have qwen2.5:14b in the loop. The lower block is the ladder on the same streams. Per-system tables, gates and the second adjudicator are in Appendix K.
Table 6: Positioning: what each line of work measures, and what it cannot see.

Table 3: current@1 as the lexical anchor is withdrawn (a = alias_p: the probability a non-introducing statement uses a short form). Test split, p=0.5, every policy re-tuned on val at every level. The last column is the keying deficit at a=1: points of current@1 below the true-key oracle, which isolates the same-fact decision from the retrieval difficulty that aliasing also creates (and which the oracle pays too). The oracle is a write-path oracle — perfect same-fact detection, ordinary similarity retrieval — so it is an upper bound only within that family, and the rungs that also resolve the query post a negative deficit against it (§5.2).

Table 19: Each policy’s own top-5 handed to qwen2.5:14b (anchored, n=150; rows carry the harness’s policy ids — reconsolidation is the threshold keyer, lexical-key the gazetteer, fuzzy-key the fuzzy linker, fuzzy-rw-key symmetric keying; the system’s row is its own rewritten memories in its own words, from the 0.1.118 run — 2.0.11 is in the text). as retrieved is what a deployment gets; the next two pairs apply this paper’s read-path fix post hoc to those same contexts, resolving the query through the keyer of §5.2 and then keeping one memory per resolved entity, at no ingestion and no model call. The two middle cur@1 columns are identical wherever the readers beside them differ by up to 1.000 against 0.293: the retrieval metric cannot see the difference the reader is made of. The last column keeps the oldest memory per entity instead of the freshest. Because facts arrive as they become true, freshest-is-current is free here (150/150 facts); withdrawing it leaves only what each write path had already removed, so the column reads near zero for anything that stores every version and near one for anything that merges on write. It is a write-path purity measure that uses no identifiers and no timestamps in its favour, and it is where the deployed system is priced.

Table 7: Where each policy’s errors go in the anchor-free regime (a=1, test, p=0.5). contamination@5 is shown with current@5 because it is not monotone (§3): the entity linker’s near-zero contamination is partly the absence of any version of the fact, not only the absence of conflict.

Table 17: Mem0 scored under the same harness as the idealized rungs, on the same streams, with the same encoder (test subsample, n=150 facts, p=0.5; anchored unless the column says otherwise; contamination@5 by id). The rightmost column is the system’s own decision histogram over its 329 ingestion calls. The library version is part of the result, not provenance: see the text.

Table 18: Every (release, vector store) pair we probed, and whether its numbers are usable. writes: the system can record its own ADD/UPDATE decisions. retrieval: a hand-scored query returns the right fact first from what the store holds. Two pairs fail, in opposite halves, and both produce plausible-looking metrics that measure the backend rather than the system — which is why the selection of runs quoted in this section is made by this table and not by which result file was written last.

Table 16: A language model as the same-fact keyer, against the mechanical rungs (test, p=0.5). For each arriving statement the model is shown the top-4 stored candidates by cosine and asked which, if any, describes the same fact; it sees statement text only — never an id, a key, or a timestamp. % split is the retrieval-independent share of facts scattered over more than one slot (§G).

Table 20: The second deployed system. Graphiti (graphiti-core 0.29.2, FalkorDB, qwen2.5:14b adjudicator, MiniLM encoder) on the identical 150-fact streams, scored by id, by text and at the reader (qwen2.5:14b, own top-5), by three read paths over the same stored graph: the library’s default search (as returned), the same hits with non-invalidated edges ranked first (the temporal-KG rung’s read path), and invalidated edges dropped. Ladder rows are the same stream; contamination@5 is by id here and by text in Table 5. An empty reader cell means that arm was not run.

Table 10: The two temporal signals, corrupted separately and together (test, p=0.5; current@1, mean over 3 permutation seeds; hyperparameters are the val-tuned values of the clean regime, since a deployment cannot retune for a corruption it does not know it has). clock permuted: timestamps permuted across statements, arrival order intact — unreliable logging, imports, clock skew. arrival permuted: arrival order permuted, each statement keeping its own timestamp — delayed or out-of-order ingestion. Every time-aware or retention policy reads one signal and is blind to the other; with both corrupted nothing recovers. The per-seed spread is at most 5.8 points in any cell.
Table 8: current@1 by per-fact version count (test, p=0.5). The cheap fix collapses on the facts that changed most — exactly the motivating population.

Table 9: A late stale report: for a fraction q of the 468 test facts the final version arrives before its predecessor, timestamps intact (p=0.5; current@1, mean of 3 draws). Overwrite loses its margin in proportion to q with contamination@5 fixed at 0.000: one confidently stale memory, not a contradiction.

Table 21: A second adjudicator model. Mem0 0.1.118 (chroma) under its stock, user-centric extraction prompt and under a prompt that admits facts about any named entity, each driven by qwen2.5:14b and by glm-4.6; Graphiti with both models, as returned and with valid edges first. Same 150-fact streams as Table 17; contamination@5 by id. slots for Graphiti is active/total edges; the last column counts UPDATE+DELETE decisions (Mem0) or invalidations (Graphiti).

Table 25: v1.1 scale track: the same ladder on every changing TempLAMA fact rather than only the single-valued ones. 2,904 test facts (2,436 of them multi-valued, mean 1.23 currently valid values each) against 468 in v1.0, scored identically — a top-1 is current when its value is valid in the final year — plus set recall@5: the fraction of a fact’s distinct currently valid values whose statements appear in the top-5.

Table 4: Reader accuracy when each policy’s own top-5 becomes the context (test split, anchored configuration a=0, p=0.5). Retrieval columns are the same policies’ current@1 and contamination@5. Readers are qwen2.5:14b, glm-4.6; the last two columns repeat both readers with the stored year surfaced in the context. Retrieval hyperparameters are inherited from the val tuning of §5.1 and are never tuned against reader accuracy. The two read-path rows are the controlled pair: identical retrieval columns except contamination@5, because they return the same statement at rank 1 for all 468 queries of this configuration.
Table 1: Terms used throughout.

Table 2: TempLAMA test split (468 facts), paraphrase p=0.5. Mean over queries; brackets = bootstrap 95% CIs; tuned hyperparameters from val (k=2 for time-rerank, τ=0.60 for the threshold keyer). Reconsolidation (τ ) is the threshold keyer and Lexical key the gazetteer keyer, both with overwrite. All four pre-specified paired comparisons (sign-flip permutation, Holm-corrected; the family is hard-coded before test evaluation and its store-all comparator is selected on val) are significant at p < 10−3. Two go against our own policies: time-rerank > cosine, and the best store-all fix > the threshold keyer on current@1; two go with them: the threshold keyer < the best store-all fix on contamination@5, and oracle > threshold keyer.

Table 12: Same-fact decisions scored directly as a clustering of statements against the true fact partition, independent of any retriever. Merge err. counts slots holding statements about more than one fact; % split is the fraction of facts scattered across several slots.

Table 14: current@1 on the 7,078-statement corpus (6,083 distractor statements from fact keys that are never queried). Keyers hold either an open-world inventory (the 468 queried subjects) or a closed-world one (all 2,995 subjects in the stream). Store-all policies use no inventory, so their columns coincide.
Table 13: Retention mechanism at fixed keyer (p=0.5): invalidation matches overwrite’s accuracy and contamination while keeping every superseded statement recoverable.

Table 15: The anchor-free ladder at a=1 with short forms drawn from Wikidata aliases and English Wikipedia redirects instead of generated mechanically (test, p=0.5; current@1, and the keying deficit in points against the write-path oracle of the same configuration; every tunable re-tuned on val, whose own inventory covers 288 of its subjects). natural: a subject with no real short form stays anchored (270 of the 467 distinct subjects behind the 468 test facts have one; 59.6% of alias-eligible statements are aliased). natural+fallback: such a subject takes the mechanical forms instead (95.1%), the like-for-like comparison with Table 3.

Table 22: The third deployed system. LangMem 0.0.30 (LangChain’s long-term memory: one structured-output call per statement returns the memories to insert or patch; inserts and updates on, deletes off, as installed) on the identical 150-fact streams with the benchmark’s MiniLM encoder as its store index, scored by id, by text and at the reader (qwen2.5:14b, own top-5). Ladder rows are the same stream. contamination@5 is by text, since the library rewrites what it stores and adds memories no statement wrote.

Table 23: The fourth mechanism: ERASE, rewrite-on-arrival (Li et al., 2025), reimplemented from the paper because no release pins it. When a statement arrives, the 5 stored facts nearest to it are retrieved and one model call decides, for each, KEEP, REWRITE or DELETE; the statement is then inserted. Same 150-fact streams, MiniLM encoder, reader (qwen2.5:14b, own top-5). contamination@5 is by text, since a rewrite can keep the superseded value’s string in a past-tense clause.

Table 29: current@1 as verbalization diversity and anchor availability are varied together (test split, re-tuned on val in every cell). p is the probability a statement uses a paraphrased template rather than the relation’s base one. The write-path ladder’s ordering is identical at every level; including the symmetric rung it is identical except that the symmetric rung overtakes the write-path oracle once any paraphrasing is present. Magnitudes move — store-all cosine by 4.3 points across the range, the entity linker by 5.1 — while the symmetric rung moves 0.4, because resolving the query to a key never asks how the sentence was phrased.

Table 11: Surface variation stresses similarity keying: current@1 [95% CI] and contamination@5 on the test split as the paraphrase probability p grows. The oracle’s keying is unaffected by construction; the gazetteer keyer (values in the text) is unaffected while subjects stay verbatim.
Table 24: Constructed contexts: reader accuracy when contamination is manipulated rather than observed (test, n facts per condition), with and without the stored year surfaced in the context.
Table 27: Slot budget B (gap 0.4, E=12 entities): current@1. Store-all fixes need the store; retention keeps one slot per fact and is budget-immune once B ≥ E.

Table 26: Controlled diagnostic, current@1 (mean ±95% CI half-width over 20 seeds). Left: update visibility (value_gap). Right: surface variation (key_jitter) at gap 0.4. Every policy is re-tuned per column on 10 held-out generator seeds; the selected values vary across columns; their ranges are given in Appendix U.

Table 28: τ sensitivity (current@1). Clean: perfect across τ ∈ [0.3, 0.75], false-merging below and falsesplitting at τ=0.9. Under jitter 0.4 the optimum moves to τ=0.2 and buys 0.24 → 0.54 — real, and still short of the oracle.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses agent memory and stale retrieval, matching the LLM memory subtopic's agent-memory scope.
papers.title: StaleBench: Isolating Stale Retrieval in Agent Memory, and Pricing the Fix
papers.tldr: StaleBench shows that similarity-based retrieval can favor outdated facts, while contamination-aware evaluation and entity resolution substantially improve freshness.

papers.abstract: When a coding agent runs out of room, its earlier findings are cut and it forgets them. We tested a simple fix: automatically putting the agent's last finding back in front of it. We fixed the rules in advance and ran 98 paired coding tasks with and without this reminder, using Gemma 4 31B (QAT, 4-bit) in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent harness. The reminder made no measurable difference: across all 98 tasks, 47 were solved with it and 48 without (-1.0 points, 95% interval [-8.3, +6.3], exact McNemar p=1.0). The primary outcome (a documented deviation from our preregistration), the first 48 pairs, was 29/48 with memory against 25/48 without (+8.3 points, [-2.1, +18.3], p=0.22); the extension of 50 tasks, decided after that result, pointed the other way (18/50 against 23/50, -10.0 points, p=0.125), so the sign did not replicate. With 19% of tasks flipping between two identical no-memory runs, the combined interval excludes harms larger than about 8 points and gains larger than about 6, and the design had 80% power only for effects of about +-12 points or more. The model almost never wrote notes (2 of 16 and 4 of 32 runs), and memory cost context: the first request is larger and something was injected at only 47% to 65% of compactions. The registered secondary, repeated actions per compaction, was also null. Two directional hypotheses found on Modal did not replicate on Kaggle. We also report an A/A calibration and a validity funnel (129 tasks, 105 valid). Together these results show that single-run memory claims on task sets of this size sit inside run-to-run noise. The treatment is a harness mechanism and does not test agent-written memory.
bullets: The study tested a fixed reminder mechanism that reinserts the agent’s last finding after context loss.
Across 98 tasks, 47 were solved with reminders versus 48 without; the estimated effect was compatible with ordinary run-to-run noise.
An initial 48-task result favored reminders, but a later 50-task extension reversed direction and did not replicate the finding.
The agent rarely wrote notes, and reminder injection occurred in only 47%–65% of compactions; repeated actions per compaction were also null.
The results do not evaluate agent-written memory and suggest that task sets of this size cannot reliably support single-run memory claims.

papers.abstract: LoCoMo is a widely reported benchmark for long-term conversational memory, but published scores mix memory quality with choices of answer prompt, judge and baseline layout that are rarely reported together. We measure how much these choices move a score, and evaluate Becos, a team memory system for coding agents, as a black box under all of them: ten conversations (1,540 questions), two answer models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini), two answer prompts and three LLM judges, against a whole-conversation baseline rerun under identical conditions. Changing only the judge moves a score by up to 7.2 points and changing only the answer prompt by up to 9.3. A blind human check of 150 answers finds the judges reliable when they agree, and the primary judge's errors on disputed answers working against Becos rather than for it. Becos answers from a context with 90% fewer characters than the whole conversation. Its configuration was developed on LoCoMo itself, so there is no held-out set. With gpt-4o-mini answers it scores clearly higher than the whole conversation (79.7 vs 73.0 with the short prompt, paired 95% interval for the difference +3.8 to +9.5; 88.8 vs 77.5 with a step-by-step prompt). With gpt-4.1-mini answers the two score about the same (83.2 vs 83.1; 92.5 vs 92.1). We release every answer and verdict and the scoring script.
bullets: Judge choice changes scores by up to 7.2 points, and answer-prompt choice by up to 9.3 points.
The study evaluates Becos across 10 conversations, 1,540 questions, two answer models, two prompts, and three LLM judges.
Becos outperforms the whole-conversation baseline with gpt-4o-mini, but performs about the same with gpt-4.1-mini.
A blind human check suggests judges are reliable when they agree; disputed- answer errors by the primary judge favored the baseline over Becos.
Becos was configured using LoCoMo itself, so the evaluation has no held-out set; answers, verdicts, and scoring code are released.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can improve long- horizon interactive decision-making through test-time evolu- tion, yet existing methods face three information bottlenecks: memory retrieval overemphasizes textual similarity, candi- date harnesses are often behaviorally redundant, and whole- harness rewriting may overwrite useful evidence or introduce cross-component inconsistency. We introduce Trident, which improves experience utilization, behavioral exploration, and harness evolution through boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion- based updating, respectively. We evaluate Trident on five benchmarks spanning text games, web interaction, and cod- ing tasks. Across qwen-32B, mistral-small-3.2-24B, and gpt- oss-20B, Trident achieves the best average performance and consistently outperforms non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and automated prompt optimization base- lines. Compared with the strongest baseline, APEX, Trident yields relative average gains of 30.7%, 30.8%, and 38.3% on the three backbones, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity stud- ies further show that the three designs provide complementary gains and remain robust to parameter variations.
authors: Kaijie Chen, Liang Yan, Yilan Wei, Jiachen Luo, Zhihao Dou, Jiashu Qu, Haoran Liu, Junli Wang
bullets: Addresses three bottlenecks: similarity-biased memory retrieval, redundant candidate harnesses, and risky whole-harness rewriting.
Uses boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion-based updates.
Evaluated across five text-game, web-interaction, and coding benchmarks with three LLM backbones.
Achieves the best average performance and outperforms several non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and prompt-optimization baselines.
Ablations show the components provide complementary gains and are robust to parameter variations.

papers.tldr: Trident robustly improves LLM agents’ test-time evolution by better retrieving experiences, routing diverse candidates, and incrementally updating harnesses.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_\alpha$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.
authors: Lihuan Li, Ruiyi Yang, Jiru Wang, Yifan Duan, Xiachong Lin, Hao Xue, Yang Song, Flora Salim
bullets: Addresses context growth and the trade-off between missing key details and retaining irrelevant history.
Uses a learned evidence selector and adaptive retention policy without extra LLM calls for context management.
Combines compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence.
Introduces Sα, which balances success and resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS).
Reaches 75.7% macro-averaged task success across three benchmarks and three LLM Actors, 6.7 points above the strongest baseline; it also leads on both metrics.

papers.abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.
authors: Yue Zhao, Angela Huyue Zhang, S. Alex Yang, Hua Wei, Xiyang Hu
bullets: The study applies presupposition theory to determine when agents should act, ask the user, or disclose reversible actions.
Listing multiple matching records prevents unsafe actions far more reliably than merely counting them.
User statements such as “the folder is empty” can stop actions when tool evidence contradicts them.
In a retail benchmark, returning a same-name, same-zip customer first caused wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations.
Safe writes require lookups that reveal competing records or verify distinguishing details, and evaluations should vary tool visibility.

papers.selection_reason: Studies the interaction between tool outputs and user input in LLM agents, focusing on grounding and safety, relevant to LLM agent tool use and reasoning.
papers.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
papers.tldr: LLM agents often act on ambiguous or contradicted assumptions unless tools expose competing records or verify user-stated claims.

papers.abstract: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements $\times$ personas $\times$ scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search's product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a $\tau^2$-bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect's traced footprint holds $b$ scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most $b/N$ to a suite of $N$. For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold $\theta = 0.10$, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator's own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property.
bullets: Suite generation is framed as diversity-driven search over requirements, personas, and scenario kinds, with the generated suite serving as an archive.
Coverage limits detectability: for most traceable defects, the affected scenarios cannot shift the suite score beyond the 0.10 detection threshold.
Suite-level pass rates can move in the wrong direction, including when a tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario.
Per-cell scoring recovers trace-aligned defects and can expose behavioural, trace-orthogonal defects such as forced escalation.
Generator diversity helps only when aligned with the defect: kind-diverse suites detected an orchestration defect, whereas happy-path-only suites detected none.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the generation of evaluation suites for agent regressions, providing a methodological framework for testing and diagnosing LLM agent behavior.
papers.title: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions
papers.tldr: Generated evaluation suites can miss real agent regressions when scored only by overall pass rate; per-cell scoring and explicit coverage reveal defects more reliably.

papers.abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
bullets: The study analyzes 516 multi-agent configurations using a six-dimensional resource vector and four-category baseline ladder.
Against single greedy passes, results are negative overall and near zero when the largest contributing study is excluded.
Against matched-sample or matched-budget baselines, multi-agent accuracy averages -0.042 and is no better in 74% of comparable contrasts.
Switching from a greedy to a sampled baseline reduces the apparent multi-agent advantage by 0.038 on average.
Positive coordination returns may require partitioned evidence, external verification, or model error diversity; the paper provides a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The Baseline Ladder: Single-agent baseline categories and inferential validity. Gray rungs represent comparisons that do not control test-time compute: Category A (Greedy single pass): A single model forward pass (N = 1) without sampling; observed gains are confounded with sample count and token budget. Category B (Sampled baseline): k samples drawn without communication; isolates gains beyond sample multiplicity, though token volume and dollar cost may still diverge. Teal rungs represent comparisons controlling a named compute resource: Category C (Budget-matched baseline): A declared dimension of the resource vector R (such as thinking tokens or iteration steps) is held equal between systems; isolates coordination gains at that matched budget. Category D (Pareto frontier): Sweeps compute budgets to trace the accuracy-versus-cost boundary, establishing whether multi-agent coordination outperforms scaled single-agent reasoning across diverse compute regimes.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a comprehensive empirical analysis of multi-agent LLMs, untangling the effects of coordination, sampling, and test-time compute, directly relevant to LLM agent research.
papers.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
papers.tldr: Across nine evaluations, multi-agent LLMs generally do not outperform single-model baselines when sample count or inference resources are matched, suggesting gains come from compute, evidence diversity, or verification rather than coordination alone.

papers.abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.
authors: Snehalkumar `Neil' S. Gaikwad, Dhruv Dixit, Bryen Alvarez, Pratik Patekar, Anika Sharma, Akshara Kolipaka, Paritosh Pandey
bullets: Addresses the lack of public participation in shaping rules that define AI-related decisions and harms.
Processes 3,653 government governance documents while preserving page and edition information.
Uses bounded agentic search to retrieve and verify evidence for each answer, with passages linked to source text.
Achieved 83.0% macro recall on 360 new questions, compared with 80.5% for the strongest baseline and 73.7% without iterative search.
A 24-person study found that participants often proposed clarifications about how provisions would apply; citations indicated grounding but rarely prompted source checking.

figures.caption: Figure 3: AI-Voyager’s architecture for human-AI civic reasoning. (a) Society in the loop: Users find governance documents, read them, ask questions, verify cited evidence, revise provisions, and share proposals for public discussion. They can combine these steps freely and view legislation through different analytical lenses. (b) Voyager-RAG: For each question, the system identifies which documents are in scope, retrieves and fuses relevant passages, and assembles the evidence used to generate an answer. An agentic controller decides whether more retrieval is needed. A verifier checks each generated statement against its cited evidence and can trigger targeted retrieval if statement lacks support. (c) Governance corpus: The ROAR pipeline processes five collections of governance documents, along with user-uploaded policies, into versioned passages that keep their source provenance and are embedded for retrieval. Summaries, mind maps, and key concepts serve as additional reading aids.

Figure 2: AI-Voyager’s Bill Library. (a) Users search AI governance legislation across jurisdictions and filter by collection, jurisdiction, topic, and keyword. Each bill card shows the bill’s identifier and legislative status. (b) Selecting a bill opens its details panel, shown here for North Carolina Senate Bill 963. The panel lists the bill’s title, status, session, and collection, followed by a summary covering its overview, technical terms, challenges, stakeholders, and sponsors. From the panel, users can open the bill in the Human AI Laboratory to read and analyze it with the AI Companion.

Figure 4: How Voyager-RAG grounds an answer in versioned policy text. Top: North Carolina Senate Bill 963 is traced from its policy record to the introduced version, page 2, a source block, and finally the passage containing the explicit user consent provision in proposed Section 114B-4(b)(3). Each passage records its document metadata, page and block references, character span, and source hash, so any citation can be traced to its exact location in the source. Bottom: Voyager-RAG answers a question about consent requirements. Scoped retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion finds relevant passages, which are combined with surrounding context into an evidence ledger. The controller checks that the evidence is sufficient before the model drafts claims with citation identifiers. The verifier checks each claim against its cited passages and requests targeted retrieval when support is missing. The final answer links the consent requirement to its source provision in the original document.

papers.abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.
bullets: Resolver errors can reverse hard-drop’s benefit, turning accuracy gains into losses.
False-dropping critical facts is more damaging than falsely keeping stale ones.
Non-deleting memory can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation.
A deployment-matched gate achieved 0.655 accuracy, below the 0.662 test-informed oracle and above the 0.641 always-drop baseline.
Deletion should be treated as a cost-sensitive decision and validated on matched data.

papers.abstract: Digital cultural heritage collections encode rich relations among objects, places, periods, providers, images, and source institutions, yet users typically access them through keyword search and faceted browsing. We present CULTUREBOT, an interactive framework for natural-language exploration of cultural heritage collections that combines knowledge-graph-guided retrieval, lexical-semantic retrieval, and source-linked generation. CULTUREBOT maps user queries to structured catalogue relations, enriches retrieved records with textual evidence, and generates answers that link back to the underlying repository records. We instantiate the framework on 81,852 SearchCulture records and release an online demonstration. In an expert evaluation involving six cultural-heritage specialists, 55 persona-grounded queries, and 250 evaluations, the graph-guided system was rated significantly higher than two general-purpose assistants and a non-graph ablation, with the largest gains in evidence grounding, diversity, reasoning, and completeness. These results support graph-guided retrieval as a practical way to expose the relational structure of cultural collections through conversational access while preserving links to catalogue evidence.
bullets: Addresses the limits of keyword search and faceted browsing for collections with rich object, place, period, provider, and institution relations.
Maps natural-language queries to catalogue relations, combines graph, lexical, and semantic retrieval, and enriches results with textual evidence.
Generates answers linked to underlying repository records to preserve evidence grounding.

Evaluated on 81,852 SearchCulture records using 55 expert-authored queries and 250 assessments; it outperformed two general-purpose assistants and a non-graph ablation across several quality dimensions.
An online demonstration is released; the evaluation focuses on cultural-heritage specialists and the SearchCulture collection.
