papers.abstract: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.
bullets: Evolves complete memory programs from minimal seeds using a standardized lifecycle and iterative diagnosis–proposal loop.
Evaluated on LoCoMo and LongMemEval, achieving up to 12% absolute accuracy gain at 35% of the serving cost of manually designed baselines.
Finds that retaining raw conversations preserves details lost in extracted memories, while query-intent-based evidence composition improves answer use.
The composition module transfers across five existing memory systems and improves accuracy in each.
Jointly optimizing accuracy and serving cost shifts computation toward selective query-time processing; scope is supported by evaluations across backbones and benchmarks.

papers.tldr: MAPE uses program evolution to automatically discover effective, efficient agent memory designs, improving accuracy over manual baselines while reducing serving cost.

papers.abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.
authors: Peiwen Li (Yale University), Harshit Verma (Yale University), Sophia Zhou (Yale University), Haiwen Wang (Yale University), Ngoc Bui (Yale University), Heng Chang (Tsinghua University), Fei Fei (Goodvision AI), David van Dijk (Yale University), Rex Ying (Yale University)
bullets: Targets memory selection when future tasks are unknown and repositories evolve.
Builds compact memory from repository-location and executable-check anchors using segment-level prospective valuation.
Adapts the actor with rollout-based memory valuation, provenance-gated credit, and rewards favoring resolution with fewer steps.
On ChainSWE, raises resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, while reducing steps by 17% and cache-aware tokens by 11% versus an untrained actor without memory.

Removing each of the seven segments of τk gives its value νc, and the segments that pay are kept as anchors A(m). (b) Cost-internalizing on-policy valuation. A group of G sessions mixes sessions with their own memory (m), no memory (∅) and a misplaced memory (m̃) under the reward Ri, and V̂b = R̄m − R̄∅ is the memory’s value on-policy. (c) Step-level provenance-gated value credit. Only the steps that the gate ωt marks as acting on an anchor from the memory receive the value credit.

The adapted instructions were written after observing the first runs on the set, whose memories were getting cut off because of note length.

papers.selection_reason: Cost-aware persistent memory for coding agents, fitting LLM agent memory and retrieval beyond context.
papers.title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
papers.tldr: CoReMem improves coding-agent performance on successive repository tasks by valuing memory prospectively and internalizing its writing, reading, and action costs.

papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order. We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow. Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers. This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.
authors: Anif N. Shikder, Ramit Dey, Jan Minac, Lyle E. Muller
bullets: Diagonal real- or complex-valued SSM transitions commute, so they cannot represent noncommutative group structure or reliably track input order.
The paper characterizes exactly when an SSM tracks a group: the group must be a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices.
Any SSM capable of tracking a group must decompose into real, complex, and quaternionic blocks; this motivates HyperSSM.

HyperSSM solves group-tracking benchmark tasks exactly using at most five state numbers, including an $S_5$ task where prior SSMs perform at chance, and extrapolates to sequences 25× longer than training.
The learned recurrence weights are directly interpretable and recover structure from gyroscope calibration, imperfect qubit-gate rotations, and protein-backbone geometry.

figures.caption: FIG. 4. Applications: Physical systems in which the state is represented as an ordered product of rotations. Median error as a function of sequence length; training lengths are shaded; mean ± standard deviation over three random seeds. (a) Orientation of a moving body measured by a real gyroscope (BROAD; held-out recordings); physical model: integration of the sensor readings. (b) Bloch vector of a qubit following a gate sequence, with imperfect gates (2% under-rotation and 2◦ axis tilt); physical model: simulation using ideal gates; HyperSSM achieves errors below the lower axis limit (10−3 degrees) at all sequence lengths; complex diagonal SSM uses three layers. Details on Clifford gates and ideal Clifford+T gates are provided in SM S11. (c) Orientation of residue j relative to the frame of residue i, computed from the torsion angles, on held-out PDB proteins; physical model: reconstruction using standard bond geometry. In all three cases, HyperSSM uses a single quaternion channel (four state variables); the complex diagonal SSM uses 128 state variables.

FIG. 1. Order in a linear memory. (a) One step of a selective SSM; shaded, the tracking regime (no decay, x0 = 1, one transition per symbol). (b) After a word w, a channel holds the ordered product Q(w); it tracks the group if a continuous readout recovers π(w) from Q(w) at every length. (c) A complex channel stores a phase; turns add, and order is lost. (d) A quaternion channel stores a 3D orientation; 90◦ turns about x and z in either order give different states. (e) q and −q are the same rotation; a sign-invariant readout tracks A5, a sign-aware one tracks Q8. (f) H tracks A5 but not S5; M2(H) tracks S5.

FIG. 3. A HyperSSM layer. Each channel follows the linear recurrence of a diagonal SSM, with input uk, hidden state x (j) k , transition a(j)(uk) and input term B̄(j)(uk)uk, with multiplication in its own algebra A(j). Channels evolve independently, mix only in the readout C, and are computed by the same parallel scan.

TABLE I. Regular languages. Accuracy (%) on lengths 40–256 after training on 3–40, mean ± s.d. over 5 runs. Baselines from [19]. HyperSSM algebras, with numbers of state: R± (1), C (2), M16(C) (32). Discovered n: the smallest n for which snapping each complex transition to an n-th root of unity is exact on validation, found after training without being told the task. Details in SM S9.

TABLE II. Group word problems. Accuracy (%) on lengths 40–256 and, for HyperSSM, 256–1000, after training on 3–40; best of 3 runs. Chance: 1.67% (A5), 0.83% (S5); –: not reported. Baselines from [19] (PD-SSM: 128 complex numbers of state). HyperSSM: H (4), R±→H (5). All runs in SM S9.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a quaternion state-space model with representation-theoretic analysis of recurrent memory, directly relevant to LLM architectures and recurrent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory
papers.tldr: A representation-theoretic analysis shows why diagonal SSMs lose sequence order, and HyperSSM fixes this with quaternion-valued state channels while preserving efficient inference and training.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon language agents accumulate tool results and replies until the history no longer fits the context window. Current agents shrink this history by having a model summarize it, so each compaction rereads and rewrites the history it replaces, and cache-aware triggers decide when to compact while taking the size of the result as given. We present Folio, a context manager that records, folds, and recovers history through one set of handles. While the agent runs, Folio records three linked levels: a short turn note the model writes as part of its ordinary reply (L1), an event manifest of every call written by the runtime (L2), and the captured source records (L3). Because these views already exist, the runtime folds the context programmatically, selecting coarser views for older turns. The fold prints the handles that index L2 and L3, so recovery tools that read bounded pages, compute over full text in files, and keep findings in a persistent dossier reach the evidence the agent needs with little added input. The fold trigger prices an explicit landing point that includes the retained budget. On 75 LOCA-bench tasks with DeepSeek-V4-Pro behind every system, Folio solves 66 tasks against 54 for the same runtime with model-written compaction and 49-59 for Claude Code, Codex, and SoL-Pi, in about half their working time, at 2.4 times lower cost than that runtime; each fold takes a median of 0.6 seconds.
authors: Yubo Ruan, Tao Peng, Jiao Zhang, Chuanguo Ma, Lei Xu, Han Zhou, Wenwu Wang, Xiafei Lv, Xingjie Zhou, Guiju Fan, Hao Wang, Fenghui Zhang, Mao Miao, Shuo Li
bullets: Addresses context-window overflow from accumulating tool results and replies in long-running agents.
Records linked history views: model-written turn notes (L1), runtime event manifests (L2), and source records (L3).
Programmatically folds older turns into coarser views while preserving handles for bounded, evidence-focused recovery.
Uses a fold trigger that accounts for an explicit retained-context budget and landing point.
On 75 LOCA-bench tasks, solved 66 versus 54 for model-written compaction, with roughly half the working time and 2.4× lower cost; folds took a median of 0.6 seconds.

papers.selection_reason: Context folding and recovery for long-horizon language agents directly targets LLM memory and long-context management.
papers.title: Folio: Recoverable Multi-Resolution Context Folding for Long-Horizon Language Agents
papers.tldr: Folio manages long-horizon agent context by programmatically folding multi-resolution history and enabling targeted recovery, improving task completion while reducing time and cost in the reported evaluation.

papers.abstract: We argue that a binding constraint for personal agents is not model capacity but the form in which context is represented: the agent does not know which entity a phrase denotes, when a fact held, or which source record licenses a claim. We call the missing representation spatio-temporal context (STC) and define it on two axes. The temporal axis carries event time, validity intervals and ingestion time. The spatial axis is a relational space in which entities are points, typed relations are edges, and distance is semantic rather than geographic; physical places are one entity type among many. Every relation is anchored to immutable source records, and every answer must be closed over those records. We formalise the substrate and six invariants, a context operator that composes temporal intersection with relational expansion, an ambiguity-preserving resolution state machine, a conflict detector that converts mutually exclusive facts into user adjudication rather than silent overwrite, and a four-regime consumption taxonomy spanning query, insight, triage and proactive reminder. We describe a local-first prototype of the retrieval layer built on SQLite with on-device embeddings and hybrid lexical-dense recall, report measurements from a deployed store of 341 documents, 340,079 chunks and 190,271 embedded vectors, and specify, but do not yet implement, the analytic layer on which the framework depends. We close with an evaluation protocol with per-invariant metrics for evidence coverage, temporal correctness, conflict precision and interruption cost. The proposal targets the representation of context rather than the volume of it.
authors: Haitao Cheng, Jerry Hu, Longdong Mao, Dong Huang, Dongming Li, Lijuan Zhang, Mengting Zhang
bullets: Motivates STC as a solution to unresolved entity references, temporal validity, and unsupported claims—not insufficient model capacity.
Represents context across temporal dimensions and a semantic relational space, with every relation anchored to immutable source records.
Defines six invariants, temporal-relational context composition, ambiguity-preserving resolution, and conflict handling through user adjudication.
Introduces four consumption modes: query, insight, triage, and proactive reminder.

Describes a local-first SQLite retrieval prototype and an evaluation protocol covering evidence coverage, temporal correctness, conflict precision, and interruption cost; the analytic layer remains unimplemented.

Candidates for the next word are enlarged and coloured by rank with preset probabilities (65%, 25%, 10%); the arrow points to their probability-weighted centre, which lands near, but not on, the top candidate. (a) "I": like 65%, want 25%, need 10%. (b) "I like": eat 65%, drink 25%, watch 10%. (c) "I like eating": apple 65%, banana 25%, pear 10%. (d) "I like eating apples": and 65%, also 25%, because 10%. Figure 1: The substrate. Source artefacts become immutable records that keep event time and ingestion time apart. Entities and relations form the relational space, with validity intervals on the temporal axis. The context operator composes neighbourhood expansion with interval intersection, and four consumption regimes apply different policies to the same representation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an evidence-grounded spatio-temporal context substrate with retrieval and conflict resolution for personal agents, directly relevant to agent and LLM memory.
papers.title: Time and Space: A Dual-Axis, Evidence-Grounded Context Substrate for Personal Agents
papers.tldr: The paper proposes spatio-temporal context (STC), an evidence-grounded representation for personal agents that links entities, time, relations, and source records to support reliable answers and actions.

papers.abstract: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment information to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering (\ace{}) harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. Our method, \acerl{}, evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks, \acerl{} achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit.
authors: Doyoung Kim, Byeongguk Jeon, Kailin Zhang, Sherry Yang
bullets: Scalar-reward RL overlooks useful trial information such as error logs.
The work learns experience handoff within a fixed Agentic Context Engineering harness.
ACERL evaluates artifacts by their downstream impact on future actor rollouts.
One model jointly learns to act, reflect on insights, and curate task-specific playbooks.
Experiments report higher held-out performance than baseline methods across agentic benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Experience-Handoff RL. (a) Outcome-only RL compresses each trial into a scalar reward. (b) A harness runs several calls to the same model (cis; in ACE, actor, reflector, and curator) and preserves experience as a model-written context, such as a playbook, handed to the next attempt (blue), but the model never learns to write better playbooks. (c) Experience-handoff RL trains the model for the harness it runs in, from task outcomes alone. For example, ACE-RL rewards each handoff artifact for what it does to a future rollout: (i) each new context is scored by a fresh rollout, and (ii) each role is compared within its own group (stacked boxes), which lowers the variance of its credit.

papers.selection_reason: Learns and optimizes experience-handoff artifacts/playbooks that persist across LLM agent rollouts, directly relevant to agent memory.
papers.title: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: ACERL trains agents to improve both their current actions and the experience artifacts handed to future rollouts, yielding higher held-out performance across agentic benchmarks.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.
authors: Sikui Zhang, Haowei Liu, Ziyun Gan, Chunfeng Yuan, Guangze Gao, Nian Liu, Boyu Cai, Bo Li, Xiaolei Lv, Jun Gao, Bing Li, Weiming Hu
bullets: Addresses context compression when relevant evidence may be local, scattered, or distributed across a document.
Uses query-guided memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query.
Applies contrastive compressor learning with same-document, multi-query hard negatives to distinguish differing evidence needs.
Enables bidirectional attention among memory slots to improve information flow despite causal masking.
Outperforms existing compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of CoMem. The QA objective LQA provides an end-task generation signal, while the contrastive learning objective Lcl imposes a more explicit representation-level signal, aligning memory slots with their source context while using same-context, different-query examples as hard negatives to encourage query-guided memory representations.

papers.abstract: Language models rely on finite token contexts, limiting access to earlier interactions. We introduce Recursive State-Augmented Language Models (Recursive SALM), a framework in which a persistent latent state evolves with each observation and generates adaptations of a pretrained language model. A modular read-transition-write architecture separates observation encoding, latent dynamics, and predictor adaptation. We develop deterministic and stochastic formulations. The experiments evaluate only deterministic SALM with frozen GPT-2 small and exclude earlier evidence from its decoder context. On a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, latent-gated LoRA reaches 89.1% accuracy, comparable to 88.0% for a trained full-context LoRA baseline, with earlier evidence available solely through a 64-dimensional state. Zeroing or shuffling the state substantially reduces accuracy. In a two-turn task with codewords unseen in training, several interfaces improve candidate ranking over chance, but rarely generate the exact codeword under the evaluated training schedule. These experiments show that persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when earlier evidence is absent from the decoder context.
bullets: Addresses the limited memory of finite-token contexts by maintaining a state that evolves with each observation.
Uses a modular read–transition–write architecture to encode observations, update latent dynamics, and adapt the predictor.
In deterministic experiments with frozen GPT-2 small, latent-gated LoRA achieved 89.1% accuracy on a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, close to the 88.0% full-context baseline.
Removing or shuffling the 64-dimensional state substantially reduced accuracy, supporting its role in retaining earlier evidence.
On unseen-codeword tasks, interfaces improved candidate ranking over chance but rarely generated the exact codeword under the tested training schedule.

papers.abstract: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.
authors: Zhicheng Jia, Shuchen Wu, Zhuoshi Tong, Haisen Liao, Sicheng Zhou
bullets: Targets the limits of similarity-based memory, which often retrieves topical facts but misses relationship-critical experiences.
Asynchronously consolidates interactions into source-linked mental states for the character, user, and their relationship.
Uses a mental-state reasoner to anticipate user needs, form proactive intentions, and retrieve relevant episodic evidence.
Introduces MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark evaluating factual recall and situated use of shared history in dyadic and group conversations.
Achieves 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, outperforming the strongest baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Enterprise agents accumulate memory across dozens of sessions in which facts contradict, get superseded, and blur as similarly named entities collide in embedding space. The field treats this as a retrieval problem; we show it is not. On ENT-310, a synthetic enterprise sales-agent memory benchmark of 310 queries (210 answerable, 100 unanswerable), a vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) reader over a memory store already matches strong memory systems on the recall pillars. Retention and currency are near-saturated, roughly 0.93 to 0.98 for every competent system, so recall is essentially solved. What remains unsolved is resolution: which entity a query refers to, which time-state is current, and whether to commit an answer at all or decline when evidence is insufficient. We propose DISCERN (DISambiguation and Cross-session Episodic memoRy Navigation), an agent-memory framework built on a single rule: preserve at write, resolve at read. At write time DISCERN builds a strictly additive bi-temporal provenance graph that never merges confusable entities and never drops superseded values. At read time a zero-LLM tool surface drives an agentic loop that navigates this graph and commits exactly one of four gated terminal actions. A four-judge LLM-as-a-Judge council scores two axes: answer correctness on answerable questions, and the answer-versus-abstain decision as a classification problem. On ENT-310, DISCERN is the best-calibrated system on abstention (F1 0.924 versus at most 0.802 across eight baselines) and leads macro answer correctness under equal pillar weighting (0.861 versus 0.806 for the strongest baseline), a lead driven by entity resolution (0.800, where no baseline exceeds 0.40). Applied with zero tuning to the full LoCoMo corpus, the same pipeline again leads macro answer correctness (0.663 versus 0.638) and stays among the best-calibrated on false-premise abstention.
authors: Chirag Ahuja, Vladislav Tanov, Ramcharan Kakarla, Jonathan Taws
bullets: Frames persistent memory as a resolution problem—not primarily retrieval—because retention and currency are already near-saturated.
Builds an additive bi-temporal provenance graph that keeps confusable entities separate and preserves superseded values.
Uses a zero-LLM tool surface and agentic read loop with four gated terminal actions, including abstention when evidence is insufficient.
On ENT-310, achieves abstention F1 of 0.924 and macro answer correctness of 0.861, driven by substantially better entity resolution than baselines.
Also leads macro answer correctness on LoCoMo without tuning, while remaining well calibrated for false-premise abstention.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The DISCERN memory graph. (a) Changed values are kept as bi-temporal edges so both history and current state remain recoverable. (b) Confusable entities are kept co-equal and merely linked, never merged. (c) Episodic turns are preserved and linked to entity nodes.

Figure 3: DISCERN read-time routing. The agent orients (Phase 1, read_profile_summary), runs a mandatory ambiguity check for underspecified queries (Phase 2, find_similar_entities), gathers targeted or raw evidence (Phases 3–4), and commits one of four terminal actions. The EarnedAbstainGate abstains only on demonstrated absence, a DeclineRouter sends a surviving decline to CLARIFY when confusable candidates remain and to ABSTAIN when none do, and a citation-or-abstain renderer requires every committed answer to cite its evidence. This procedure realizes the predicates of Eq. 1.

Right (read time resolves): an adaptive policy navigates the views with a small read-only tool surface and commits one of four governed actions (answer, update, clarify, abstain) under the EarnedAnswerGate and EarnedAbstainGate, the DeclineRouter, and the near-miss guard.

papers.abstract: As memory-augmented agents increasingly support long-term and personalized interactions, reliable recall of emotional experiences while preserving their associated affect becomes necessary. However, existing evaluations usually assess emotion accuracy and factual memory grounding separately, overlooking event-affect correspondence. In this work, we formulate Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as a task that explicitly evaluates the recovery of past events, associated affects, and their correspondence, and define Event-Affect Decoupling as a failure mode where the correct emotion is recalled but associated with the wrong episode. To diagnose Event-Affect Decoupling, we propose EM-TRACE, a stage-wise framework that decomposes AER into retrieval, affect recovery, and realization. On a controlled GoEmotions-based benchmark, Emotion-only retrieval achieves 28.65% affect recovery but retrieves the target episode for only 4.44% of queries, yielding a UAR of 24.21%. Further analysis reveals that event retrieval and affect assignment introduce distinct binding failures. These findings show that reliable AER requires grounded recall of emotional experiences, where episode retrieval, affect recovery, event-affect binding, and generation quality should be evaluated jointly. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/A412/.
authors: Tingna Xie, Ming Wang, Shi Feng, Yongkang Liu
bullets: Defines Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as jointly recovering past events, their affects, and event–affect correspondence.

Proposes EM-TRACE, a stage-wise diagnostic covering retrieval, affect recovery, and realization.
On a controlled GoEmotions-based benchmark, emotion-only retrieval achieved 28.65% affect recovery but only 4.44% target-episode retrieval, with a 24.21% UAR.
Finds distinct binding failures in event retrieval and affect assignment, motivating joint evaluation of grounded emotional recall.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents can share conversational history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, a Conversation ESAA extension inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR), and an exploratory synthetic evaluation comparing chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR, and variants under three output budgets. With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, versus 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling; with 4,096 tokens it recalled all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations, as expected when the active decision set and the adapter ordering are the same. The isolated contribution of ringing to decisions was not measured: comparator D1 cuts facts before the graph is built, and the product retains active decisions by rule. Before the output limit, full-RRR conflict F1 was 0.615 at all three scales; after it, at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, it was 0.000. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raised that F1 to 0.431 in that scenario, at the cost of lowering decision recall from 0.44 to 0.34, and to 0.930 at 4,096 tokens without decision loss. Fixtures are repetitive, comparators are simplified, and the evaluation was not independently replicated; the results support an engineering analysis, not a claim of selectionist superiority.
bullets: Persistent conversation history does not ensure retrieval of current decisions and their provenance.
The study compares chronological retrieval, recency- and authority-aware baselines, full RRR, and variants across three output budgets using synthetic conversations.

Simplified baselines and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall, so the isolated contribution of ringing was not established.
Conflict F1 fell to 0.000 after the output limit in the 480-fact, 1,024-token setting; reserving 20% of the budget improved it to 0.431 but reduced decision recall to 0.34.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action. We introduce MemCredit, a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility. MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.
authors: Quanjiang Guo, Sijie Wang, Qianyang Zhu, Ben Zhang, Jinchuan Zhang, Ke Yan, Zhao Kang
bullets: Targets the mismatch between semantically relevant memories and memories that actually improve actions.
Uses controlled counterfactual interventions to estimate each memory’s state-, context-, and policy-conditional utility.
Distills intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator; relevance only generates high-recall candidates.
Retains memories by predicted utility without changing the agent policy or requiring extra environment interaction.
On ALFWorld, reaches 86.57 SR@50 with a 500-token memory budget versus 65.67% for BM25; utility is sparse and state dependent.

papers.abstract: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.

papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Anurag Koul, Hongjun Liu, Bo Pang, Shafiq Joty, Erik Nijkamp
bullets: The study tests whether identical information helps differently depending on how it is represented in history and whether the world reflects it.
With the world fixed after a wrong value, a truthful note improved recovery from 51% to 66%, while presenting the correction as a completed action reduced it from 50% to 44%.
In AppWorld, success receipts helped when their effects were present (38% to 49%) but hurt when effects were absent (45% to 28%).
History edits and world state interacted across receivers, showing that the value alone does not determine recovery.
Scope: results concern mid-task, tool-using agents and history/world edits evaluated on AgentCE-Bench and AppWorld.

papers.abstract: Recurrent sequence models must decide how strongly to overwrite their memory at each token. Read as Bayesian filtering, this write is the gain of a Kalman update, set by uncertainty from two sources that pull it in opposite directions: volatility, how quickly the underlying associations change, and stochasticity, how noisy each observation of them is. First, we show that the update of gated delta-rule memories is the form this filter takes under isotropic uncertainty. Next, we introduce Voltic, a recurrent memory that keeps the covariance anisotropic and makes both noise variances input-dependent, so the write is vector-valued and carries uncertainty accumulated over the sequence. A dense covariance would have to be propagated token by token, ruling out the parallel training these models depend on. We therefore give two assumed-density approximations, diagonal and quasi-diagonal, both of which leave the memory update in delta-rule form and reuse its chunked kernels. On controlled recall tasks in which associations change and observations are corrupted, Voltic leads all baselines. On the task combining volatility and stochasticity, its margin over the strongest baseline is larger at both extrapolation sizes than at the training sizes. In 45M-parameter language models it leads an eight-task reasoning average and achieves higher retrieval accuracy beyond the training context length than gated baselines, at throughput close to those baselines. Deriving the write from an uncertainty recursion therefore makes memory more responsive to change.
bullets: Recasts gated memory writes as Kalman-style updates driven by uncertainty.
Introduces input-dependent volatility and stochasticity with anisotropic covariance, producing vector-valued writes.
Uses diagonal and quasi-diagonal approximations to preserve parallel, chunked training.
Leads baselines on controlled recall, combined volatility–stochasticity, reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks.
Scope: approximations trade full covariance modeling for computational efficiency.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $\tau$-Retail/$\tau$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.
authors: Runxuan Tang, Haoyu Gao, Yuyan Ding, Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, Zecheng Sheng, Liwei Hou
bullets: Addresses the risk that local episode success leads agents to store unsafe or non-transferable lessons.
Represents each candidate update with a precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier.
Tests updates temporarily using transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, then commits, refines, or rejects them based on gain and risk.
Reports strong performance across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks.
Reduces falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%.

The right-side annotation reports the sign-consistency score C(h). Figure 10: Memory-growth Pareto analysis. We vary the retention budget and evaluate longhorizon self-evolving agents under different memory policies. Left: task success rate versus committed memory size. Right: violation rate versus committed memory size. The x-axis is update gain ∆upd, and the y-axis is either harmful update rate H (left) or regression damage R (right). Point size indicates verifier cost C (average verifier calls per candidate update), and color denotes the update-selection strategy. The black dashed line shows the empirical Pareto frontier, where larger gain and smaller harm are jointly preferred. The left panel shows bad-update detection rate D(K), and the right panel shows harmful update avoided A(K). papers.abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace
authors: Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: External memory can hurt performance when lessons are incorrect, misapplied, or misread.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon personalized agents maintain an evolving memory by continuously deciding what to add, modify, or discard. However, learning an optimal update policy remains challenging. Conventional training relies solely on terminal question-answering accuracy, yielding a coarse feedback signal that treats all intermediate updates identically. Furthermore, update utility is inherently user-specific, as identical memory actions may yield opposite effects across different user personas. Existing methods fail to address this heterogeneity, relying on globally shared evaluation standards with at most a single scalar intermediate reward. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{Personalized Memory Rubrics} (\textbf{PMR}), a framework that translates terminal feedback into fine-grained, per-step, and per-user credit assignment. PMR decomposes evaluation into a universal layer capturing cross-persona failure patterns and a per-user adaptive layer modeling individual traits as a specialized delta over the universal baseline. Through \textbf{Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment}, PMR redistributes credit at the token level, selectively amplifying validated decisions on successful trajectories while falling back to standard policy optimization on failed ones to avoid unreliable attribution. The rubric and memory policy \textbf{co-evolve} in a closed loop with anti-circularity guarantees. Crucially, PMR incurs zero inference overhead, operating without any rubric or external judge during deployment. Extensive experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines.
authors: Yupeng Han, Kai Zhang, Shuochen Liu, Ze Liu, Xianquan Wang, Zhihong Pan, Xiangyu Zhao, Qi Liu, Enhong Chen
bullets: Addresses coarse terminal-only feedback and the fact that memory actions can help one user but harm another.
Uses a universal rubric for cross-user failure patterns plus an adaptive per-user layer capturing individual traits.
Redistributes credit at the token level, reinforcing validated decisions on successful trajectories and using standard policy optimization on failed ones.
Co-evolves the rubric and memory policy with anti-circularity safeguards.
Shows consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines across four benchmarks, with zero inference overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PMR. PMR first induces a personalized rubric 𝑅𝑢 from shared cross-user patterns and residual per-user failures, and then uses it to shape direction-safe, per-step credit while preserving the trajectory-level update direction. A co-evolution loop iteratively updates the student, rubric, and credit assignment, with standard GRPO used as a fallback for failures. At inference, only the student model is required.

Figure 1: Long-horizon memory learning involves multiple updates but only a terminal QA reward, making fine-grained credit assignment difficult. Hand-crafted methods use fixed, non-personalized rules, while RL-based methods rely on sparse scalar feedback with ambiguous step/token attribution. PMR decouples direction from magnitude: the QA advantage determines the learning direction, while personalized rubric evidence modulates credit magnitude through direction-safe gating.

PMR selectively adapts rubric dimensions to user behavior: Malia emphasizes timeliness and conciseness, Maria largely retains universal criteria, and Alex strengthens completeness and conciseness. papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.
authors: Lirui Luo, Kelong Mao, Xinwei Yang, Rongqing Li, Luyu Chen, Kieran Wong, Yudong Guo, Xinrui Wang, Jiayin Zhu, Gu Simiu, Sulong Xu, Cong Fang
bullets: Long-horizon agents need to decide what information to save, retrieve, and when, as histories exceed active context.
CAMG-II evaluates memory behavior across Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual environments using Bash and persistent workspaces.
CAMP-II jointly trains one policy across all five environments with a frozen teacher that already understands file operations.
The learned file-based memory behavior transfers to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2 with improved success rates.

papers.abstract: Practical Web applications increasingly require agents to interpret long conversations or documents. For inputs exceeding the context windows of large language models (LLMs), memory agents process segments sequentially and retain past information in bounded memory. However, they typically divide inputs into flat token segments without preserving structure or hierarchy, causing three limitations for structured data such as API responses or HTML documents. First, fixed-length segmentation can split fields of the same record, breaking their relationships. Second, segments lack hierarchical information, obscuring their structural context and positions. Third, successive memory updates may discard details of earlier sibling records needed for reasoning on later segments. To address these limitations, we propose TreeAgent, a structure-aware agent that uses the input hierarchy to guide both segment-wise context processing and access to past information. Specifically, TreeAgent constructs segments from complete subtrees and groups of adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structural relationships. We provide theoretical guarantees on segment counts to guide token budget selection toward matching the segment count of fixed-length segmentation. We further attach structural paths to the segments for the agent to identify their ancestors and hierarchical positions. We also introduce residual memory links from the segments of low-level children to the segments of high-level parents, enabling direct information flows beyond successive memory updates. We evaluate TreeAgent with four representative memory agents on eight retrieval and aggregation tasks. The inputs are derived from real-world application data in JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript and range from 8K to 1M tokens. TreeAgent improves the average score across the four datasets for all four agents, with 3.61% performance gain on average.
authors: Wei Gu, Weiwei Qi, Jiajun Tang, Tianhang Zheng, Bo Chen, Zhibo Zhang, Jinfei Liu, Kui Ren
bullets: Targets flat, fixed-length segmentation that breaks relationships, loses hierarchy, and forgets earlier sibling details.
Builds segments from complete subtrees or adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structure.
Attaches structural paths to expose each segment’s ancestors and position.
Adds residual links from low-level child segments to high-level parent segments for direct information flow.
Evaluated on retrieval and aggregation tasks over JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript inputs spanning 8K–1M tokens; improved all four tested memory agents on average.

The memory-agent block represents the agent’s original workflow, including its internal actions and stopping behavior. After processing each section, TreeAgent saves the updated memory. Parent–child relations determine which saved states are linked and accessed by later updates.

papers.tldr: TreeAgent improves long hierarchical-data processing by preserving structure during segmentation and memory access, yielding an average 3.61% gain across evaluated memory agents.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems. In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed. In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).
bullets: Focuses on attacks that manipulate agents’ semantic memory and alter their behavior.
Uses signed knowledge-base entries to prevent unauthorized or malicious knowledge manipulation.
Combines a local Prolog-like Horn-clause inference system with private access to an external knowledge base.
Describes Python implementations offering privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy via IT-PIR.
Scope is semantic memory; episodic and short-term memory attacks are not addressed.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. We present Synapse-Control, an agent runtime whose lightweight control plane selects advice and determines when to send it to the task-executing model. Rules shortlist relevant advice, and a lightweight 1.7B classifier fine-tuned on teacher-labeled state-suggestion pairs scores those candidates instead of generating a diagnosis. Micro-contracts encode reusable interface checks, such as required arguments or valid options, without prescribing complete task programs. A Prompt Value Table records earlier guidance and feedback to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget checks. Across 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively.
authors: Zhiyuan Huang, Shengan Zheng, Chenghu Yang, Song Zhang, Lingyun Li, Chen Yu, Weiquan Huang, Linpeng Huang

Uses rules to shortlist advice and a fine-tuned 1.7B classifier to score candidate suggestions.

In AppWorld and WebShop, it achieved 270 successes—29.8% more than Base—and replaced 4,987 diagnosis calls.
Reduced auxiliary control time versus Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0% across the two environments.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.
authors: Mingchen Li, Yongkang Xiao, Rumeng Li, Rui Zhang, Hong Yu
bullets: Evaluates five memory approaches across four LLMs in biomedical reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversation settings.
Analyzes task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness.
Finds that memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history strongly affect downstream performance.
HMRU improves results by an average of 8.6%, reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9%, and closes 48.0% of the gap to full-context inference.
The study highlights persistent challenges in retrieving relevant information, preserving fidelity, and using memory effectively for biomedical reasoning.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.
bullets: Motivation: Query relevance alone may be insufficient for long-lived AI systems that must recover causally and temporally linked memories.
Method: Request and goal cues seed a memory graph; activation and fan attenuation bound traversal, while retrieved entities recursively emit cues.
Output: A typed evidence graph is reconstructed before language-model generation.
Analysis: The work specifies architectural consequences, cost estimates, ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol.
Scope: This is a preprint with no benchmark measurements; the claim is testable against a simpler graph reranker under equal budgets.

Authorization is evaluated before content-bearing activation or expansion; only qualified downstream outcomes update future availability.

papers.selection_reason: Activation-conditioned memory graph retrieval for long-lived language-model systems, fitting persistent LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems
papers.tldr: An architecture proposes reconstructing memories by activation-guided traversal of an authorized graph, returning evidence paths rather than only relevance-ranked context.

papers.abstract: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. A memory manager decides how each input changes this memory and which records the agent acts on. It can fail in two ways: keeping a fact that has since changed (outdated memory), or storing a planted passage or injected instruction (memory poisoning). Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.
bullets: LLM memory managers must handle two conflicting failures: retaining changed facts and storing injected or malicious content.
The paper introduces evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which evaluates both answer correctness and whether selected memory contains complete, updated, attack-free evidence.
Existing memory systems and defenses are no more robust than an untuned manager on the authors’ test sets.
Fine-tuning on synthesized episodes built from a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks improves every tested category across three backbones.
The method more than doubles overall ECA versus the untuned manager, but robustness remains incomplete.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to maintain personalized and temporally coherent interactions, but repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization introduces substantial cost and latency. We present SLICE-Mem, a lightweight memory framework that combines salience-guided admission and predicate-centered information extraction. A compact classifier identifies user turns worth retaining, and a semantic-dependency-based extractor converts admitted turns into concise memory entries. This online pipeline requires no generative LLM calls, while cross-entry reconciliation is deferred to an offline consolidation stage. We evaluate SLICE-Mem on the weekly subset of Memora and LongMemEval-S using 8B and 30B Qwen backbones for memory construction and consolidation on both benchmarks. Compared with the generative-memory baseline MemOS under the Qwen3-30B configuration, SLICE-Mem's online pipeline achieves 46.60 versus 46.68 FAMA (Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy) on Memora Weekly and 56.8% versus 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S, while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that SLICE-Mem can preserve useful evidence for long-term memory with substantially less reliance on LLM-based memory construction.
bullets: Targets the cost and latency of repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization.
Uses a compact salience classifier to select user turns and a semantic-dependency extractor to create concise memory entries.
Runs online memory construction without generative LLM calls, deferring cross-entry reconciliation to offline consolidation.
On Memora Weekly and LongMemEval-S, it achieved near-baseline quality while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively.
Quality was slightly below MemOS under Qwen3-30B: 46.60 vs. 46.68 FAMA on Memora Weekly and 56.8% vs. 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems can separate contextual computation, persistent storage, and exact execution instead of updating all capabilities through one shared parameter system. We investigate FEM-ASM, a finite-element-method-inspired organization in which independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills contribute typed proposals to a shared language-model state. An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes. We evaluate this organization through controlled experiments and negative results rather than claiming a physical finite-element formulation of language. An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype learns causal language modeling but does not establish competitive general capability. A versioned store contains 52,809 reconstructive memory elements near a 1.7-billion-floating-value budget; reconstruction is incomplete, with approximately 75\% token accuracy. Support-aware lexical indices make these elements addressable under provenance-controlled query construction. For executable arithmetic, positional result observations substantially improve neural rendering relative to a repeated global result vector, and output substitutions change the model's preferred answer. A bounded attachment demonstration further measures the effect of making selected evidence available, without establishing the utility of loading an entire multi-billion-value store. The results support a separation of storage, execution, and neural coordination, while identifying unresolved limitations in question-only retrieval, unrestricted answer generation, and end-to-end efficiency.
bullets: Uses independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills that submit typed proposals to a shared model state.
An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes.
An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype supports causal language modeling, but does not demonstrate competitive general performance.
Reconstructive memory contains 52,809 elements with about 75% token accuracy; support-aware lexical indices enable provenance-controlled addressing.
Positional arithmetic-result observations improve neural rendering, while unresolved issues include incomplete retrieval, unrestricted generation, and end-to-end efficiency.

papers.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.
authors: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Separates task-solving from applying a previously derived solution to new instances.
Constructs agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces for CPU execution.
Matches frontier LLM performance across difficult mathematical and scientific tasks.
ARCs are explainable, continually trainable, and robust to input perturbations.
Reported invocation cost is 16–291× lower than the source model.

papers.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
papers.tldr: CPU-ARC reuses LLM-derived reasoning through explainable, CPU-executable caches, achieving frontier-level performance at 16–291× lower invocation cost.

papers.abstract: A conversational agent that remembers has to decide what to keep. Retrieval-augmented generation keeps the transcript and searches it; the alternative is to compact each turn into atomic facts and search those. We compare the two on LoCoMo, with both arms answering all 1,985 questions in one window, against the same stores, with the same generator and judge, and both predictions on one row, which licenses McNemar's exact test on the 512 questions where they disagree. On the four categories comparable work reports, compaction scores 71.4 per cent against 64.6, a lead of 6.8 points (p = 5.5e-08) at 34 per cent fewer prompt tokens. On all five, including the adversarial set comparable work drops, the lead falls to 2.0 and stops being significant, because the baseline leads adversarial by 14.6. That loss has a structure. Our lead falls as the reference answer demands more source wording, 9.6 points ahead at one or two reference words and 3.1 behind past eight, with token overlap moving the same way, so the judge is not the cause. Compaction keeps what a fact asserts and discards how it was said, so it wins where the answer is a value and loses where it is a phrasing. We also report four negative results with their power calculations.
authors: Osamudiamen Edogun, Joshua Obigwe, Irfan Mehmood
bullets: On four comparable LoCoMo categories, compaction scored 71.4% versus 64.6% for retrieval-augmented generation, using 34% fewer prompt tokens.
Across all five categories, the advantage fell to 2.0 points and was not significant because retrieval performed better on the adversarial set.
Compaction’s lead declined as answers required more source wording: from 9.6 points for one or two reference words to 3.1 points behind beyond eight.
The paired evaluation used identical stores, generator, and judge, with McNemar’s exact test on 512 disagreements.
The approach preserves asserted facts but loses the original phrasing, limiting performance on wording-sensitive questions.

papers.abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.
authors: David H. Yang, Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Giorgio Severi
bullets: Targets memory poisoning in long-horizon, multi-session LLM agents.
Provides 155 trajectories across four domains and supports five memory systems.
Traces poisoned information from storage through retrieval to downstream agent behavior.

papers.abstract: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.
authors: Tong Guan, Alexander Chemeris, Yiqing Guo, Warren Jin, Zhao Li, Shirui Pan, Ming Jin
bullets: Introduces Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), replacing offline one-shot processing with persistent stateful reasoning over open-ended streams.
Presents LiveTS-Suite: 18 tasks across six capabilities, covering over 5K streams, 2.2B timesteps, and 15K response events.
Combines hybrid temporal encoding, persistent memory for historical evidence and task states, and elastic inference synchronization to reduce lag.
Reports a score of 90.0 versus 79.3 for Opus 5, with 206× lower p95 latency than its backbone using a 4B-parameter model.
Demonstrates real-time continuous understanding on a Jetson edge device.
