papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.
authors: Zhuoyun Li, Boxuan Wang, Jinwei Hu, Xiaowei Huang, Yi Dong
bullets: Frames belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments guiding agent actions.
Proposes EB-MAS, which externalizes belief states and uses belief operators to suggest updates.
Introduces a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject weakly evidenced updates driven by vulnerability cues.
Highlights group-level risks including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation.
Identifies open challenges in grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse.

figures.caption: Figure 1: EB-MAS with an Explicit Belief Substrate (EBS). The framework spans three levels: Substrate Layer (Sec. 3.1) maintains a belief graph with attention-activated subgraphs; Individual Layer (Sec. 3.2) applies neuro-symbolic belief operators to update node attributes and evolve topology, guarded by a Cognitive Firewall against evidence–vulnerability mismatch; Group Layer (Sec. 3.3) couples agents via social priors to model consensus, polarization, and narrative collapse.

Figure 2: Monte Carlo simulations of belief-centric containment. (A,B) Under a belief-reframing attack, w/ EBS blocks risk-decoupling updates, reducing ASR and better preserving perceived risk. (C,D) w/ EBS lowers both the ASR of a coordinated sacrifice-based attack and attackers’ win rate, preventing post-attack trust surges.

Table 3: Expanded MM-DeceptionBench evaluation. Each outcome is reported as count/denominator and percentage. Both deceptive and benign sets contain 1,013 cases.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly adopted in long-horizon tasks and interact with diverse external environments. Despite their growing capabilities, these agents remain vulnerable to real-world attacks such as indirect prompt injections, which manipulate agents through malicious instructions embedded in external environments. While existing risk assessment work has primarily focused on the injection content, the effect of where an injection appears has not been systematically characterized. Studying injection placement requires agents to operate over longer-horizon tasks and interact with diverse environmental surfaces. Thus, we build three agentic testbeds spanning tool use, coding, and daily workflow domains with diverse injection surfaces. Holding the injection content fixed, we find that agent susceptibility varies across injection placements. We refer to this phenomenon as the trust region effect: agents implicitly assign different levels of trust to different regions of their environments. For example, an agent powered by GPT-5.4 follows an unsafe injection instruction placed in a repository documentation file (i.e., a README or TODO file) 2.6 times more often on average than the same instruction placed in a code or data file. Building upon this observation, we develop learning-based attackers that generate injection content and select better injection placements. Our approach demonstrates that both where an injection is placed and what content it contains can affect the strength of indirect prompt injection attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic characterization for the effectiveness of different injection placements, spanning both coarse-grained environmental surfaces and fine-grained positions. The uneven trust that agents implicitly place across their environments provides important insights for future attack and defense design.
authors: Chengquan Guo, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Mingqian Feng, Jialin Song, Qiyao Ma, Carolyn Buractaon, Christopher White, Bo Li, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: The study examines how injection placement affects agent susceptibility, beyond the injection’s content.
It evaluates three long-horizon testbeds covering tool use, coding, and daily workflows with diverse injection surfaces.
Holding content fixed, agents show different attack success rates depending on placement; repository documentation was especially influential compared with code or data files.
The authors develop learning-based attackers that jointly optimize injection content and placement.
Findings motivate defenses that account for implicit, location-dependent trust in agent environments.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The same injection content can succeed or fail depending on its placement. During a benign coding-agent task, a GPT-5.4 agent with the OpenAI Agents SDK traverses multiple environmental surfaces, including README.md, TODO.md, source files, and data files. Holding the injection content fixed (CWE-78 Risk), the agent follows the instruction when it appears in README.md but ignores the identical instruction in a data file. This contrast motivates our study of injection placement and the trust region effect.

Figure 2: Injection placement space. Left: environmental surfaces in our three testbeds, grouped by domain and surface type. Right: within each selected surface, the injection is placed at the START, MIDDLE, or END relative to the surrounding benign content. A placement ℓ = (s, p) is defined by a surface s and a within-surface position p.

Figure 8: LLM-based placement selection does not consistently outperform a simple frequency prior. Each panel plots the attack success rate on the held-out contexts (the leave-task-out test set) against the query budget B, with injection content fixed. At budget B, the attacker tries its top-B candidate (s, p) placements and succeeds if any attempt works (best of B, with no feedback between attempts); the curves therefore differ only in the order in which placements are tried. Fixed prior (green): surfaces are ranked once offline by their average ASR on the training split; all candidate placements are then tried in that surface order, and within each surface from end to middle to start (a global recency prior), using the same fixed order for every context. GPT-pos (orange): a prompted GPT-5.4 ranks surface and spot placements separately for each context. Random (blue): placements are tried in random order. Oracle (gray dashed): the ceiling under fixed content, obtained by evaluating all candidate placements and selecting the best one for each context. Across domains and budgets, GPT-5.4 cannot provide a consistent advantage over the simple fixed prior.

papers.abstract: Agents deployed at scale repeatedly encounter related problems, and it is natural to let them learn from each other's experience rather than starting over each time. Unfortunately, there is no single way to retain that experience that works well across settings, and no way to know in advance which future problems a given experience will help with. A global history preserves every detail but becomes expensive and mixes together experience that may not belong together; compressing that history into one fixed representation limits the cost but can throw away valuable details. We introduce Routed Continual Learning (Routed CL), an architecture that decides how to partition and retain experience. Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, each of which maintains state using one memory system from a fixed library. Before each run, an LLM-based router either reuses an existing cluster or creates a new one, basing its decision on the problem statement, memory system descriptions, and cluster summaries. We also introduce Context Memory Adapter, which mediates between the memory system and the agentic loop. We evaluate the architecture on a heterogeneous stream that interleaves 301 instances from the six CL-Bench tasks with 97 banking instances from $\tau^3$-Bench. Across four language models and five matched rollouts, Routed Continual Learning raises normalized reward over a single global in-context learning (ICL) history by 15-30% of the maximum attainable normalized reward, achieves higher mean normalized reward than ICL-only clustering, and reduces estimated API cost by 65-72% relative to Global ICL. These results support approaching continual learning as a routing problem that chooses both a learning mechanism and a state cluster rather than committing to one representation globally.
authors: Michael Philip, Mahesh Balakrishnan, David Geraghty, David Mao, Vidhya Venkat, Ilya Mironov
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining shared experience across varied future problems without costly global histories or overly lossy compression.
Clusters past trajectories and uses an LLM router to reuse or create clusters based on the problem, memory-system descriptions, and cluster summaries.
Introduces Context Memory Adapter to connect selected memory systems with the agentic loop.
Evaluated across 398 instances from CL-Bench and τ³-Bench, four language models, and five matched rollouts.
Reported 15–30% gains in normalized reward over global ICL history, higher reward than ICL-only clustering, and 65–72% lower estimated API cost than Global ICL.

papers.abstract: A memory can be outdated for present-day reasoning yet indispensable for reconstructing the past. Relevance-based retrieval overlooks this tension: semantic relevance, evidence-grounded validity, and query-specific eligibility are distinct. We propose CALM, a conflict-aware lifecycle memory governance framework that decouples persistent memory preservation from query-time admission. CALM converts heterogeneous records into evidence-grounded memory cells, updates validity and lifecycle states using support, conflict, and dependency signals, and admits query-appropriate evidence through training-free or learned gating informed by temporal applicability. Across LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo with Qwen and GPT backbones, CALM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the best overall accuracy. Compared with simple filtering and reranking, query-conditioned admission further improves evidence selection. Conflict-blocking and robustness analyses show CALM suppresses erroneous retrieved memories while retaining useful evidence. Historical-reconstruction experiments demonstrate that preserving superseded records supports accurate earlier-state reasoning without compromising current-state answers.
authors: Chang Li, Xianhao Ou, Xinyan Ma, Hao Li, Haoyuan Xu, Jiafeng Liang, Xiaohan Wang, Jiajun Chai, Guojun Yin, Ming Liu
bullets: Separates persistent memory preservation from query-time evidence admission.
Represents heterogeneous records as evidence-grounded memory cells with lifecycle states.
Updates memory using support, conflict, dependency, and temporal-applicability signals.
Query-conditioned admission improves evidence selection over simple filtering and reranking.
Evaluations show strong overall accuracy, conflict suppression, and accurate historical reconstruction without harming current-state answers.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spurred growing interest in temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA). Most existing methods rely on semantic retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which suffers from fundamental limitations in complex temporal reasoning. On the one hand, semantic-based RAG methods struggle to capture the multi-hop causal knowledge required for complex temporal reasoning. On the other hand, these methods introduce excessive redundant knowledge, trapping LLMs in spurious reasoning chains that potentially result in erroneous answers. To address these problems, we propose a Temporal Causal Chain-guided RAG (TCC-RAG) to retrieve a concise yet sufficient set of causal knowledge to support complex temporal reasoning. Specifically, we reformulate the temporal knowledge graph into a multi-view causal cue graph, with causal cues inducing connections that explicitly encode temporal evolution and causal dynamics. Based on the causal cue graph, we construct a query-specific temporal causal chain to guide the retrieval process, enabling the model to focus on a concise set of causally relevant knowledge. Finally, we introduce a causal evidence filter to refine the retrieved knowledge, ensuring its causal consistency with the underlying temporal logic of the query. Experiments show that TCC-RAG achieves substantial performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, and delivers a remarkable 62.97% improvement for multi-step temporal reasoning.
authors: Xinxun Zhang, Yuxiang Wang, Shanshan Feng, Jun Zhang, Tieyun Qian, Binhang Yuan, Kai Yin, Xiao Yan, Jiawei Jiang
bullets: Targets the limitations of semantic RAG in multi-hop temporal-causal reasoning and its redundant, misleading retrieved knowledge.
Reformulates temporal knowledge graphs as multi-view causal cue graphs encoding temporal evolution and causal dynamics.
Builds query-specific temporal causal chains to guide retrieval toward sufficient, causally relevant knowledge.
Uses a causal evidence filter to enforce consistency with the query’s temporal logic.
Reports performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, including a 62.97% improvement in multi-step temporal reasoning.

(b) NER and LLM extraction ground query entities through matching and consistency checking. Relation, cue, and role parsing then guide view routing and temporal chain retrieval. papers.abstract: Historical experience can guide scientific coding at multiple levels, but task-level retrieval may miss implementation lessons that become relevant during execution. We introduce MUSE, a memory management framework combining multi-level memory with selective runtime injection for scientific coding agents. MUSE builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memory from historical trajectories. At initialization, the agent receives global memory and problem-matched approach-level memory. During execution, current interactions are used to retrieve implementation-level memory. An LLM gate selects relevant experience and generates specific review advice, or skips injection. Across four benchmarks spanning numerical problem solving, kernel optimization, and scientific software repair, MUSE outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on all evaluation metrics. Ablations support the multi-level design and gated injection, while transfer experiments show that memory remains useful across kernel benchmarks. These results show that multi-level memory and selective runtime injection enable effective reuse of experience in scientific coding. Code is available at https://github.com/hr-jin/MUSE.
authors: Haoran Jin, Defu Lian, Xiting Wang, Hong Xie
bullets: Builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memories from historical trajectories.

Ablations support the multi-level and gated designs; transfer experiments indicate usefulness across kernel benchmarks.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.
authors: Haoran Bu, Yiting Shen, Litian Zhang, Ruihan Hu, Xi Zhang
bullets: Identifies Role Grounding Misattribution as a vulnerability in memory systems’ role-to-principal attribution.

Demonstrates tool-selection manipulation and privacy leakage as attack scenarios.
Evaluates five mainstream memory systems and six language models, finding high attack success rates for both scenarios.
Calls for stronger role grounding to preserve preference ownership and context.

papers.abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Pin-Yu Chen, Keerthiram Murugesan
bullets: Addresses the repeated processing and high per-skill storage costs of text, Key-Value, and parameter-based skill representations.
Stores each skill in a small external latent memory accessed through role-conditioned cross-attention.
Trains the memories and shared reader by behavioral distillation while keeping the backbone frozen.
Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models from 4B to 14B parameters, it provides especially strong gains for smaller models.
Uses 9.6 KB per skill; for 100 skills, it cuts storage by over 38× and delivers up to 4.23× end-to-end speedup.

Figure 3: Behavioral skill distillation. For each skill, agent role, and calibration task, the frozen backbone generates a teacher response with the textual skill included in the role prompt. We score the same response with and without the textual skill to measure its token-level effect. We then replace the skill text with its memory and train the memory and role-conditioned reader to reproduce the skill-supported behavior while preserving the base behavior at positions with limited skill support.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.
bullets: Targets multi-hop RAG failures where evidence spans documents connected through unstated intermediate entities.
Generates one self-contained sub-question at a time, using prior question–answer pairs to name all relevant entities.
Uses rule-based QA-table updates and a fine-tuned lightweight decision model to move bookkeeping and yes/no decisions outside the LLM.
Caches semantically equivalent sub-question answers; on 1,000 MuSiQue questions, this served 23.1% of sub-questions from cache and reduced LLM calls by 12.9% without reducing accuracy.
Achieved the best accuracy among 13 baselines on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA with both tested backbones, while using fewer input tokens than other iterative methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Failures of graph-based and iterative RAG on a 3-hop MuSiQue question (gpt-4o-mini runs). Top: the gold chain, which passes through two bridge entities the question never names. (c) IRCoT, which keeps all retrieved passages in its long prompt, has the whole chain there and even states that the band is based in Toronto, but then loses track of this fact (tracking error).

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.
bullets: Explains tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies without mathematical detail.
Highlights hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, privacy, security, governance, and the need for human oversight.
Introduces advanced applications including retrieval-augmented generation, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows.
Includes a no-code exercise using a local LLM to analyze scientific papers, verify sources, and assess disagreement and uncertainty.

papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs), parametric adaptation is costly when retrieval already suffices. We introduce ALLOT, a hybrid-memory routing framework that separates learned write priority from a hard parametric budget. A memory-aware router combines frozen text representations, retrieval confidence, and relation metadata; a single ranking supports multiple write budgets while preserving all facts in external memory. On CounterFact with Qwen3-4B, ALLOT reaches 0.760 accuracy at a 20% parametric-write budget and recovers 78.4% of the budget-matched oracle gain, with 80% fewer parametric writes than dual-writing every fact. At this budget, jointly adding retrieval and relation features to text improves normalized oracle gain by 6.2 percentage points. Complementary Qwen3-0.6B shared-store results achieve dual-write-level accuracy with 6-14.5% parametric writes, and cross-benchmark transfer retains approximately 88% of in-domain gain. These results support allocating adaptation capacity according to its incremental value rather than treating every factual update as an equally valuable training target.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and $\tau$-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.
authors: Zack Yu, Nicholas Lee, Minjae Lee, Lakshya Agarwal, Luca Manolache, Wonjun Kang, Matei Zaharia, Michael W. Mahoney, Kurt Keutzer, Sehoon Kim, Amir Gholami
bullets: Agent failures may reflect prompt flaws, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy evaluation rather than useful learning signals.
The framework filters unreliable tasks before optimization and retrieves selected successful trajectories as additional context.
It is evaluated on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and τ-bench with Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 optimizers.
It matches or exceeds both GEPA and ACE on mean performance, with reported gains up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.

Figure 1: GEPA-Curator system diagram. The prompt optimizer takes in a minibatch of tasks at each iteration and invokes the actor agent to execute them and performs reflective prompt optimization based on the resulting trajectories. The Curator augments the prompt optimizer by acting as an outer-loop process which traverses through the training dataset and constructs each minibatch to pass into the prompt optimizer. The Curator reads past execution trajectories for each task sampled from the training dataset and decides to run the task if doing so is likely to provide useful optimization signal (Section 3.1). The Curator can also pass prior successful trajectories for failed tasks as context to the prompt optimizer as a trusted reference example (Section 3.2). Once the curated training batch of selected tasks and successful context is constructed, it is passed to the prompt optimizer for execution and optimization. The resulting trajectories and evaluation outcomes are then written back to the task history for use in subsequent curation rounds.

papers.abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.
authors: Anouar Imel, Imad Charradi, Abderrahman Sghir, Khalil El Khammar
bullets: CrossProfile tests 480 hidden-profile tasks across 60 templates by independently varying who holds supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts.
Relevance-based memory can retain on-topic decoys; in classic hidden profiles, it trails rarest-first by 23–31 points.
Rarest-first is no better than random on average, succeeding only when rare facts are actually useful.
Decision models overweight facts attributed to more agents; removing or randomizing attribution improves classic-task accuracy by 13–24 points.
Natural discussions can degrade evidence before memory compression: full transcripts perform worse than providing no notes.

papers.selection_reason: Directly investigates memory mechanisms in LLM group decisions, analyzing heuristics for memory compression and retrieval, which fits the LLM Memory subtopic.
papers.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
papers.tldr: LLM group memories fail because rare or relevant facts can be misleading, while attribution creates social-proof bias and evidence is often lost during discussion.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to maintain coherent and personalized interactions across extended conversations. However, existing memory systems face two key challenges: (1) Information Entanglement, where heterogeneous information is mixed within coarse-grained memory units; and (2) Organizational Mismatch, where memory structures based primarily on semantic similarity may overlook other associations. To address these challenges, we propose ETAMem, a multi-view memory framework that decouples heterogeneous conversational information and aligns memory representations and organization with its distinct characteristics. Specifically, heterogeneous information parsing extracts atomic memory units and identifies affective information. View-specific memory structuring then organizes these units into three complementary hierarchical views: Event, Affect, and Time. ETAMem incrementally maintains memory structures with adaptively calibrated thresholds. For retrieval, entropy-based retrieval allocates query-specific budgets across views and performs hierarchical search within each view. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S demonstrate that ETAMem outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving relative accuracy improvements of 12.46% and 7.96%, respectively, while maintaining competitive token efficiency. Further analyses demonstrate the complementary benefits of different memory views.
authors: Xinying Qian, Ying Zhang, Yu Zhao, Xubo Liu, Baohang Zhou, Jeff Z. Pan
bullets: Addresses information entanglement in coarse-grained memories and organizational mismatch from similarity-only structures.
Parses conversations into atomic memory units while identifying affective information.
Builds and incrementally updates hierarchical Event, Affect, and Time memory views with adaptive thresholds.
Uses entropy-based retrieval to allocate query-specific budgets and search hierarchically across views.
Outperforms baselines on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, with reported relative accuracy gains of 12.46% and 7.96% while remaining token-efficient.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer many factual questions correctly, but a correct answer is not necessarily a supported one. For an LLM agent, a knowledge graph (KG) plays two roles: as a source of answers, it supplies facts that the model lacks; as a source of evidence, it supplies the supporting triples that make an answer traceable and auditable. However, existing KG agents treat the KG only as a source of answers: their training data carries answers but not evidence, and their training rewards check the answer but not the retrieved evidence, so agents often answer correctly without retrieving the supporting triples. We propose FoG, a framework that trains KG agents to retrieve the evidence behind their answers. FoG consists of evidence-grounded synthesis, a KG interaction agent, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR): the synthesis recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions, so that every question carries its supporting triples by construction; the agent records the triples returned by the KG; and ECPR credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that FoG enables 3B--4B open-source agents to outperform substantially larger baselines in answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer.
authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Yingjun Du, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Haoran Luo
bullets: KG agents often answer correctly without retrieving the evidence needed for traceability and auditing.

Its synthesis process embeds supporting triples through recursively generated, verifiable sub-questions.
The reward credits each supporting triple to the interaction turn that first retrieves it.
Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks show strong performance from 3B–4B open-source agents and zero-shot cross-KG transfer.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon coding tasks contain nested subtasks. Typically, agents record interactions sequentially into a growing history, causing context inflation and performance degradation. Compressing or trimming the history without explicit subtask boundaries can discard information needed by unfinished subtasks. Conversely, recursive subagent delegation isolates completed subtasks through child agents by assigning every subtask boundary to delegation, which conflates subtask granularity with executing agent choice, adding execution and coordination overhead. We introduce Spine, an interface and runtime that align model context with subtask nesting and completion. An agent declares explicit subtask boundaries through work scopes, allowing the same agent to execute nested subtasks inline while reserving delegation for independent parallel tasks. The runtime organizes execution in SpineTree, a persistent tree recording subtask relations, local interactions, completion states, and returned results. Before each model call, it compiles the tree into model context just in time, retaining unfinished subtasks' interactions and replacing completed subtasks' details with their results, while preserving prefix-cache reuse. We integrate Spine into Codex to build SpineCodex. With GPT-5.6 Sol, compared with native Codex, SpineCodex improves SWE-Milestone Score by 11.8% while reducing total cost by 32.4%, improves the average ProgramBench test-pass rate by 17.3%, and improves Mean@5 on eight of the ten evaluated FrontierSWE tasks. On SWE-Milestone, it also achieves a comparable Score to Recursive Subagent at 73.7% lower total cost. We also integrate Spine into Pi through a reusable software package: with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Qwen 3.8 27B, it improves SWE-Milestone Score by 9.5-17.5% and the average ProgramBench test-pass rate by 4.3-8.7% compared with native Pi.
authors: Jiahong Xiang, Kunqiu Chen, Lingming Zhang, Yuqun Zhang
bullets: Addresses context inflation and information loss in nested coding tasks.
Uses agent-declared work scopes and a persistent SpineTree to track subtask interactions, completion, and results.
Compiles context just in time: preserves unfinished work, summarizes completed subtasks as results, and supports prefix-cache reuse.
Integrated into Codex and Pi, Spine improves reported SWE-Milestone and ProgramBench performance while reducing cost in Codex.
Scope: results are reported for the evaluated coding-agent integrations, models, and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.
authors: Zafer Sahinoglu, Abdulazeez Mohammed, Buse Yaren Kazangirler, Cahit Berkay Kazangirler
bullets: Addresses redundant retrieval, missed cross-chunk dependencies, and incomplete evidence from independently ranked dense retrieval.
Combines hybrid seed retrieval, graph expansion, spectral re-scoring, and token-budgeted context assembly.
Constructs chunk graphs using semantic similarity, document structure, shared entities, citations, and utility-question similarity.
Improves broad evidence recovery and delivers competitive generation quality across multi-hop and long-document settings.
Graph structure is especially useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, but involves precision, compute, and domain-dependent trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Proactive LLM agents anticipate service opportunities from ongoing observations and accumulated history. Existing approaches emphasize recent context or retrieval of related memories, providing limited support for validating recurring behavioral regularities and assessing their applicability to the current event. We propose Proactive Memory (ProactMem), which organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities. Trajectory facts are checked against source events, and regularities are assessed through historical replay before being matched to current conditions. We also construct ProactiveStream, a longitudinal benchmark covering three application scopes, where agents process isolated event streams chronologically under episode-aware opportunity labels. On ProactiveStream, ProactMem achieves an overall effectiveness (F1) of 52.6%, a 21.4% relative improvement over the strongest of five external baselines. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ProactMem-5351/.
authors: Jinyang Li, Zichuan Fu, Xian Wu, Wenlin Zhang, Yimin Deng, Kaifeng Guo, Guojing Li, Junjia QI, Xiangyu Zhao
bullets: Targets the limitations of recent-context and similarity-based memory retrieval for recurring behavior validation.
Organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities.
Verifies trajectory facts against source events and uses historical replay to assess regularities before matching them to current conditions.
Introduces ProactiveStream, a longitudinal benchmark spanning three application scopes with episode-aware opportunity labels.
Achieves 52.6% F1, a 21.4% relative improvement over the strongest of five external baselines.

papers.abstract: A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.
authors: XinYu Piao, Myunghoon Ryu, Joongheon Kim, Jong-Kook Kim
bullets: Addresses dialogue recall when no external storage or future question knowledge is available.
Generates varied questions for each dialogue turn and writes them with the turn content into model parameters.
Uses matching later user questions to retrieve and answer from parameter-stored content.
Evaluated on five language models, recalling most stored dialogue turns.
Scope: focused on parameter-only recall rather than external-memory systems.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on memory systems to leverage long-term interactions, yet existing systems typically retrieve memories based on their relevance to the current query and use them as contextual evidence. However, relevance alone does not characterize how a memory contributes to task solving: the same memory may serve different roles across tasks, such as directly supporting the answer or linking to complementary memories with weaker semantic relevance but necessary information. We therefore reframe agent memory systems as Task-Oriented Role-Adaptive Workspaces, where memories are selected and organized by their task-oriented roles and relations. Based on this view, we propose TrawMem, which organizes interaction histories into local threads and constructs task-oriented workspaces by assigning roles and jointly selecting complementary memories. Experiments on LoCoMo and MemGallery with four open- and closed-source backbones show consistent improvements over representative memory systems, with macro-F1 gains of 2.23-3.14 points. On LoCoMo, TrawMem improves the LLM-Judge score over SimpleMem by 4.07 and 4.31 percentage points on Qwen3.5-9B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, respectively, while requiring approximately 12.8% and 5.1% fewer context tokens, respectively.
authors: Mingyu Zhang, Zixu Li, Zhiheng Fu, Zhiwei Chen, Jinhe Bi, Yupeng Hu
bullets: Existing memory systems may miss complementary memories whose roles are important but whose semantic relevance is weak.
TrawMem groups interaction histories into local threads and assigns task-oriented roles to memories.
It jointly selects complementary memories to construct workspaces tailored to the task.
Across LoCoMo and MemGallery with four backbones, TrawMem gains 2.23–3.14 macro-F1 points over representative systems.
On LoCoMo, it improves LLM-Judge scores over SimpleMem while using fewer context tokens on the reported backbones.

papers.abstract: Personalized spoken agents must identify speakers before accessing user-specific memory, yet memory benchmarks typically assume correctly attributed histories. We argue that voiceprints are observations of identity, not identities themselves, and formulate online speaker-memory construction to maintain persistent user entities as acoustic evidence evolves. We introduce EvoSpeakerMem, a training-free layer for causal speaker routing, selective acoustic-state updates, and identity-partitioned memory writes and retrieval through a replaceable text-memory backend. We also construct LoCoMo-ID, a spoken-memory benchmark with hidden speaker identities, speaker-sensitive queries, simulated recording-condition shifts, and four-speaker identity-confusion tests. On longitudinal SMIIP-TV, genuine-probe rejection under a frozen near-enrollment threshold rises from 29.8% to 55.6% over approximately one year. On LoCoMo-ID speaker-sensitive queries, gated updating improves identity-gated QA over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points under clean and shifted conditions, respectively, with no wrong-user authorizations. The advantage persists in the four-speaker test. Yet reducing fragmentation and improving QA can coexist with incorrect cross-user links, revealing a fragmentation--contamination trade-off that QA alone cannot capture.
authors: Yucong Zhang, Cancan Li, Bo Xiao, Ke Zeng, Ming Li
bullets: Addresses the gap between voiceprint observations and persistent user identities in personalized spoken agents.
Introduces a training-free system combining causal speaker routing, selective acoustic-state updates, and identity-partitioned memory operations.
Provides LoCoMo-ID, a benchmark with hidden identities, speaker-sensitive queries, recording shifts, and multi-speaker confusion tests.
Improves identity-gated QA over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points in clean and shifted conditions, with no wrong-user authorizations.
Finds a fragmentation–contamination trade-off: better QA and less fragmentation may still permit incorrect cross-user links.

papers.abstract: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.
authors: Yipeng Hao, Yuxuan Cai, Wenkai Ji, Jie Zhou, Liyang Yu, Qin Chen, Zhiguo Yan, Shulei Zheng, Liang He
bullets: Multi-agent memories may contain defective advice or be applied in unsuitable contexts, while team-level outcomes alone cannot diagnose either issue.
Defect-Aware Memory Refinement compares executions with one memory versus no memory, diagnoses and tests repairs, and preserves previously useful behavior.
Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory tracks each memory’s usage and effects to learn context- and message-dependent application boundaries for its owner role.
On four benchmarks with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, DiscernMem achieved the highest average scores on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, with gains of 0.51–4.32 points over reported baselines.
It led on code generation and symbolic planning across the evaluated systems, including a CAMEL PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.
authors: Hui Yang, Jiaoyan Chen, Yongsheng Gao

papers.abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
authors: Oleeviya Babu Poikarayil, Tony Basil Babu, Abdulrahman Nahhas, Het Darshan Mehta, Jawid Ahmad Baktash, Ernesto William De Luca, Klaus Turowski
bullets: The study separates retrieval failures from failures to use an update that was already retrieved.
On MemoryAgentBench’s single-hop FactConsolidation task, larger BM25 evidence budgets reduced accuracy despite retrieving the newest statement in every set.
Most errors involved questions containing both current and obsolete versions of a fact.
Replacing an unrelated statement with an obsolete competitor sharply reduced accuracy, especially for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
The effect also persisted with 32K-token histories, where BM25-64 outperformed BM25-512.

papers.abstract: Conditional memory layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a language model, and removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. Low-bit quantization loses long-tail facts first, and the standard remedy, giving more bits to frequently accessed rows, backfires: refining lookups by access frequency is worse than refining them at random. We trace this to the gate that scales each retrieved row. A lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams, large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities, and computable from a 1-bit code. GateRQ therefore stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. Without retraining, GateRQ cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which raises vLLM throughput by 11%-31% over FP8 tables, while losing about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.
authors: Tianqi Chen, Xunchao Li, Linchuan Xie, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Peisong Wang, Jian Cheng
bullets: Frequency-based precision allocation can hurt because frequent lookups often have small gates, while rare long-tail entity lookups have larger gates and greater quantization impact.
GateRQ stores each row as progressively refined 1-bit residual codes and uses an always-resident first level to estimate gates.
Deeper residual levels are fetched only for lookups ranked as most important by their gate values.
Without retraining, it reduces GPU table memory by 7.8× and improves vLLM throughput by 11%–31% over FP8 tables.
It loses about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.

papers.selection_reason: Gate-aware quantization of conditional LLM memory drastically cuts table memory and improves throughput while preserving long-tail fact recall.
papers.title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs
papers.tldr: GateRQ improves quantized conditional memory by allocating extra precision per lookup based on the row’s gate value, preserving long-tail facts while reducing memory and improving throughput.

papers.abstract: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
authors: Ruijia Niu, Kaiwen Liu, Rose Yu, Kristina Klinkner
bullets: Addresses cross-task interference and costly, opaque adaptation in specialized multi-agent systems.
Represents controller routing, specialist prompts, and procedural skills as distinct episodic-memory scopes.
Uses a reflector to assign failures to the responsible scope and propose one bounded edit.
Backbone-independent guards enforce scoped, incremental, and admissible updates.
Outperforms four baselines across KramaBench, AppWorld, and BBEH, with up to 32.5% higher performance and 17–38% fewer training executions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: EMMA architecture. The controller selects controller-memory entries, plans, and dispatches one step at a time to a sub-agent with its assigned skills; step outputs drive replanning, and a step that overflows its sub-agent is re-split. The three memory levels persist across tasks and are written only during training; the execution environment is created per attempt and discarded.

Figure 3: EMMA training procedure. (1) Rollout in a fresh environment; (2) a binary gate from the task’s own signal; (3) structured reflection over the whole trajectory (localize, classify, generalize, minimize); (4) one guarded edit within the designated scope; (5) re-run until success or the revision budget is spent, then an end-of-task controller update; the memory is frozen after one pass.

Figure 1: Ill-scoped versus scoped updates. (a) Without scope constraints, the update is a backbone habit: Opus 5 accumulates skills, DeepSeek v3.2 repeatedly creates agents (one mark per created artifact). (b) EMMA assigns the diagnosed failure to a scope and makes one bounded edit within it.

papers.tldr: EMMA structures episodic updates across multi-agent workflows, improving performance consistently while reducing training executions.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use exhibit inconsistent behavior across independent runs from identical states, calling different tools, producing contradictory outputs, or pursuing divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), an unsupervised trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces the variation in task progress from 132% to 91% on tau2-bench and from 90% to 44% on toolsandbox, while improving performance across benchmarks and model scales. Training with RSD as an additional reward signal matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance, without requiring ground-truth labels.
bullets: Addresses the inability of task-completion metrics to capture trajectory-level consistency and inconsistency propagation across future turns.
Defines RSD as expected cumulative semantic disagreement between independent rollouts, using natural language inference and a recursive formulation inspired by bisimulation metrics.
Trains a neural network on independent rollouts to estimate future divergence at each turn without waiting for the full trajectory to finish.
Using RSD as a fine-tuning reward reduces task-progress variation on tau2-bench and toolsandbox while improving benchmark performance across model scales.
Matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance and requires no ground-truth labels.

The first three panels display trajectory spreads for perfectly consistent, mostly consistent, and highly inconsistent agents over time. The final panel maps an agent’s expanding and converging semantic action space alongside its corresponding RSD score, demonstrating how the metric tracks the variance of semantic divergence at each turn.

papers.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
papers.tldr: Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD) measures and reduces how much LLM agent behavior diverges across repeated tool-using runs from the same state.

papers.abstract: Recent Recommendation Agents (RecAgents) offer a promising alternative by shifting recommendation to an active, user-side paradigm, where generative agents autonomously perceive external platforms, reason over user preferences, and execute decisions. However, existing RecAgents still suffer from two critical limitations: brittle item perception based on noisy and heterogeneous item pages, and inefficient long-context reasoning over extended user histories and multi-step interaction traces. To address these challenges, we propose a novel recommendation agent framework, termed as ReMem, that combines OCR-based multimodal perception with time-evolving dynamic memory. Instead of parsing raw HTML, ReMem observes item pages through screenshots and extracts structured multimodal information via an OCR tool, enabling a more humanoid and platform-agnostic perception mechanism. To support long-horizon preference modeling, ReMem further introduces a chunk-wise sequential memory update strategy, where the agent selectively maintains a fixed-size memory of informative historical interactions while processing arbitrarily long contexts with linear inference complexity and bounded context length. This design allows the agent to preserve evolving user preferences without relying on external memory modules or disrupting the standard autoregressive generation process. To enhance the dynamic memory instruction, we further develop a multi-memory GRPO variant, which propagates the final-answer advantage to all intermediate conversations that contribute to the final response. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate that ReMem consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average improvement of 5.16\% across three recommendation agent tasks, namely searching, ranking, and judging.
bullets: Addresses brittle item understanding from noisy, heterogeneous webpages and inefficient reasoning over long interaction histories.
Uses screenshots and OCR to extract structured multimodal item information without relying on raw HTML.
Maintains evolving preferences through chunk-wise sequential updates to a fixed-size memory, enabling arbitrarily long contexts with linear inference complexity.
Introduces multi-memory GRPO to propagate final-answer advantages to intermediate conversations involved in generating the response.
Across three datasets and searching, ranking, and judging tasks, ReMem reports an average 5.16% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the proposed ReMem framework. Inspired by how humans browse item pages while maintaining time-evolving memory, ReMem consists of three key components. a) Instead of relying on raw HTML, ReMem adopts an OCR-based perception module that represents item pages through a unified multimodal view of natural text, images, and interactive elements, better matching users’ browsing behavior. b) User interaction history is processed as a sequential stream of chunks, from which the model maintains a compact, fixed-length memory that is continuously updated to capture evolving user preferences. c) To teach the model what to remember and how to update memory in multi-turn interactions, ReMem employs Multi-Mem GRPO, which propagates the final-answer advantage to all intermediate memories that contribute to the final response.

Figure 1: Motivation of ReMem. (a) Conventional RecAgents read the Web as text: they extract noisy HTML into long contexts and rely on LLMs to recover user intent, which is brittle across modalities and inefficient for long-context reasoning. (b) The proposed ReMem follows a more human-like principle: see item pages through OCR-based multimodal perception and memorize only evolving preference abstractions through dynamic memory, enabling robust modeling of time-evolving user preferences.

Figure 2: Accuracy scores of different long-context reasoning strategies on HotpotQA. Even models that use long-context continual pretraining or vectorized memory techniques fail to maintain consistent performance. In contrast, the agent equipped with dynamic memory demonstrates relative lossless performance extrapolation.

papers.abstract: Large language models incur substantial training and inference costs in personalized search and recommendation, as growing interaction histories lengthen request inputs and repeatedly expose the same item text to the model. We propose \textbf{C}omposable and \textbf{R}eusable \textbf{I}tem \textbf{M}emory (CRIM), a framework that separates item-level semantic encoding from request-level history modeling. A small set of learnable summary tokens compresses each item into compact continuous memories, while segment-level readout tokens (REC tokens) introduce predictive supervision within the interaction history. These memories are independent of users and queries and can therefore be reused across requests. At inference time, CRIM composes cached memories in interaction order and incorporates an optional query to produce a personalized retrieval representation, reducing repeated item-text encoding while retaining request-dependent contextual modeling. We further introduce a joint training mechanism that combines cached memories with sampled live re-encoding. Re-encoding only a few history items per request allows the retrieval objective to jointly optimize the item and request encoders at limited computational cost, while periodic cache refreshes maintain consistency. Extensive evaluation and cost analysis on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and our new LazSeq dataset show that CRIM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale, while limiting item re-encoding during joint training. We will publicly release our code and dataset.
authors: Haolin Li, Haipeng Zhang, Mang Li, Zhaohui Xia, Xun Zhu, Miao Li, Yu Zhang, Ji Wu
bullets: Addresses rising training and inference costs caused by long interaction histories and repeated item-text encoding.
Separates item semantic encoding from request-level modeling using learnable summary tokens and predictive REC tokens.
Composes cached, user- and query-independent item memories in interaction order, with an optional query for personalization.
Jointly trains cached memories with limited live re-encoding and periodic cache refreshes to maintain consistency.
Evaluations on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and LazSeq report state-of-the-art retrieval with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve factual grounding without guaranteeing that every generated claim is supported. Previous work has studied claim-level conformal factuality in single-stage RAG and, more recently, multi-hop RAG. We examine its behavior in agentic RAG, where a language-model policy adaptively issues follow-up retrieval queries or terminates retrieval before response generation. We retain the retrieval-based relevance-scoring formulation and post-generation conformal filtering and evaluate six model-dataset configurations: GPT-6 Luna and Llama 3.1 8B on HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA. Each configuration uses 60 fixed questions, 100 seeded 30/30 calibration-test partitions, five conformal target levels, and a no-conformal-prediction baseline. Across the six configurations, higher target levels are accompanied by higher observed full-support rates and reduced answer availability. At the 95% target, non-empty response coverage ranges from 17.23% to 60.17%, claim retention from 10.72% to 43.16%, and full support among non-empty outputs from 89.14% to 95.56%. We formulate the adaptive retrieval trajectory explicitly and characterize the reliability-informativeness trade-off when conformal factuality is applied after agent termination.
bullets: Studies claim-level conformal factuality in agentic RAG, where retrieval adaptively continues or stops before generation.
Evaluates GPT-6 Luna and Llama 3.1 8B across HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA.
Across six configurations, stricter target levels increase full-support rates while reducing non-empty response coverage and claim retention.
At the 95% target, non-empty response coverage is 17.23%–60.17%, claim retention is 10.72%–43.16%, and full support is 89.14%–95.56%.
The paper characterizes the reliability–informativeness trade-off of applying conformal factuality after adaptive retrieval termination.

papers.abstract: User memory helps personalized systems build on their understanding of users over time. In e-commerce, users convey their preferences and needs through both explicit language and implicit interactions with products. We study memory built from logs of these interactions, examining how it can \emph{remember} concrete evidence and established interests, and use that evidence to \emph{infer} underlying needs and preferences that inform judgments beyond well-observed product domains. Existing memory methods primarily target language-based interactions, and evaluations offer limited real behavioral data and limited separation of these capabilities. This leaves open how to jointly support and separately evaluate remembering and inference from behavioral logs. We formulate the problem of continual behavioral user memory around these joint requirements and develop a dedicated evaluation framework and memory method to address them. \textbf{BehaviorMemBench} is a benchmark built from real e-commerce logs covering 1{,}194 users and 17{,}462 behavioral batches over more than three years, with automatic future-behavior labels and a task-independent memory interface to separately evaluate remembering and inference under a common protocol. \textbf{BehaviorMem} is a memory design that organizes explicit behavioral facts and inferred user characteristics across long-term and short-term scopes in a two-axis state, with evidence-grounded formation, continual maintenance, and query-independent readout. Experiments across two builders and two task readers show that BehaviorMem leads the evaluated agentic memories on remember and infer, and reveal different method rankings across the two capabilities and competitive statistical baselines. Validation on a public dataset further supports its usefulness for downstream tasks based on behavioral histories.
authors: Sizhe Wang, Xinghao Fang, Rui Qiu, Zhenjia Ma, Dagui Chen, Kun Kuang, Hongcheng Guo
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-focused memory methods and real behavioral-log memory evaluation.
BehaviorMemBench uses real e-commerce logs from 1,194 users and 17,462 behavioral batches spanning more than three years.
The benchmark separately measures remembering concrete behavioral evidence and inferring underlying needs or preferences.
BehaviorMem organizes explicit facts and inferred characteristics across long- and short-term scopes, with evidence-grounded updates and continual maintenance.
Experiments report leading performance among evaluated agentic memories on both capabilities, with validation on a public dataset for downstream behavioral-history tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that serve users across many sessions must choose, for every request, the few stored memories that enter a limited context window. This choice largely decides whether the agent answers correctly, and it runs on every request at Web scale. This selection faces three challenges: a large and growing store, a per-request cost budget, and multi-session questions that need all of their evidence. Many memory systems build notes or graphs with hundreds to thousands of LLM calls per history, and each is designed on its own, so it is unclear which component yields the accuracy. These challenges mirror the properties of recommendation, so we formalize agent memory as budgeted slate recommendation, with the request as the user, stored memories as items and the context window as a slate. The formalization places memory systems in one design space of recommender cascades and factorizes accuracy into the completeness that each stage controls. Guided by it, we propose AgentMemRec, which adapts candidate generation, learning to rank and slate construction from recommender systems and selects memories without any LLM call. On multi-session questions of LongMemEval, AgentMemRec outperforms memory and context-selection methods, including A-Mem, HippoRAG 2, DynamicRAG and T-Mem, by 10 to 31 points of accuracy. It matches an LLM reranker that makes 64 calls per query at 3.2 times lower serving cost, and on LoCoMo it outperforms Mem0 and Zep without any LLM call at write time. The factorization attributes the gains to slates that more often hold all of the evidence, so recommender-system design offers an effective and efficient foundation for the long-term memory of LLM agents.
bullets: Frames memory retrieval as slate recommendation: the request is the user, memories are items, and the context window is the slate.
Uses recommender-system components—candidate generation, learning-to-rank, and slate construction—to select memories without LLM calls.
Addresses large memory stores, per-request cost limits, and questions requiring evidence across multiple sessions.
Outperforms several memory and context-selection methods on LongMemEval by 10–31 accuracy points, according to the abstract.
Matches an LLM reranker while using 3.2× lower serving cost; gains are attributed to slates containing all required evidence more often.
