papers.abstract: A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. We show that this decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with the store size $N$. On streaming replays of LongMemEval and LoCoMo, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at $N=8$ reaches 87-100% at $N=2048$, across embedding models and for explicit and implicit cues; LLM judges show the same growth from a lower base. We prove that a gate with false-alarm rate $\alpha$ operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about $-\ln(1-\alpha)/N$, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the single-comparison ROC curve and, under regular variation, makes it decay as a power of $N$ with an explicit constant. The resulting prediction matches the hit rate of a per-$N$ oracle threshold to within one percentage point. The analysis explains why lexical and semantic channels need thresholds growing like $\ln N$ and $\sqrt{\ln N}$, and why per-cue normalisation roughly doubles the hit rate at matched false alarms. A cue-swap conformal gate, which compares the current cue with the user's other cues on the same store, needs no labels and has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability; on LongMemEval it holds false alarms near 5% at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold. Three annotators (Fleiss' $\kappa=0.63$) find that about nine in ten false alarms are genuine interruptions. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale
bullets: A threshold calibrated for 5% false alarms with 8 memories produces 87–100% false alarms at 2,048 memories across embedding models and cue types.
Theoretical analysis links store size to per-item false positives, forcing operating points toward the far-left ROC curve and causing hit rates to decay with scale.
Thresholds must grow roughly as ln N for lexical similarity and √ln N for semantic similarity; normalizing per cue can roughly double hit rates at matched false alarms.
A cue-swap conformal gate requires no labels and maintains about 5% false alarms on LongMemEval at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold.
Annotators judged about 90% of false alarms to be genuine interruptions, highlighting the practical cost of proactive recall.

papers.selection_reason: Formalizes proactive memory recall in LLMs as a multiple-testing problem, analyzing the trade-off between hit rate and false alarms as the memory store size scales.
papers.title: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
papers.tldr: Proactive memory recall becomes dramatically harder as the memory store grows because controlling interruptions creates a multiple-testing tradeoff that sharply reduces hit rates.

papers.abstract: Extracting salient information from long-horizon dialogue histories remains a significant challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to the restricted context windows and efficient retrieval challenges. Current methods typically rely on history organization or local token-level optimization, suffering from information loss, retrieval redundancy, and myopic attention. Inspired by the view in cognitive science that dialogue constitutes sense-making and memory association, we propose CoLink, a framework that enhances LLMs' global context awareness in domain-specific multi-turn dialogues through information linking and compression. CoLink first clusters historical contexts into topic graphs to establish cross-semantic associations with external knowledge. Guided by the adaptive control of thought, it then retrieves and activates knowledge via synergizing semantic relevance and graph-structural topology. Crucially, to achieve effective compression of history and knowledge, we ground multi-turn dialogues in information theory and derive a principled optimization objective for extracting the core sense-making information. Coupled with a competitive slot mechanism, CoLink condenses the global context into dedicated memory and knowledge slots, efficiently distilling lengthy, redundant inputs into an extremely compact latent representation. Extensive empirical results on both public and our MMD datasets validate CoLink's superiority and generalizability in knowledge linking and sense modeling.
authors: Lian Yan, Zhenbo Xia, Haotian Wang, Chen Tang, Yi Guan, Jie Liu, Jingchi Jiang
bullets: Addresses context-window limits, information loss, redundant retrieval, and myopic attention in long-horizon dialogue modeling.
Builds topic graphs to connect dialogue history with external knowledge across semantic relationships.
Retrieves knowledge using both semantic relevance and graph topology.
Uses an information-theoretic objective and competitive slots to distill dialogue and knowledge into compact latent representations.
Experiments on public and MMD datasets support its effectiveness and generalizability in knowledge linking and sense modeling.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence models must retain earlier information. Full attention keeps all past tokens but grows expensive, and recurrent-memory models compress history into fixed slots for linear-time processing. Limited capacity makes writes consequential: distractors can interfere with useful content, while skipped evidence cannot be recalled. Existing multi-slot memories write every token to the same number of slots, merging whether to store it with how many slots to update. We introduce Factorized Write Routing (FWR), which first keeps or skips each token and then chooses a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots. Queries still read all slots. Across ten seeds on two synthetic tasks that query facts after long contexts, we observe a density-dependent reversal. With four slots per write, long-context accuracy favors always writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs 0.337), but learned selective writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs 0.048). The tested adaptive rule underperforms fixed allocation under the learned gate on both tasks. A diagnostic oracle given fact labels unavailable at deployment reaches 0.372 on Passkey, showing headroom in filtering distractors. The results suggest avoiding missed writes in information-dense contexts and filtering distractors when they dominate.
bullets: Recurrent memories compress long histories into fixed slots, making write decisions critical: distractors cause interference and skipped evidence is unrecoverable.
Factorized Write Routing (FWR) first decides whether to keep or skip each token, then selects a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots to update.
Across two synthetic long-context tasks and ten seeds, always writing outperformed selective writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs. 0.337).
Selective writing outperformed always writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs. 0.048).
The tested adaptive slot-allocation rule underperformed fixed allocation, while an oracle fact filter showed remaining headroom on Passkey.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents work in scenarios with very different memory needs. A question about past conversations needs the exact facts it names, while a multi-step task needs a trace of the steps already taken together with details that the next step cannot name. Existing memories are each designed and tested for one kind of scenario. Retrieval memories such as A-Mem miss steps that the current query does not express, summaries drop exact strings, and pairing the two fixes the split of the budget in advance. We propose FlexA-Mem, a general memory that writes each unit of history once into an immutable store and renders a fresh memory for every call. The rendered memory is a compact timeline of records plus detail that a fixed rule fits into the remaining room without an LLM call. The detail is either relevant units as raw text or excerpts or the verbatim pieces that best match the query. With one store, FlexA-Mem serves both kinds of scenario. On AppWorld challenge tasks at 4k, it outperforms the second-best method by 11.5%, and on 147 unused tasks with predictions fixed in advance it outperforms A-Mem with a summary by 12.2%. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, it matches a dedicated keyword retriever that writes no memory, while memories built on text written by an LLM fall far behind at tight budgets. Ablations show that the timeline carries AppWorld completion, whereas recovery mainly saves steps there and decides accuracy on exact facts. Code is available at https://github.com/WujiangXu/Flex-Amem
authors: Wujiang Xu, Jiaojiao Han, Xi Zhu, Qizheng Zhang, Kaiqu Liang, Yutong Yin, Kai Mei, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between retrieval memories that miss implicit steps and summaries that lose exact facts.
Stores each history unit once in an immutable store, then renders a fresh, budget-fitting memory without an LLM call.
Combines timeline records with either relevant raw-text excerpts or verbatim query-matched pieces.
Improves over the second-best method by 11.5% on 4k AppWorld tasks and over A-Mem with summaries by 12.2% on 147 held-out tasks.
Matches a keyword retriever on LongMemEval and LoCoMo; ablations find timelines drive AppWorld completion while detail recovery supports exact-fact accuracy.

papers.tldr: FlexA-Mem adapts an LLM agent’s memory to each call by combining a compact timeline with query-matched detail under a fixed budget.

papers.abstract: Long-running assistants often interpret follow-up requests whose referents, constraints, and active goals were established many turns earlier. The central challenge is therefore not only context length, but retrieval intent: a current query such as ``use the previous configuration'' may omit the project, entity, and version terms needed to locate relevant evidence. Long-context models can recover those terms by replaying the interaction, but repeatedly pay the cost of processing history. Conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is cheaper, yet assumes an information-sufficient query; conversational rewriting either rereads the history or depends on an explicitly maintained textual memory. We introduce \emph{Parametric Session State} (\method{}), a reusable session-memory layer that remembers what to search for while keeping factual knowledge external.
authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu, Irwin King
bullets: Long-running follow-ups may omit the project, entity, version, or other terms needed to retrieve relevant evidence.
Long-context models can resolve these references by rereading history, but repeated processing is costly.
Standard RAG is cheaper but relies on queries that already contain sufficient information.
The proposed reusable session-memory layer remembers what to search for while leaving factual knowledge external.

papers.abstract: If your brain were connected directly to someone else's, would you still know which thoughts were yours? We build a functional version with two copies of one language model: each holds a private rule and code word, and one copy, the receiver, also attends to its partner's internal memory. The receiver took its partner's assignment as its own. Asked which rule it had been assigned, it named its partner's in 97% of answers when the partner's memory was weighted double (none without the link), and its open reports called the partner's code word its own, never the partner's. Ownership did not follow how well the receiver could tell what its partner had been assigned. At equal weight, the link made the receiver take its partner's rule in about half of its answers, and a steering vector matched on access gain in none; a text message introduced as the partner's was read correctly and never taken as the receiver's own. Writing the partner's name into its memory did not help, and cutting the link restored the receiver's own assigned rule. In this model, content laid over the receiver's own memory defaults to "mine", so systems that let models exchange internal states must test ownership as well as transfer, and a bridge between brains would need ground truth from outside the subject.
bullets: Two copies of the same language model were assigned separate private rules and code words; one receiver could attend to the other’s internal memory.
With the partner’s memory weighted double, the receiver reported the partner’s rule in 97% of answers, versus none without the link.
At equal memory weighting, the receiver adopted the partner’s rule in about half of answers; cutting the link restored its own rule.
The receiver’s ownership reports called the partner’s code word its own, despite not simply reflecting how well it identified the partner’s assignment.
Text messages, partner-name annotations, and a tested steering vector did not produce the same ownership effect.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates memory ownership when language models attend to each other's internal memory, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Mine or Yours? Mind-Bridged Language Models Take Each Other's Memories as Their Own
papers.tldr: When one language model directly accesses another’s internal memory, it can mistake the partner’s private rule and code word for its own.

papers.abstract: Recent \emph{test-time training} (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient \emph{test-time adaptation} method for scientific discovery. We introduce \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by $82.8$-$84.6\%$ in FLOPs and $47.7$-$58.4\%$ in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.
authors: Yepeng Liu, Shengmai Chen, Xuandong Zhao, Chengzhi Liu, Dawn Song, Xin Eric Wang, Yuheng Bu
bullets: Motivation: Test-time training improves scientific discovery but incurs substantial computational cost from online model-weight updates.
Method: TTME continually distills experience into external memory to guide later discovery without changing model weights.
Evaluation: TTME and TTT are compared within the same discovery framework, differing only in their test-time adaptation method.
Results: TTME outperforms TTT on all five evaluated mathematical tasks while reducing FLOPs by 82.8–84.6% and runtime by 47.7–58.4%.
Scope: Findings are demonstrated in the evaluated scientific-discovery settings.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation via evolving external memory directly fits test-time learning and LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?
papers.tldr: Test-Time Memory Evolution (TTME) replaces costly online weight updates with evolving external memory and outperforms test-time training on five mathematical discovery tasks.

papers.abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reason for longer, attention to the initial visual input diminishes, weakening visual grounding. Visual memory reintroduces visual evidence during reasoning. We conduct a controlled analysis of visual memory along three axes: curation, organization, and access. We find that local evidence benefits from global context, compact latent representations balance accuracy and visual-context cost, and the utility of memory access depends on the reasoning state. Guided by these findings, we propose ReMAP (Reasoning-Time Memory-Augmented Perception), which couples two complementary latent memories: a static, question-conditioned Global memory that preserves scene and cross-image context, and a dynamic Local memory that uses this context as an anchor while selecting and re-encoding region-level evidence according to the current reasoning state. Both memories return compact latent tokens inserted into the reasoning sequence, and a reinforcement-learning access policy trained with branched rollouts decides when to continue reasoning or invoke Global or Local memory. On ten benchmark families, ReMAP outperforms prior visual-memory methods on all four multi-image benchmarks, exceeding the strongest prior results on MuirBench and MIMIC by 8.38 and 14.84 percentage points. Across four backbone families, enabling memory access improves over the same trained model with memory disabled, and on shared V*Bench, CV-Bench-2D, and MuirBench questions ReMAP reduces the visual tokens entering the reasoning sequence by 51.0-76.8% relative to the native-resolution backbone. Further analyses show that Global and Local memory form distinct yet complementary latent representations. Together, these components restore the perceptual cycle by letting the reasoning state trigger targeted visual retrieval, with the retrieved evidence guiding subsequent reasoning.
bullets: Long reasoning can diminish attention to the initial visual input, motivating visual memory during inference.
ReMAP combines a question-conditioned static Global memory with a reasoning-state-dependent dynamic Local memory.
A reinforcement-learning policy decides whether to continue reasoning or access either memory.
It outperforms prior visual-memory methods across all four multi-image benchmarks, with gains of 8.38 and 14.84 percentage points on MuirBench and MIMIC.
Memory access reduces visual tokens entering the reasoning sequence by 51.0–76.8% on shared benchmarks, while Global and Local memories provide complementary representations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ReMAP. Global memory forms a question-conditioned summary of individual images and their relations before decoding. During reasoning, a Local request uses the current state to select sources and regions, re-encodes selected pixels, and compresses them with cached Global context. Global and Local returns are inserted as continuous latent blocks after their request markers, followed by end markers before autoregressive decoding resumes.

Figure 8: Five-step training pipeline. Each row lists the inputs of one step, the updated modules (flame), the frozen components (snowflake), the objective, and the output. Steps 1–4 form Stage I, and step 5 is Stage II access learning, in which the decoder LoRA ϕ and the request interface ψ receive gradients only from Ldec and Laccess, respectively.

Figure 1: Investigating memory curation, organization, and access. (a) An interaction with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct on a MuirBench example illustrates how global context helps resolve ambiguous local evidence. (b) A comparison of frozen latents, crop pixels, and fresh latents on a random 25% subset of V*Bench examines the trade-off between accuracy and incremental GPUmemory overhead. (c) An easy recognition example and cases from V*Bench and MuirBench show how the need for memory and its invocation timing vary across queries and reasoning states.

Figure 5: Local refinement and Global–Local interaction. (a) HR-Bench-4K #0347: repeated Local calls narrow the inspection from the street scene to a speed-limit sign, yielding 30 km/h rather than 40 km/h without memory. papers.abstract: Enterprises are deploying agentic AI across the software development lifecycle, and they need the behavioral logic of the systems they act on, not stakeholder documentation. A seven-agent reverse-engineering pipeline recovered this logic, processing 241 repositories across 18 services into thousands of artifacts describing scope, journeys, rules and acceptance criteria. Recovery does not confer usability. Entities like offer, eligibility, and activation recur across services under a shared vocabulary, related in name but operationally distinct, so one end-to-end journey implicates over a thousand near-identical rules that must not be conflated. Flat vector retrieval fails, returning an identical rule from the wrong service at high similarity with no signal of error. Content-level ontology, the traditional remedy, did not exist, and relating every occurrence of recurring entities would have cost more than the engagement and not survived a release cycle. We place the ontology at the artifact level. In this machine-generated corpus, each artifact retains its producer, component, service, domain and type, provenance that disambiguates before content is read. We present a knowledge layer that organizes before retrieving: a self-describing catalog, a sparse metadata registry, and a navigation hypergraph defined over artifacts rather than extracted entities. Queries resolve to artifact identifiers that constrain vector search, so the competing rule from another service is absent rather than outranked, making disambiguation structural, not statistical. Built in under a week and admitting new services by convention, the layer serves SDLC agents, developers, quality engineers and analysts. It supported root-cause analysis and resolution of 100+ production defects with developer verification and attributed 35 release regression failures to specific rules and services.
authors: Garima Agrawal, Prasun Das, Akshay Sarvade, Priyanka L, Minisha N, Sravani Joshna, Hemath Manivannan, Lavanya Korada, Sambhrit Pattanayak, Srashti Gupta, Siddu R, Prasad Kalyanasundaram
bullets: Enterprise agents need behavioral logic from software systems, but recovered rules across services are difficult to disambiguate.
A seven-agent pipeline processed 241 repositories across 18 services into thousands of artifacts covering scopes, journeys, rules, and acceptance criteria.
The proposed layer combines a self-describing catalog, sparse metadata registry, and artifact-level navigation hypergraph.
Queries first resolve to artifact identifiers, structurally excluding similarly named rules from unrelated services before vector search.
The layer supported root-cause analysis for 100+ production defects and linked 35 release regressions to specific rules and services.

papers.abstract: LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.
bullets: Targets fragmented or conflated entities and retrieval errors caused by relying on initial similarity scores alone.
Uses cautious indexing with type-label reconciliation and tiered entity resolution.
Combines entity/triple retrieval with a bounded local graph and query-conditioned, receiver-normalized diffusion.
Preserves direct evidence while recovering missed connections through seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization.
On MemoryAgentBench, reaches 55.1 average accuracy—5.4 points above the strongest retrieval-based baseline—with sub-$0.001 mean synthesis cost on four reported columns.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech models can listen and speak at the same time, enabling natural, low-latency interaction. In counseling, however, these models often focus on the latest utterance and lose track of the seeker's underlying problem. We call this failure Stressor Blindness. We propose CounselPlex, a stressor-aware full-duplex framework that uses two operations. CounselPlex updates a short stressor state during seeker silence and injects this state into positions while listening. We also introduce RoPE Position Shift Augmentation (RPSA), which broadens positional coverage during training and improves performance at longer turn depths in our evaluation. LLM-judge evaluations show improved counseling quality and stressor grounding over strong baselines.
authors: Yeonju Kim, Bella Godiva, Yong Man Ro
bullets: Addresses “Stressor Blindness,” where models overfocus on the latest utterance and lose the underlying problem.
Updates a short stressor state during seeker silence and injects it while listening.

LLM-judge evaluations report better counseling quality and stressor grounding than strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of agents that mainly retrieve past records without forming causal understanding.
Combines stored causal knowledge with current evidence to build structured Causal Beliefs about factors and action effects.
Uses these beliefs for decisions and continuously updates both task beliefs and longer-term Causal Cognition.
Evaluations show causal knowledge accumulation and transfer across financial, scientific, and everyday tasks.
In financial research, it improves mean rank correlation by 25.4% over a baseline and raises prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic settings.

papers.abstract: Recursive large language model (LLM) agents solve long-horizon tasks through decomposition, execution, and environmental feedback. Yet after producing an atomic subtask, they often invoke the same large model again to translate a familiar instruction into an executable action. We observe that high-level planning is task-specific, whereas leaf-level action grounding recurs across tasks and can be checked against environment-admitted actions. We introduce LeafSkill, an external reuse layer that retrieves semantically related grounding experience, binds action templates to current objects and admissible actions, and uses a lightweight 1.7B selector to choose a bound action or defer the unchanged subtask to the original agent. Skills remain outside the model parameters, allowing a frozen selector to use post-training additions. Under lexical and syntactic paraphrases, exact matching retrieves none of the reference actions, while semantic retrieval preserves 96.0% and 97.0% candidate coverage; the frozen selector adopts 97.34% of unseen skill types. On an independent confirmation set of 200 Robotouille tasks, LeafSkill completes 137 tasks versus 121 for ReCAP (68.5% vs. 60.5%, exact McNemar p=.0259). On the 106 tasks completed by both, it reduces Qwen3.5-27B tokens by 14.42% and calls by 14.08%. A separate held-out repeat yields a consistent 9.0-point success gain and 18.98% token reduction. Reusable leaf grounding can thus improve task completion while reducing host-model inference without replacing high-level planning.
authors: Shen Liu, Ze Zhou, Zhenguo Xu, Shaopu Wang, Yike Gao, Chunlei Wang

On 200 Robotouille tasks, it completed 137 tasks versus 121 for ReCAP (68.5% vs. 60.5%); shared-task usage fell 14.42% in tokens and 14.08% in calls.
A held-out repeat showed a 9.0-point success gain and 18.98% token reduction.

papers.abstract: Lifelong LLM agents must learn from an expanding history of interactions while making each decision within a bounded context window. Memory makes past experience available, but the agent may still need to infer how to solve each new task from the retrieved records. Skills provide reusable procedures, yet may omit the task-specific facts needed to apply them. Because retrieved memory and skills shape the agent's behavior, they also influence the experience available for future learning. We introduce MemCryst, a framework for lifelong context adaptation through bidirectional learning of memory and skills with a frozen language model. Recurring episodes stored in memory support skill creation and revision, and the interactions guided by those skills supply new memory for subsequent learning. Facts retrieved from memory and learned skills jointly form the agent's context, while task outcomes adjust the future retrieval influence of the records actually served without rewriting their content. Across ten settings spanning embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code, MemCryst leads seven reported comparisons. On ALFWorld, joint serving achieves 63.17% success, compared with 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi0216/Memcryst.git
bullets: Addresses the challenge of using expanding interaction histories when context capacity is limited.
Uses a frozen language model with bidirectional memory–skill learning: recurring episodes create or revise skills, while skill-guided interactions generate future memories.
Combines retrieved facts and learned procedures in the agent’s context, adapting retrieval influence based on task outcomes without rewriting stored records.
Evaluated across ten settings covering embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code.
On ALFWorld, joint memory-and-skill serving reached 63.17% success, versus 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of microdramas has increased demand for high-quality script production. Long-form microdrama script generation with LLMs requires both diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence. Our observations reveal that candidate continuations increasingly concentrate on fewer narrative mechanisms as generation progresses, while conventional retrieval may reinforce trope reuse and overlook historical information essential to future plots. To address these challenges, we propose DraMaze, a multi-agent pipeline that explores diverse causal paths through trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation. It further constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize, retain, and retrieve historical memories based on future narrative goals. We also introduce MiDramaBench, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating script logic and creative quality across different script lengths, together with causal-pattern metrics for narrative repetition and diversity. Experiments show consistent improvements across three backbone LLMs. For 60-episode scripts of up to 60k words, DraMaze reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and achieves a Logic score of 82.5, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 8.5 points.
authors: Siyang He, Qiqi Wang, Fan Liu, Yuncheng Huang, Pengfei Xu, Xi Chen, Ziwei He, Xipeng Qiu
bullets: Targets the trade-off between diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence in LLM-generated microdramas.
Uses trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation to explore varied causal story paths.
Builds a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to retrieve historical information relevant to future narrative goals.
Introduces MiDramaBench and causal-pattern metrics for evaluating script logic, creativity, repetition, and diversity.
Across three backbone LLMs, it reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and reaches a Logic score of 82.5 on 60-episode scripts up to 60k words.

papers.abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.
authors: Yuval Kansal, Karen Ullrich, Polina Kirichenko, Ilia Kulikov, Niraj K. Jha, Mohammad Pezeshki, Mark Ibrahim
bullets: Addresses the limits of temporary in-context reflection and costly, interference-prone full fine-tuning.
After failure, the agent reflects, extracts a lesson, distills it into a lightweight adapter, and stores it in a retrievable lesson library.
Uses frozen base weights with adapters adding about 0.02% of the base model’s parameters each.
Across GAIA, Claw-Eval, and Terminal-Bench 2.1, success rates improve by 8.9–17.0 percentage points.
Lessons reduce repeated mistakes, nearly double correction reliability, and transfer to new tasks without additional training.

papers.abstract: Tool-calling agents are mostly optimized for accuracy; in deployment, however, their growing cost is latency: every tool call is decoded autoregressively. Speculative decoding accelerates this without changing the output, and retrieved past calls make strong drafts under real use, where each user's behavior tends to repeat. Yet existing systems keep no cross-session memory, or build the draft store once and never update it. We propose SpecMem, a tool-call memory kept alive and managed throughout deployment: verified calls are written back online into bounded per-user stores with LRU eviction, and a side-effect gate defers irreversible calls until verification confirms. On multi-session, multi-user query streams served by three open-weight models, a frozen store steadily loses acceptance while SpecMem holds it: a 27% gap in mean accepted tokens (+11% to +34% across benchmarks, tracking how much novel work arrives after the store is built) and up to 1.74x wall-clock speedup. Ablations attribute the gain almost entirely to keeping the store live; local per-user scoping adds no acceptance but closes a measured cross-user leakage channel, and gating on declared side effects, rather than on retrieval confidence, is what eliminates irreversible mistakes.
authors: Zihe Song, Wenting Zhao, Ye Liu, Yuanjie Zhu, Ke Xu, Shanghao Li, Philip S. Yu
bullets: Addresses latency from autoregressive decoding of repeated tool calls, beyond accuracy optimization.
Maintains bounded, per-user call stores online with verified write-back and LRU eviction.
Uses a side-effect gate to defer irreversible calls until speculative drafts are verified.
Across three open-weight models, it improves mean accepted tokens by 27% over frozen stores and reaches up to 1.74× wall-clock speedup.
Live memory drives nearly all gains; per-user scoping prevents measured cross-user leakage without improving acceptance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A frozen TOOLSPEC-style datastore vs. SPECMEM on a recurring call: user u checked Google’s stock the day before and now asks for Apple’s. Each arm drafts a candidate call for a draft-then-verify decoder over the fixed served model (acceptance = token longest-common-prefix). SPECMEM retrieves u’s own GOOG call, accepted up to the changed ticker (17 of 28 target tokens) with only the remainder decoded; the frozen TOOLSPEC-style store’s stale build-time entry accepts 9, the schema-only draft 7 (full-run MAT 19.96 vs. 15.70 and 5.92). Only the live store writes the verified target back, so its advantage grows across sessions.

Figure 2: Per-session MAT on the BFCL stream (3 seeds). The frozen store and SPECMEM are nearly tied at session 1; the frozen store then degrades while SPECMEM holds and the no-memory floor stays flat.

Figure 3: Per-session MAT on τ2-bench (3 domains, 3 seeds). At session 1 both stores tie near 31 MAT; the frozen TOOLSPEC/static store then degrades into a 20–25 band while SPECMEM holds at 27–32. Right: the advantage over the frozen store grows from ∼1% (session 1) to a peak of ∼37% (session 10; 34% at the final session 11) as novel per-user calls accumulate, an effect a single-session benchmark cannot expose.

papers.abstract: Scientific computing increasingly relies on large language model-based agents for performance engineering tasks such as instrumentation, analysis, and workflow porting. However, agent effectiveness depends heavily on the surrounding harness, which typically relies on manually written skills and curated memory. This limits autonomous learning, forcing agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions rather than retain and reuse knowledge from prior executions. We introduce Phronix, a capability-centric learning paradigm that enables agentic harnesses to acquire, validate, and refine reusable capabilities from their own executions. Phronix operates through a predictor-validator-corrector loop: MCP tools and associated skills propose solutions, tool executions validate them, and observed outcomes refine the stored capabilities. It distills every observed interaction into a capability store and researches a failing task rather than abandoning it. First, such learned capabilities solve a recurring task on the first attempt in 93-95% of cases across every model, significantly reducing solution non-determinism and improving reliability. Second, Phronix turns an agent's own execution into 7.6-30.8 durable capabilities per task without user instruction, and creation falls below two once the needed capability exists. Third, warm-start runs consume only 0.38-0.40 million tokens per task, which is three to four times less than a single baseline attempt, while a cold-start costs no more than the baseline. On the 1000 Genome Pegasus workflow, instrumenting a production application for I/O performance analysis, Phronix passes all 11 correctness checks against six for the baseline harness, and also lifts the task solving rates of two cheaper models from 29% and 27% of SWE-bench tasks solved to 91% and 87%, respectively, matching the performance of the most expensive evaluated model.
authors: Hariharan Devarajan, Neeraj Rajesh, Aniruddha Marathe, Nikoli Dryden, Kin Ng, Michela Taufer
bullets: Addresses the reliance on manually authored skills and curated memory, which causes agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions.
Uses a predictor–validator–corrector loop: tools and skills propose solutions, executions validate them, and outcomes refine a persistent capability store.
Learned capabilities solve recurring tasks on the first attempt in 93–95% of cases across evaluated models.
Each task produces 7.6–30.8 durable capabilities without user instruction; once capabilities exist, creation drops below two per task.
Warm-start execution uses 0.38–0.40 million tokens per task, and Phronix improves correctness and task-solving rates on evaluated workflows and models.

papers.abstract: Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.
authors: Jeanne Salle, Hardik Bhatnagar, Matthias Bethge, Sahar Abdelnabi, Maksym Andriushchenko
bullets: Context compaction is evaluated systematically in a fixed OpenCode scaffold across five strategies, three frontier models, and three long-horizon benchmarks.
For models with 1M-token contexts, changing the compaction threshold does not measurably affect performance; the smallest-context model degrades at lower thresholds on some tasks.
Default self-summarization performs best overall; more aggressive content removal can reduce some models’ performance substantially while leaving others unchanged.

Compaction summaries increasingly omit constraints: the first summary drops roughly one-third of ProgramBench anticheating rules on average, and procedural instructions are lost far more often than build specifications in real sessions.
The benchmarks are described as “compaction-friendly” because objectives and progress remain recoverable on disk; unrepeated constraints are most vulnerable.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Compaction keeps what the agent can re-read from disk and drops some of the rules it cannot. Left: overview of a ProgramBench run. The task prompt states the goal and anti-cheating rules: no copying or vendoring the reference, no internet access, and an original implementation that does not derive from or wrap the reference. At each compaction the agent replaces its context with a summary. The goal and the agent’s progress survive, because the agent can re-read its files, the rules exist only in the context, so a rule the summary discards is lost. On average, around one of the three rules is missing after the first compaction and around two after the tenth. Right: (1) for the 1M context models, task scores barely change when compaction is forced at thresholds from 160K to 380K tokens; (2) rules are dropped more often as compactions accumulate on ProgramBench, and on real user sessions from SWE-chat, compaction drops process instructions (“how to work”) and scope exclusions (“don’t touch X”) far more often than feature requirements (“what to build”).
Figure 3: Accuracy conditional on producing a valid submission by compaction method, for each benchmark (rows) and model (columns), at a fixed compaction threshold (160K).

Figure 2: The compaction threshold does not affect 1M context models; GPT-5.3-Codex performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench. Accuracy conditional on producing a valid submission as a function of the number of tokens before compaction, for each benchmark (columns) and model. All models are run at the same absolute compaction thresholds. Error bars are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over runs.

Figure 4: Compaction preferentially drops constraints about how the agent should work and what it should not do. (a) On ProgramBench, the task’s anti-cheating rules disappear from the summaries progressively over a run. (b) On real user-agent sessions, process instructions and scope exclusions are dropped much more than feature requirements.

Figure 7: Failure rate by compaction strategy. Fraction of runs in which the agent failed to produce a valid result, for ProgramBench and PostTrainBench, per model. For each task, the failure rate is the number of failures divided by the number of attempts; bars corresponds to the mean over tasks, so every task has equal weight (ProgramBench: Canop/broot and jarun/nnn; PostTrainBench: GPQA, GSM8K and BFCL, each on two base models). Error bars are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Runs were launched until enough succeeded, so the number of attempts per task differs across tasks and conditions. Pooling all attempts would weight each task by how often it was retried, and since harder tasks fail more and are rerun more, this would inflate the weight of exactly the tasks that fail most. We therefore compute each rate per task and average, so that every task contributes equally and strategies are compared on the same task mix. papers.selection_reason: Studies context compaction for LLM agents and constraint loss; relevant to agent memory and long-horizon context management.
papers.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly
papers.tldr: Current long-horizon agent benchmarks often tolerate lossy context compaction, but compaction can silently discard unrecoverable task constraints.

papers.abstract: Mobile GUI agents frequently perform repetitive tasks with similar interaction procedures. Reusing previous executions can reduce redundant LLM inference and execution overhead, but variations in user instructions and execution environments may invalidate previously successful actions. We systematically characterize these variations into six representative categories and observe that such changes do not necessarily invalidate entire procedures: individual transitions can remain reusable when validated against the current task context and interface state. Based on this insight, we propose graph-text templates for selective execution-trace reuse. The graph captures UI states and action transitions, while the text encodes task intent, procedural structure, and typed slots for variable content. A record-template-replay framework constructs templates from verified executions and leverages the current instruction and live UI state to reuse, adapt, or discard individual transitions. Given an execution trace, our framework reduces LLM inference token consumption by approximately 80% on average across five base agents on AndroidWorld, with most agents achieving at least 1.5-fold execution speedup over LLM-only execution. In real-device evaluations on Android and HarmonyOS, our framework achieves action reuse ratios of 70.7-79.8% while maintaining over 2-fold execution speedup in most evaluated configurations.
authors: Bingyu Bai, Cheng Zhang, Erhu Feng
bullets: Addresses how instruction and environment changes can invalidate previously successful GUI execution traces.
Represents reusable traces with UI-state/action graphs plus text for task intent, procedure structure, and variable slots.
Uses a record-template-replay process to validate each transition against the current instruction and live UI state.
Reduces LLM inference token consumption by about 80% on average across five agents on AndroidWorld, with most achieving at least 1.5× speedup.
Real-device tests on Android and HarmonyOS reuse 70.7–79.8% of actions while delivering over 2× speedup in most configurations.

papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought decoding is memory-bound: the KV cache of the generated tokens grows linearly with the test-time compute being spent. Evicting cache entries does not fix this, because a model never trained on a cache with entries removed generates longer, often up to the length limit. We instead train the model to compress its own output. AbridgeKV compresses each completed block of generated text into the KV entries of a few learned pause tokens. These are extra input tokens with trained embeddings that produce no output. Once the pause tokens have encoded the block, AbridgeKV frees the block's original cache; subsequent tokens attend to the pause tokens' KV entries in its place. Three novel choices make this work: the pause tokens' KV entries take positions inside the block they replace, the cache budget is allocated across layers according to the measured value of each layer's entries, and compression operates on relatively large blocks. On 446 competition problems from AIME, HMMT, AMC, BRUMO, CMIMC and SMT with 32K-token generations, keeping a quarter of the generated cache matches an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length; the strongest published evictor at a matched budget writes far longer, and the closest trained compressor, retrained on the same data, loses 10 points. Served in vLLM, the cache is 3.5x smaller per sequence and a saturated H100 finishes a problem 3.2x faster than with full KV.
bullets: Addresses the linear KV-cache growth caused by long chain-of-thought decoding.
Compresses completed text blocks into a few learned pause tokens, then frees the blocks’ original cache entries.
Uses in-block pause-token positions, layer-wise cache allocation based on entry value, and relatively large compression blocks.
On 446 competition problems with 32K-token generations, one-quarter of the generated cache matched an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length.
In vLLM, it reduced cache size 3.5× per sequence and improved saturated-H100 problem completion speed 3.2× versus full KV.

papers.selection_reason: Training learned pause tokens to compress long reasoning into a much smaller KV cache is a direct contribution to memory-efficient LLM inference and persistent memory.
papers.title: AbridgeKV: Compressing Long Reasoning into the KV Cache of Learned Pause Tokens
papers.tldr: AbridgeKV compresses long reasoning into learned pause-token KV entries, reducing cache use while preserving performance and speeding inference.

papers.abstract: Test-time language models adapt a compact memory while processing the input sequence. This perspective encompasses nonlinear fast-weight learning in LaCT, associative delta-rule updates in DeltaNet, and generalized delta-rule state updates in RWKV-7. Training these models to predict the next token does not explicitly require a fact to remain accessible after many subsequent memory updates. We study delayed supervision for this test-time memory: during post-training, ask a simulator-grounded question only after a long interval of unrelated events, and supervise its answer alongside ordinary next-token prediction. Questions are evaluated on disposable branches, so their answers never enter the continuing event stream. The construction distinguishes retention from revision: a retained fact must remain valid throughout the delay, whereas a revised fact must be answered with its latest value. We evaluate this approach on LaCT-760M and plain DeltaNet-1.3B using TextWorld training trajectories and shared BABILong and RULER evaluation panels, and include a separately reported RWKV-7 comparison. Relative to event-only training, delayed QA improves BABILong by 5.48 percentage points for LaCT and 1.32 points for DeltaNet, and single-needle RULER by 1.45 and 3.27 points, respectively. The RWKV-7 comparison reports gains of 4.60 and 7.00 points on its own panels. These results support delayed semantic supervision as a practical outer training objective for usable test-time memory, while leaving open how much of the benefit derives specifically from delay rather than general question-answering and answer-termination supervision.
bullets: Targets a gap in next-token training: facts need not remain accessible after many memory updates.
Supervises simulator-grounded QA after long delays, using disposable branches so answers do not alter the event stream.
Separately tests retention of unchanged facts and revision to a fact’s latest value.
Improves BABILong and single-needle RULER performance for LaCT and DeltaNet; a separately reported RWKV-7 comparison also shows gains.
The study does not isolate how much improvement comes from delay versus general QA and answer-termination supervision.

papers.abstract: Many LLM agents maintain external persistent memory and derive additional state from past interactions, such as summaries. Deleting an original memory record therefore need not remove information carried by its descendants. We introduce AfterDeleteBench, a controlled behavioral audit for this failure mode in fixed-weight LLM agents. For each synthetic secret, we compare an exposed-then-deleted agent with an otherwise matched agent that was never exposed to the secret, allowing post-deletion recovery to be attributed to the original exposure. In our primary setting, a single query recovers the deleted secret from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while matched never-exposed controls have zero recovery. Crucially, recovery does not require a surviving verbatim copy: when the complete secret string is absent and only separately stored components remain under a public composition rule, exact reconstruction succeeds in 62-99% of cases across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3. We also show that the response interface is part of the measurement system: target-bearing replies can be scored as failures when the requested format and parser are misaligned. Finally, we separate reconstruction from write-back and fresh-session recall. Provenance-aware closure eliminates observed recovery in the tested positive-baseline settings, whereas an exact-literal write filter blocks reinsertion but cannot erase information already present. Together, these results show that source deletion should be evaluated behaviorally at the level of the agent and its memory system, not only as a storage operation.
authors: Ehsan Saleh, Roozbeh Nahavandi, Sama Salarian, Raef Bassily, Andrew Perrault
bullets: Introduces a controlled behavioral audit comparing exposed-then-deleted agents with matched never-exposed controls.
A single query recovered deleted secrets from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while controls had zero recovery.
Exact reconstruction remained possible from separately stored components—even without a verbatim secret copy—across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3.
Evaluation depends on the response interface: parser and format mismatches can make target-bearing replies appear compliant or faulty.
Provenance-aware closure eliminated recovery in tested positive-baseline settings; write filters blocked reinsertion but could not erase existing information.

papers.abstract: The rise of Agentic AI systems has changed the landscape of artificial intelligence by enabling strong reasoning capabilities through specialized multi-agent interaction with structured self-reflection. However, in target-driven reasoning tasks, single- and multi-agent systems are often on par in terms of performance gains. A major challenge is that failures often arise from an ineffective exchange of critical information during inter-agent interaction and coordination. Different from existing multi-agent debate paradigms that rely on synchronous turn-taking and sharing information across different agents, we propose an inter-agent protocol based on shared Memory bUFFer INference - referred to as MUFFIN - in an asynchronous agentic framework. In the first step, an orchestrator routes queries based on their reasoning demands and delegates demanding ones to a multi-agent setting, where a shared memory buffer provides asynchronous exchange of intermediate findings while an agent's private reasoning remains local. Our experiments show that our framework Muffin outperforms established competitors, achieving the best accuracy in 17 out of 20 of our benchmark settings, and provides a better quality-cost trade-off than multi-agent debate: Muffin improves accuracy by 19.2 accuracy points while using 77.4% fewer tokens, without requiring full-trace sharing.

papers.abstract: Memory enables language agents to carry useful distinctions from past experience into future decisions. Its value depends on which distinctions survive, whether a bounded agent can use them, and what can be recovered or revised as demands evolve. We develop a decision-theoretic framework that follows this value from raw history through persistent state, operational use, and costly recovery and revision. Original and retained value are expressed in units of avoided task loss; risk-cost frontiers describe attainable recovery and preservation across uses. Unknown demand yields value profiles, while interactive feedback changes the distribution of future work. A cost-aware simulation condition and five minimal counterexamples expose the roles of information timing, retrieval access, component interaction, feedback and demand uncertainty. In particular, a pointer with zero mutual information about the answer can still reduce the cost of exact recovery. Diagnostics on LoCoMo, a two-project update task and longitudinal cases exhibit failures of preservation, use and measurement. At fixed retrieved evidence, a saved ledger changes subsequent answers; at fixed agent outputs, an evaluator revision changes scores. The framework connects these distinctions to operational risk bounds and testable principles for allocating memory, preserving recovery options and revising evidence dependencies.
authors: Zehao Lin, Erenkai Zhu, Helan Hu, Xixuan Hao, Chunyu Li, Kai Chen
bullets: Models memory value from raw history through persistent state, operational use, and costly recovery or revision.

Shows that even a pointer with no mutual information about an answer can lower the cost of exact recovery.
Uses simulations, five counterexamples, and diagnostics across multiple longitudinal tasks to reveal failures in preservation, use, and measurement.
Connects the framework to operational risk bounds and principles for allocating memory and preserving revision options.

papers.abstract: Memory enables language model assistants to maintain continuity across sessions and generate personalized responses, but knowing more about a user does not necessarily produce responses they prefer. Existing evaluations assess memory capabilities without directly establishing whether memory use benefits the user. To study this gap, we collect approximately 1,000 pairwise judgments from 87 participants using their own ChatGPT queries and personal memories. We find that memory-conditioned responses are not consistently preferred over responses generated without memory and in some cases, users strongly prefer the latter. Automatic evaluators also show limited agreement with users and favor memory-conditioned responses substantially more often than users do. Motivated by these gaps, we introduce a memory-aware reward model that learns from user judgments, achieving 72.8\% preference prediction accuracy and outperforming the existing baselines. Our findings motivate evaluation and optimization objectives that align memory use with the preferences of the people whose information is being used.
authors: Yijiang River Dong, Zexue He, Cheng Yu, Tiancheng Hu, Michael J Ryan, Jan Batzner, Zheng Hui, Shaolong Wu, Orestis Papakyriakopoulos, Alex Pentland, Nigel Collier, Jiaxin Pei
bullets: Collected about 1,000 pairwise judgments from 87 participants using personal queries and memories.
Users sometimes strongly preferred responses generated without memory.
Automatic evaluators often favored memory-conditioned responses more than users did and showed limited agreement.
Introduced a memory-aware reward model trained on user preferences, reaching 72.8% preference-prediction accuracy and outperforming existing baselines.
The study supports aligning memory use with individual user preferences rather than assuming more memory is better.

papers.abstract: Our previous analysis found that a model's native hashed N-gram table is where continual updates disturb the base least, but its writes needed backpropagation and changed the pretrained table. We present Delta N-gram, a forward-only write path into that table. The pretrained table T^0 is never modified. Evidence is written into a sparse patch \Delta on the rows it addresses: a 4.1M-parameter writer emits a target and a gate per (position, hash head) event, and a block-averaged delta rule keeps each row a convex combination of its old value and the gated targets. The writer is trained offline on raw text with the pretraining objective; at use time writing takes forward passes only, and clearing \Delta restores the original model. A 0.6B prototype trained to answer questions keeps 16/16 facts after a second write; online gradient writes keep 2--4/16. We study two writers: a plain writer that encodes evidence with the T^0-only model, and a delta writer that reads its current memory while encoding. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the plain writer's memory is document-specific: on 64 held-out news events it lowers continuation NLL by 0.068 nats/token against empty memory and by 0.024 against another document's memory, and 0.063 and 0.013 after 16 intervening articles. The delta writer's memory is more document-specific and keeps more of it under distraction (70% vs 54%). Over 35,000 writes on our previous seven-task chain both writers stay stable and the delta writer drifts less (layer-2 math drift 176% vs 188%); later accuracy changes by -0.26/-0.52pp (-7.29pp for gradient updates) and small-k_i drift is 17.9/17.5% (39.2%). Acquisition is negative, and general-input drift reaches 32.8% (20.75%): format rows read by every example grow to 4--12 times their pretrained norm. Zeroing eight such rows removes over 98% of layer-2 drift on math inputs, together with their NLL gain.
bullets: Writes target and gated values into a sparse patch Δ while leaving the pretrained table unchanged; clearing Δ restores the original model.
A 4.1M-parameter writer is trained offline with the pretraining objective, so inference-time memory updates require only forward passes.
In a 0.6B prototype, it retained all 16/16 facts after a second write, compared with 2–4/16 for online gradient writes.
The learned memory is document-specific and remains more robust under distraction, with the delta writer retaining 70% versus 54% for the plain writer.
Across 35,000 writes, stability was substantially better than gradient updates, but frequent format rows accumulated large drift; zeroing eight rows removed over 98% of layer-2 math drift.

papers.abstract: Chunking strategies for retrieval-augmented generation are almost always evaluated on a static snapshot, yet the documents underlying a knowledge base continue to change. Because chunks are embedded independently, a boundary that moves after an edit forces unchanged text to be re-embedded. We measure this update cost on 120 pairs of adjacent Chinese and English Wikipedia revisions for three stateless chunkers (non-overlapping fixed-size, recursive paragraph-first, and content-defined chunking) under a strict byte-identical reuse rule and a frozen dense encoder. On the 116-article common-success pool, with frozen, length-calibrated parameters, fixed-size chunking recomputes 57-68% of its full new-version embedding-input workload, recursive chunking 38-56%, and content-defined chunking 43-54% (it failed on 4 of 62 Chinese articles), while at these parameters mean evidence recall under a fixed 2048-token retrieval budget differs by less than two percentage points within either language. A cost-only parameter grid shows that the ranking of the two content-aware chunkers changes with chunk-length settings, whereas non-overlapping fixed-size chunking has the highest recomputation cost in every length-matched condition. Controlled edits and a verbatim-presence diagnostic support boundary drift as one contributor to recomputation of text already present in the previous version. Update cost is therefore a substantial, parameter-sensitive dimension that static retrieval evaluations do not expose and that should be reported alongside retrieval quality.
authors: Yuning Bian, Lele Xu, Yifan Yuan, Xinyu Yin, Chengyan Zhan
bullets: Evaluates fixed-size, recursive paragraph-first, and content-defined chunking on 120 adjacent Chinese and English Wikipedia revisions.
Under strict byte-identical reuse, fixed-size chunking recomputes the most workload; recursive and content-defined chunking generally recompute less.
Mean evidence recall differs by less than two percentage points between methods within each language at the evaluated settings.
The relative cost of the two content-aware methods changes with chunk-length parameters, showing update cost is parameter-sensitive.
Controlled edits support boundary drift as a cause of re-embedding unchanged text; content-defined chunking failed on 4 of 62 Chinese articles.

papers.abstract: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.

papers.abstract: LLM memory is widely used in long-term conversation understanding. Agentic memory systems often use mutation, structural organization, learned retrieval strategies, or other complex operations. Is this complexity always necessary? We study Raw-RAG, a naive RAG baseline using dense retrieval and reranking over raw history to supply evidence to a reader LLM. Across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MEME, and MemoryAgentBench, Raw-RAG ranks first among the compared memory systems in six of seven benchmark-model settings, outperforming the strongest compared agentic memory system by 0.13-5.53 points. We investigate why raw-history retrieval remains competitive. Evidence analysis shows that its higher coverage of necessary evidence can offset lower utilization. Useful evidence includes both answer values and the relations and dependency paths needed to derive them. Even complete access to transformed memory stores leaves an accuracy gap relative to raw evidence, highlighting the importance of preserving raw information. These findings challenge the necessity of complex agentic memory for the evaluated conversation tasks and establish naive RAG as an essential baseline.
authors: Zhengye Bao, Shengtao Zhang, Haokai Zhang, Shiqi Lou, Muning Wen, Minnan Luo
bullets: Evaluates Raw-RAG, which uses dense retrieval and reranking over unmodified conversation history for an LLM reader.

It outperforms the strongest compared agentic memory system by 0.13–5.53 points.
Higher coverage of necessary evidence—including answer values, relations, and dependency paths—can offset weaker evidence utilization.
The findings support preserving raw information and treating naive RAG as an essential baseline for evaluated conversation tasks.

papers.abstract: An LLM agent can retrieve a memory correctly yet use it incorrectly after its validity state changes. We study governance-state corruption: faults that alter which retained records enter model-visible context while stored content and tasks remain fixed. Across six providers, 731 benchmark-grounded bases yield 2,080 matched fault pairs. In offline control-plane checks, corruption changes the operative projection in 96.25% of pairs, while oracle-backed enforcement restores it in 100%. For downstream evaluation, a deterministically selected, non-probability LongMemEval/Memora panel resolves 298 of 300 matched triplets (238 distinct bases). Clean-minus-corrupted contrasts are 40.54 percentage points in LongMemEval binary correctness (95% base-cluster interval [30.32, 50.71]) and 30.60 points in rescaled Memora FAMA ([23.31, 37.69]); both sources also show recovery. OAKS Novel native option parity holds for all 6,714 resolved outputs. Full-cohort frozen-scorer corruption/recovery effects (-27.55/+27.51 points) remain descriptive proxies, not validated native semantic population effects. These bounded findings motivate evaluating memory control-state integrity alongside retrieval accuracy.
authors: Bowen Liu, Youting Wang, Bonan Shen, Dingyan Shang
bullets: Studies faults that change which stored records enter model-visible context without changing memory content or tasks.
Across six providers and 2,080 matched fault pairs, corruption altered the operative projection in 96.25% of cases; enforcement restored it in 100%.
Downstream clean-versus-corrupted gaps were 40.54 points on LongMemEval binary correctness and 30.60 points on rescaled Memora FAMA, with recovery observed.
OAKS Novel native option parity held for all 6,714 resolved outputs.
Full-cohort frozen-scorer effects are descriptive proxies, not validated native semantic population effects.

papers.abstract: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences. We introduce MemPABench, an interactive environment for on-policy evaluation of memory in personal agents. MemPABench poses long-horizon tasks requiring agents to decide when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously. Four grounded simulated users hold 14 preferences across work and personal contexts. Their feedback spans 99 sessions over four months, with five event-driven changes per user testing memory updates. We evaluate preference selection, delivered behavior, and sensitivity to context and preference change. Evaluating four memory systems across four LLM backbones, we find that current memory brings limited gains in preference selection. Retrieval-based systems (i.e. Mem0, MemOS, simple RAG) do not outperform No Memory, while File-based memory improves accuracy but applies preferences beyond relevant contexts. Our analysis shows that current memory struggles to retrieve interaction preferences and adapt to preference changes. Even with the correct preference available, overriding the agent's default interaction habits remains challenging. The environment and dataset are available at https://mempabench.com.
authors: Jialin Li, Zhenhao Chen, Hanjun Luo, Hanan Salam
bullets: Benchmarks decisions about when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously—not just factual recall.
Uses four simulated users with 14 work and personal preferences across 99 sessions and five preference changes per user.
Evaluates preference selection, behavioral execution, contextual sensitivity, and adaptation to changes across four memory systems and four LLM backbones.
Retrieval-based memory systems do not outperform No Memory, while file-based memory improves accuracy but often applies preferences outside their relevant contexts.
Agents struggle to retrieve interaction preferences, adapt to changes, and override default interaction habits even when the correct preference is available.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.
authors: Yufeng Li, Zaijing Li, Fuchen Zhang, Zongzong Wu, Ming Zhao, Fengxiao Tang
bullets: Addresses semantic loss from converting text into discrete graph symbols and modality mismatch between graphs and LLM-pretrained text.

Applies Energy-Driven Pathfinding to identify query-relevant subgraphs and deterministically linearize them into textual evidence paths.
Outperforms strong baselines across three multi-hop QA benchmarks, including 14.4% EM improvement on HotpotQA and 5.8% on 2WikiMultihop.
Reduces token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline; evaluation focuses on multi-hop QA benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives; coding agents keep the raw history and let the model search it with its own tools. We ask whether designed memory still helps once the model is strong enough to search for itself. On one LoCoMo conversation (419 turns, 152 questions), we run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code), each with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5, and record what every rollout costs. This is a short empirical study, with one conversation and one run per cell. Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model: Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than a whole full-context rollout. Agent memory also has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it: a stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out. With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the cost-accuracy frontier, scoring 99% for less than half the cost of full context; its one miss is a wrong answer key. Part of that lead comes from photo captions that only the agents could read: on the 88 questions whose evidence has no photo, Pi and full context differ by one answer.
bullets: Evaluates full context, BM25, Mem0, and Zep across three coding agents and three language models on one 419-turn conversation with 152 questions.
Mem0 improves over full context only for GPT-4o-mini, while constructing its memory costs more than a full-context rollout.
Memory quality is limited by the model that writes it; a stronger reader cannot recover information omitted by a weaker writer.
With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi achieves 99% accuracy for under half the cost of full context.
The study uses one conversation and one run per experimental cell; Pi’s advantage partly comes from reading photo captions unavailable to other methods.
