papers.abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.
authors: Ido Levy, Segev Shlomov, Leshem Choshen
bullets: Introduces LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled, compositional RAG evaluation.
Evaluates 450 pipeline configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora from 5K to 200K documents.
Three individually strong retrieval techniques predicted a 47% combined gain but achieved only 17% together.
Design choices that improve retrieval may reduce answer faithfulness, showing the objectives can diverge.
The best component combination changes with corpus scale, limiting conclusions from small-corpus tests.

papers.abstract: Long-term agent memory is shifting from predefined workflows toward learnable policies for memory construction and retrieval. Existing learning-based methods either optimize construction alone or combine retrieval-side online reinforcement learning (RL) with offline construction supervision, limiting co-adaptation between the two stages. In this paper, we explore end-to-end online RL for a unified memory manager (Uni-Mem) that learns both capabilities under a shared policy. However, joint optimization with existing RL algorithms such as GRPO faces confounded group comparisons and sparse feedback over long memory-management trajectories. To this end, we propose Stage-Decoupled GRPO, which alternates construction and retrieval optimization while controlling variation from the other stage within each rollout group, yielding stage-specific learning signals. We further introduce Event-Wise Credit Assignment (ECA), which localizes feedback to responsible events and propagates event-level advantages to their constituent operations. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show that Uni-Mem outperforms the strongest RL-based memory, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly learning memory construction and retrieval via Stage-Decoupled GRPO and ECA.
authors: Zhiqian Xia, Jielong Tang, Ling-An Zeng, Shixiong Kai, Rong Yao, Hao Kong, Xiao Dong, Wei Wang, Mingxuan Yuan, Siyu Xia, Haifeng Xia
bullets: Existing methods typically optimize memory construction or combine offline construction supervision with online retrieval learning, limiting co-adaptation.
Uni-Mem uses a shared policy to learn construction and retrieval end to end with online RL.
Stage-Decoupled GRPO alternates optimization stages while controlling cross-stage variation to produce clearer learning signals.
Event-Wise Credit Assignment assigns feedback to responsible events and their constituent operations.
On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, Uni-Mem outperforms the strongest RL-based memory method reported.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user's state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two-threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2 show consistent state-of-the-art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non-stationary belief drift without over-reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.
authors: Jian Zhong, Zeyu Liu, Pingchuan Cao, Rongduo Han, Shunye Tang, Guohuan Xie, Mingyuan Qin, Ran Ji, Xiao Liang, Wei Wang, Haining Zhang
bullets: Represents user memory as confidence-weighted beliefs rather than simple append-or-overwrite entries.
Uses Effective Surprisal, combining semantic deviation and contradiction evidence while discounting unreliable retrieval.
Applies a two-threshold gate with three updates: MAINTAIN, PROFILE, and CORRECT.
PROFILE serves as a low-confidence waiting room for ambiguous or potentially noisy evidence.
Reports consistent state-of-the-art accuracy on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2; DiMoBench evaluates adaptation to belief drift.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
authors: Hong Ting Tsang, Boyi Zhang, Haoyu Huang, Jiaxin Bai, Yufei Li, Yisen Gao, Zhongwei Xie, Hongyu Luo, Jeff Z. Pan, Yangqiu Song
bullets: Evaluates 923 questions across persona-grounded histories spanning 11–24 sessions and four modalities.
Targets meaningful spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media.
Uses matched controls to isolate failures in representation, retrieval, delivery, and reading.
Finds modality-dependent representation loss, substantial residual reading errors even with gold evidence, and weak abstention.
Moves evaluation beyond a single leaderboard score toward component-level diagnosis.

papers.abstract: Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $\tau^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.
authors: Tanqiu Jiang, Min Bai, Sadat Shahriar, Wanyu Du, Sandesh Swamy
bullets: Addresses memory injection and poisoning, which hinder safe memory sharing among agents.
Allows agents to retain multi-turn planning and tool choice while mediating environment-derived values.
Proves and machine-checks two Lean 4 integrity theorems under the assumption that only user inputs and gate-confirmed values are trusted.

Reports zero observed attack success on Trojan Hippo with self-verification and lightweight verifiers; up to 90 agents built shared knowledge bases without directly promoting injected memories on τ²-bench.
Community endorsements reduce verification burden and, under stated assumptions, lower both poison promotion and benign-knowledge eviction risks as communities grow.

papers.abstract: Scanning every passage in a long document seems thorough, but does it preserve more useful evidence or produce better answers? We compare 11 retrieval configurations spanning lexical and dense search, hybrid reranking, and full-document scanning with Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and Cloudflare Clef. Our evaluation uses 396 QASPER questions and 80 questions from eight complete textbooks, with common passages, a five-passage limit, and a fixed answer generator. On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), compared with 88.7% for Jev full scan and 81.3\% for OpenAI dense retrieval. Full scans examine every passage initially, yet later reduction steps can discard relevant evidence. Higher evidence coverage also does not consistently produce better answers: Hybrid + Decisions achieves the highest observed book Answer Accuracy among retrieval methods (0.892), despite recovering less reference evidence. Full scanning incurs substantially higher latency on books under the tested deployments, while reusable dense retrieval has lower projected API cost than paid decision-based methods as queries accumulate. Most QASPER articles already fit within the hybrid candidate pool, limiting the benefit of scanning. These results highlight evidence retention, answer quality, and reuse cost as complementary criteria for choosing a long-document retrieval strategy.
authors: Juan Terven, Diana-Margarita C\'ordova-Esparza, Julio-Alejandro Romero-Gonz\'alez, Edgar Chavez-Urbiola, Juan Irving Vasquez, Julian Andres Ramirez-Bautista, Silvia L. Chaparro-C\'ardenas, Gendry Alfonso-Francia
bullets: Compares 11 lexical, dense, hybrid, and full-document retrieval configurations across QASPER articles and textbook questions.
On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), exceeding Jev full scanning (88.7%).

papers.selection_reason: Compares retrieval configurations for long-document RAG, directly relevant to external memory and retrieval for LLMs.
papers.title: Scan or Index? large Evidence Coverage, Answer Quality, and Cost in Long-Document RAG
papers.tldr: For long-document RAG, hybrid retrieval can retain more useful evidence than full scanning while delivering better latency and reuse economics, though evidence coverage does not guarantee answer quality.

papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.
authors: Pedro H. Barcha Correia, Matheus Azevedo de S\'a, Paulo H. Gomes de Senna, Giovanni Mandel Martignago, Victor Takashi Hayashi, Charles Christian Miers, Marcos A. Simplicio Jr
bullets: Introduces a general threat model for memory injection in LLM-as-a-service platforms.
Shows that all evaluated services—ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash—can collectively achieve all NIST attack goals under this model.
Identifies attack vectors spanning personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and MCP-connected resources.
Finds persistent manipulation in fresh sessions, including disinformation, harmful content, and simulated unresponsiveness; Claude also enables organizational spread and prompt exfiltration.
Reports that nearly half of the proposed mitigations are not implemented across the evaluated services.

papers.selection_reason: Studies persistent memory vulnerabilities in LLM services; directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
papers.tldr: Persistent memory turns prompt injection from a session-limited attack into a cross-session compromise that can spread harmful behavior and misinformation across users and connected resources.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by directly retrieval without any adaptation for the current task, while the retrieved memory may contain much history noises waiting to be preprocessed. In contrast, MAS characterized by task-specific guidance often lack long-term memory specifically designed for the guidance. To address these challenges, we propose M-Plan, a closed-loop MAS framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory. By combining global-local and past-current guidance, M-Plan enhances agents' performance on multi-turn tasks while maintaining a plug-and-play design. During task execution, agents receive task-specific milestones and insights, and are provided with local hints only when confusion arises, which form global-local guidance together. These guidance generation and utilization construct the short-term memory as well. After task completion, relevant information about the current task is optimized or reorganized before being sent to the long-term memory storage for future retrieval. The designments mentioned above build a comprehensive framework different from other individual long-term or short-term memory works. Extensive experiments on multi-turn tasks including ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models demonstrate that M-Plan outperforms multiple baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency.
bullets: Targets LLM agents’ difficulty with continuous reasoning and long contexts in multi-turn, long-horizon tasks.
Uses global-local guidance: task milestones and insights provide global direction, while local hints appear when agents become confused.
Builds short-term memory from guidance and reorganizes relevant task information before storing it in long-term memory.
Evaluated on ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models, where it reportedly improves accuracy and efficiency over multiple baselines.
Its plug-and-play design integrates memory arrangement with task-specific guidance rather than relying on direct retrieval alone.

papers.selection_reason: LLM-agent framework combining long-term and short-term memory for long-horizon tasks; relevant to agent memory.
papers.title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement
papers.tldr: M-Plan is a closed-loop multi-agent framework that combines organized long- and short-term memory with task-specific guidance to improve LLM agents’ long-horizon task performance.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. We propose SPEM, a lightweight structure-aware procedural memory framework for efficient skill use in LLM-based agents. SPEM maintains Atomic Skill Memory for individual skills and Skill-DAG Memory for reusable compositions derived from successful executions. For a new task, SPEM reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates when available. Otherwise, it retrieves atomic skills and invokes Skill-GNN for state- and structure-aware skill selection. Successful executions are written back as new Skill-DAGs, allowing procedural memory to accumulate over time. Experiments on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show that SPEM achieves the best overall effectiveness--efficiency trade-off, reaching 87.1% ALFWorld success and 38.38% SkillsBench reward while reducing token and runtime costs against strong baselines.
bullets: Addresses the overhead and inaccuracy of loading or retrieving skills from large, flat libraries.
Stores individual skills in Atomic Skill Memory and reusable successful compositions as Skill-DAGs.
Reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates or applies Skill-GNN for structure-aware skill selection.
Learns over time by writing successful executions back into procedural memory.
On ALFWorld and SkillsBench, reports 87.1% success and 38.38% reward while reducing token and runtime costs versus strong baselines.

Figure 2: Overview of trajectory-DAG extraction. Successful trajectories are converted into execution graphs, from which necessary steps are identified through backward slicing, pruning, and dependency repair. The resulting backbones are stored as reusable Skill-DAG templates for future tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Structured procedural memory for LLM-agent skill reuse; fits LLM and agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: SPEM improves LLM-agent skill reuse by combining structured procedural memory with state- and dependency-aware skill selection, reducing resource costs while maintaining strong task performance.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
bullets: Controlled results across 22 benchmarks show that merely increasing inference-time reasoning yields modest gains.
A capability layer standardizes tool access and renders tool outputs as model-readable evidence.
Persistent memory stores images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts across reasoning steps.
A coding interface enables computations that combine outputs from multiple tools.

Across eight open and proprietary backbones, it improves average scores by 9.7–12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, with substantially lower token cost than maximum-effort alternatives in one comparison.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of OpenVLHarness. The MLLM orchestrator invokes capabilities through typed interfaces. Persistent multimodal memory retains image artifacts, structured data, and web references under reusable handles. An Environment Update advertises the available artifacts to the orchestrator, allowing subsequent calls to reuse earlier evidence, including through memory-grounded computation.

Figure 9: Object-count distribution across counting benchmarks. Each bar shows the percentage of samples falling into binned object-count buckets, with the per-dataset maximum count annotated above. Widely used benchmarks such as TallyQA, CountBenchQA, and PixmoCount are dominated by low counts: nearly all of their samples contain ten or fewer objects (and a majority of TallyQA fall in the 0–1 bucket), capping at 10–15. Only FSC-147 and FSCD-LVIS contain substantial mass in the high-count regime (> 50 objects), reaching into the hundreds or thousands. This skew means accuracy on standard counting benchmarks largely reflects performance on small object counts and reveals little about high-count visual measurement.

Figure 10: Object-count distribution across grounding benchmarks. Each bar shows the percentage of samples falling into binned object-count buckets, with the per-dataset maximum count annotated above. Referring-expression benchmarks such as RefCOCO/+/g and Ref-L4/GroundingME ground a single target per sample (100% in the 0–1 bucket, max = 1), and even detection-style sets like OdinW-13 (97%) and LVIS (86%) are overwhelmingly concentrated at one object per image. Only the FSCD variants exercise dense, many-object grounding. As with counting, this distribution implies that progress on common grounding benchmarks is measured almost entirely in the singleor few-object regime.

papers.abstract: Large language models are expected to estimate their own uncertainty, with confidence signals used to guide retrieval, adaptive compute allocation, routing, and selective abstention. We investigate whether confidence signals measured at different temporal stages of problem solving encode distinct forms of epistemic information and remain reliable beyond English-centric settings. Inspired by classical meta-memory theory, we distinguish anticipatory pre-solve confidence (Feeling-of-Knowing, FOK) from retrospective post-solve confidence (Judgement-of-Learning, JOL). We evaluate these signals across two frontier LLMs, multiple reasoning domains, translated Marathi benchmarks, and a newly constructed benchmark of genuinely local Marathi factual questions. Across settings, the cheaper pre-solve signal remains weakly calibrated, while post-solve confidence generally provides stronger epistemic alignment despite its additional inference cost. Confidence behaviour transfers surprisingly well under direct language translation, with calibration trends largely preserved between English and Marathi, but degrades substantially on local Marathi knowledge, suggesting that linguistic transfer alone is insufficient for region-specific information needs. Finally, hallucinated responses maintain persistently elevated confidence after answer generation, highlighting important limitations of current LLM self-assessment mechanisms.
bullets: Studies confidence signals at two reasoning stages: pre-solve Feeling-of-Knowing (FOK) and post-solve Judgement-of-Learning (JOL).
Evaluates two frontier LLMs across reasoning domains, translated Marathi benchmarks, and locally sourced Marathi factual questions.
FOK is weakly calibrated, while JOL usually shows stronger alignment with epistemic correctness despite higher inference cost.
Calibration trends transfer well between English and translated Marathi, but degrade substantially for genuinely local Marathi knowledge.
Hallucinated answers retain elevated confidence after generation, exposing limitations in current self-assessment.

papers.abstract: LLM agents have become capable kernel engineers on mainstream GPU stacks, but they struggle on emerging accelerators such as Ascend NPUs, whose programming model is barely represented in pretraining data. Recent NPU agents address this gap largely through experience: they accumulate memory from their own generation and optimization trials and reuse it on later tasks. We argue that experience alone is not enough for kernel generation. An agent can only remember what it has tried, and it rarely tries a mechanism it does not know. As a result, such memory offers little help when a new operator calls for a different mechanism, and even familiar operators raise unseen situations as optimization proceeds. We present ASCENDEVOLVE, which grounds every step of an evolutionary kernel search in a large external knowledge base built from platform documentation, toolkit headers, and operator repositories. Because this corpus far exceeds any context window, ASCENDEVOLVE indexes it and routes each agent to a small, task-specific slice of evidence instead of the corpus itself. The retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementation strategies, guides repair when a candidate fails, and constrains how strong candidates are recombined. On 53 Ascend C operators from CANN-Bench spanning four difficulty levels, ASCENDEVOLVE achieves an overall score of 71.39, improving over Reflexion and OpenEvolve by 11.6% and 17.2%.
authors: Xi Chen, Ming Shen, Haotian Yan, Ruoyu Sun, Tianjun Yao
bullets: Experience-based NPU agents may miss unfamiliar implementation mechanisms and optimization situations.

Retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementations, supports candidate repair, and constrains recombination of strong kernels.
Evaluated on 53 Ascend C operators across four difficulty levels, it achieves an overall score of 71.39.
It improves over Reflexion and OpenEvolve by 11.6% and 17.2%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech agents must update persistent memory while listening and speaking, yet it remains unclear which events should be stored, revised, or excluded. Existing benchmarks isolate interaction timing from memory outcomes, obscuring the state transitions behind a correct answer. We introduce DuplexLedger, a bilingual benchmark of 1,094 persistent sessions aligning four full-duplex scenarios with event-level Write/Update/Ignore/Retain supervision, explicit pre/post memory states, and 6,564 same-session questions and checks. Evaluating five full-duplex models reveals an interaction-memory gap: no system combines strong boundary control with coherent final-state memory, and the best final-state fact coverage is 2.01%. We propose ACT-Mem, an 8.92M-parameter sidecar comprising an event controller, a versioned transactional ledger, and a typed retriever coupled with a frozen MiniCPM-o 4.5 backbone. On 219 held-out sessions, ACT-Mem increases latest-value accuracy from 4.11% to 8.68% while reducing stale assertions and distractor adoption. It improves interaction boundaries but slows interruption stopping. These results motivate selective, auditable full-duplex memory rather than indiscriminate transcript retention. Code is available at https://github.com/lyx-researcher/DuplexLedger.

papers.abstract: Code agents increasingly work on evolving real repositories, and memory systems aim to help them reuse earlier experience. However, such experience is diverse and evolving, so it remains unclear how memory systems organize it and thereby affect code agents. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this reliably because they lack either temporally valid histories or control over prior-task relevance. In this paper, we present MemDev-Bench to evaluate how memory systems affect code agents over diverse repository histories. It pairs each task with relevance-annotated earlier tasks from the same repository to build histories with controlled relevance. We also build an automated pipeline that reliably makes these earlier tasks executable and verifiable, producing 4,869 historical tasks for 555 base tasks. Based on MemDev-Bench, our systematic evaluation of memory systems across diverse development scenarios yields three main findings. (1) Memory mainly improves fine-grained localization and editing, increasing functional correctness. (2) Memory also causes failures on otherwise solvable tasks even with related history, and unrelated history tends to increase such failures. These failures mainly stem from agents reusing memory without reassessing its applicability. (3) Compared with using memory systems, directly providing agents with raw historical trajectories substantially reduces their steps. Further analysis suggests that agents save these steps by reusing process information that compressed memories tend to omit. These results suggest that future memory systems should preserve process information and reassess memory applicability against current task context.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.
authors: Ruhan Wang, Kishan Panaganti, Dongruo Zhou
bullets: LLM agents can self-improve by storing execution experience without changing model parameters.
Stored rules, summaries, and skills enable strategy reuse but may propagate errors through retrieval and reuse.
The paper identifies “error reproduction,” where faulty abstractions influence executions that generate further faulty abstractions.
Anti-Persistence stores trajectories and outcomes but synthesizes task-specific guidance only when needed, discarding it afterward.
Across benchmarks and backbones, it achieves the highest overall held-out success and lowest average LLM-call cost among evaluated memory designs.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now autonomously complete long-horizon tasks, such as repository-level coding, through hundreds of think-act steps, yet the experience each run produces is rarely reused on the next. Prior memory systems concentrate on retrieval, finding the most relevant past trajectory. Retrieval cannot observe the running agent, so it cannot decide whether the agent needs an experience, at which point, or for how long. We introduce REM (Reusable Experience Memory), a framework that manages the memory lifecycle from inside the agent's think-act loop through three explicit decisions. What to store: each completed trajectory is consolidated into a phase-structured document, two orders of magnitude smaller than the trajectory. When to recall: the document is injected at the start of the task; the costlier implementation record is withheld until an in-loop gate detects the agent struggling. What to forget: the record is evicted after a single exposure. On repository-level bug fixing (SWE-ContextBench Lite), REM retrieves the related trajectory more accurately than every state-of-the-art memory system (68.7% vs. 55.6% match@1) and improves, in every replicate, end-task resolution (27.6% vs. 24.9%) at 17% lower cost. Injecting the same experience as a summary or raw trajectory, even when oracle-retrieved, does not. Ablating any of the three decisions reduces resolution. Altogether, these results demonstrate that the bottleneck in experience reuse is not retrieval fidelity but how experience is stored and governed across its lifecycle, opening a control-theoretic perspective on agent memory.
authors: Xinyi Lisa Chen, Pedro Herrero-Vidal, Xiaohan Chen, Xiaojing Yu, Cris Liu, Bingqing Song, Bin Xu, Suleiman A. Khan, You-Lin Chen
bullets: Targets the failure of retrieval-only memory systems, which cannot observe when an agent needs past experience or how long it should retain it.
Consolidates completed trajectories into compact, phase-structured documents; exposes detailed implementation records only when an in-loop gate detects difficulty.
Evicts implementation records after one exposure to prevent unnecessary persistence.
On SWE-ContextBench Lite, REM achieves 68.7% match@1 retrieval accuracy and 27.6% end-task resolution, at 17% lower cost than the comparison system.
Ablations and oracle-retrieved summary/raw-trajectory variants show that lifecycle governance—not retrieval alone—is critical to effective reuse.

papers.abstract: Checking whether a text complies with a body of law is slow when done by hand and fragile when done with keyword rules. This paper presents ComplianceAgent, the legal compliance sub-agent of COMPASS, a multi-agent framework that evaluates texts along four axes: digital sovereignty, carbon impact, compliance, and ethics. The agent relies on a large language model that scores a text on a fixed rubric, grounds its judgment in a reference legal corpus, and, when the score falls at or below a critical threshold, runs a corrective chain made of self-healing rewrites, a compliance label, an explainability report, and escalation to a human reviewer. We describe what the language model does at each step, how the memory of the agent is organized, and how the same implementation can be pointed at different reference corpora. We evaluate the agent in a Canadian and Quebec context, on a corpus of thirteen legal instruments that brings together federal and provincial texts, international treaties, and municipal documents of the City of Trois-Rivi\`eres. The evaluation relies on a hand-annotated gold standard of fifteen texts and combines classification metrics, a repeated-query stability test, retrieval precision, and a composite score. On this gold standard the agent separates every conforming text from every non-conforming one, its scores remain stable under repeated queries, and the index returns relevant passages.
bullets: Addresses the slowness and fragility of manual and keyword-based legal compliance checks.
Scores texts against a fixed rubric grounded in a configurable reference legal corpus.
Triggers self-healing rewrites, compliance labels, explainability reports, and human escalation for critically low scores.
Evaluated on 13 legal instruments and 15 hand-annotated texts using classification, stability, retrieval, and composite metrics.
Separated all conforming from non-conforming texts in the evaluation, with stable repeated-query scores and relevant retrieval results.

papers.abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.
authors: Tao Jiang, Benjamin Navet, Yousouf Taghzouti, Fabien Gandon, Louis-F\'elix Nothias, \'Elise Dumont
bullets: Integrates computational protocols, lab notebooks, and chat logs across docking, molecular dynamics, and quantum chemistry.
Uses three memory tiers: session observations, project-level learnings, and human-validated cross-project rules.
Demonstrated across four chemistry case studies, tracking 317 runs and producing 116 project-tier entries and four promoted rules.
In controlled replays, memory-enabled runs passed checks that memory-free runs failed, including docking-configuration checks.
Combines automation, reproducibility, direct analysis, and human-in-the-loop feedback; its scope is illustrated by four case studies.

papers.abstract: RL agents trained on a single trajectory-level return face a credit-assignment problem: when a reward arrives many steps after the decision that caused it, every action gets the same signal regardless of causal responsibility. This paper studies Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking (VCBM), which concentrates credit on the decision points that determine an episode's return, via two instantiations. The first targets a fully observed, low-dimensional MDP (a delayed-reward watch-repair task), where VCBM statistically discovers which state components the agent causally controls and estimates per-decision-point action values directly, evaluated against ground truth and RUDDER, an LSTM-based baseline. VCBM converges to 95.07% correct decisions in a mean of 1,532.3 episodes across 20 seeds, versus RUDDER's slower, more variable convergence (mean 3,327.1 episodes; p<0.001); VCBM's discovered causal structure exactly matches ground truth in all seeds. The second targets a partially observed, language-based setting: an LLM agent trained with Leave-One-Out PPO (LOOP) in AppWorld, where causal discovery is intractable and a structural heuristic (state-mutating tool calls) substitutes for it, with credit distributed via retrieval over episodic memory and blended with LOOP's advantage. Over 200 iterations on identical Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/LoRA/FSDP2 configurations, VCBM-blended LOOP improves task success over plain LOOP (0.354 vs. 0.458), reduces final-step max importance weight, and improves token efficiency, with a small KL exception favouring LOOP. The watch-repair result supports the claim that weighting causally relevant steps is more sample-efficient than an undifferentiated baseline or a learned return-redistribution network; the AppWorld result, limited to one seed per arm by a 2-GPU budget, is a compute-limited demonstration at a harder, natural-language scale, not a statistical confirmation.
bullets: Addresses the problem of assigning equal credit to all actions when rewards arrive long after their causes.
In a fully observed watch-repair MDP, VCBM discovers causal state components and directly estimates per-decision action values.
VCBM reached 95.07% correct decisions in a mean of 1,532.3 episodes across 20 seeds, versus 3,327.1 for RUDDER; its causal structure matched ground truth in every seed.
In AppWorld, a retrieval-based heuristic blended with LOOP improved task success from 0.354 to 0.458, while also improving token efficiency and reducing final-step maximum importance weight.
The AppWorld result used one seed per arm and is therefore a compute-limited demonstration rather than statistical confirmation; a small KL metric favored plain LOOP.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning on agent trajectories is an effective way to improve coding agents, but selecting useful training examples requires more than identifying successful runs. A resolved patch may follow inefficient reasoning or unnecessary tool use, while a failed run may still contain useful intermediate steps. Training pipelines therefore rely on rules and qualitative assessments to filter trajectories, yet designing these filters typically requires substantial human expertise, and validating improvements through repeated training and evaluation is expensive. We introduce MetaCurate, a training-free framework that evolves executable trajectory curation filters using pairwise LLM judgments. Disagreements between the filter's rankings and the judge's preferences provide targeted feedback for jointly revising its rules, rubric, and aggregation policy. The resulting filter scores trajectories independently, so pairwise comparisons are required only during search. Starting from a blank filter, MetaCurate autonomously discovers a curation strategy that achieves competitive downstream performance without task-specific handwritten criteria. We validate downstream utility through controlled SFT experiments on our uncurated trajectory pool and the Nemotron v3 SWE dataset, with random selection and hand-authored filtering as baselines. In our experiments, MetaCurate achieves the highest mean SWE-Verified score among the compared methods, including hand-authored rule-based filtering and a training-loop baseline whose search costs 3.5x as much.
bullets: Successful trajectories may contain inefficient reasoning, while failed runs can include useful intermediate steps, making curation difficult.
The framework uses pairwise LLM judgments to identify ranking disagreements and revise a filter’s rules, rubric, and aggregation policy.
After search, the learned filter scores trajectories independently, avoiding pairwise comparisons during deployment.
Controlled SFT experiments on an uncurated pool and the Nemotron v3 SWE dataset found the highest mean SWE-Verified score among compared methods, including hand-authored filtering.
The approach is training-free during curation search and reportedly costs less than a training-loop baseline.

papers.abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

papers.abstract: Multi-chain reasoning is a challenging task not only because the multi-chain evidence is dispersed, but also because different parts of reasoning may require distinct, interacting chains of support. Flat retrieval can flood a model with loosely related text, whereas early selection of a single reasoning path can discard evidence that becomes useful only after other facts are considered. We introduce RESIN (Reasoning with Entity Structured Indexing), which uses structure to locate evidence while keeping the original source as the basis for reasoning. RESIN decomposes a question into focused one-hop needs, retrieves a small set of source-grounded units for each hop, and places only this relevant evidence in a compact reasoning buffer. The buffer preserves alternative supports until final composition, making intermediate decisions explicit without forcing a brittle path. On the full HolisQA benchmark, RESIN achieves 82.92 context recall and 76.70 answer relevancy over all questions, with higher reported CR and AR across five domains and higher F1 in four domains than the published baselines. Ablations show that both typed evidence diversity and hop-wise decomposition are essential, supporting a clear conclusion: Precise evidence organization and delayed commitment make multi-chain reasoning effective and auditable. Our code is available at https://github.com/RamonMeng/RESIN.
authors: Xuanyu Meng, Jash Rajesh Parekh, Jiawei Han
bullets: Addresses dispersed, interacting evidence that flat retrieval may over-select or prematurely discard.
Decomposes questions into focused one-hop needs and retrieves source-grounded evidence for each.
Uses a compact reasoning buffer that preserves alternative supports for explicit final composition.
On HolisQA, reports 82.92 context recall and 76.70 answer relevancy across all questions, with stronger domain-level results than published baselines.
Ablations identify typed evidence diversity and hop-wise decomposition as essential; the approach emphasizes auditable reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: RESIN at a glance. Offline, entity-structured records serve as addresses into source-grounded evidence. Online, a dependency-aware plan creates focused one-hop needs; each retrieves a small candidate set, and the resulting evidence buffer remains available until final composition.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses decide what a language model sees across turns: they drop old turns, summarize them, or replay the model's own earlier reasoning. We ask when these choices change whether an agent succeeds, not only what it costs, and report three findings. First, in a pre-registered synthetic probe, truncating the context window costs a low-cost reasoning model nothing in success when a needed fact can be looked up again (it looks the fact up instead), but drops its success to chance when the fact cannot be re-observed: the two penalties differ by 92.5 percentage points (90% CI [89.5, 95.5]). A pre-registered replication on one model from a second provider showed the same contrast. Once the fact was lost, that model chose no answer rather than guessing. Second, on ARC-AGI-3, where the benchmark's Standard harness trails its Provider Adapter harness by a wide margin, we decompose that gap one component at a time, for one model on four games. Summarizing old turns instead of dropping them, while keeping the Standard harness's invitation to take notes, recovers 86% of a 63-point gap without replaying the model's reasoning. The same harness without the invitation recovers 43%, and adding the provider's native replay of the model's reasoning recovers the remaining 57%. These are point estimates from one counted run per configuration and game, and the replay share depends on a single run. Third, in the benchmark's published runs and in ours, the Adapter's advantage in the probability of clearing a level it has reached is larger at deep levels than at early ones. This largely restates where runs stopped and does not separate a growing advantage from a constant one.
bullets: Truncating context had little effect when the model could look up a needed fact again, but reduced success to chance when the fact was irretrievable—a 92.5-point penalty difference.

On ARC-AGI-3, summarizing old turns recovered 86% of the Standard-versus-Adapter harness gap without replaying prior reasoning; note-taking and reasoning replay accounted for the remainder in tested configurations.
The Adapter harness showed a larger probability of clearing reached levels at deeper levels, though this may reflect where runs stopped rather than a growing advantage.

papers.abstract: Latent memory is gaining ground as a lightweight history supplement for GUI agents. It supplies history to a frozen vision-language model via prefix vectors trained with step-wise cross-entropy (CE). While resulting gains are naturally attributed to encoded history, our controlled experiments show they primarily stem from action revision. The prefix learns to alter the model's default actions. However, this revision is unscoped because step-wise CE pushes outputs toward reference actions at every step without explicitly preserving correct decisions. Consequently, it repairs errors but also breaks 8-13% of initially correct answers. Overall accuracy metrics hide these losses. We therefore propose ScopeMem, a latent-memory method for scoped revision. Its encoder conditions prefix generation on the model's initial answer and is trained to correct errors while preserving correct decisions. On the controlled ablation set, ScopeMem reduces the share of broken correct decisions to 5.6% while repairing more errors than any evaluated CE-trained prefix. On AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, and zero-shot AITW, ScopeMem outperforms all evaluated prompting and latent-memory baselines, enabling a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B to match or surpass GUI-specialized agents and Qwen3-VL-32B.

bullets: Latent-memory gains mainly come from changing the agent’s default actions, not merely supplying history.

ScopeMem conditions its prefix memory on the initial answer to enable scoped correction.
It reduces broken correct decisions to 5.6% while repairing more errors than evaluated CE-trained prefixes.
On AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, and zero-shot AITW, it outperforms evaluated prompting and latent-memory baselines.

papers.abstract: Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation, interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight online memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.
authors: Guannan Lai, Zi-Yang Bai, Jun-Peng Jiang, Han-Jia Ye
bullets: Resource constraints can make existing memory methods ineffective, as irrelevant or ineffective retrieval consumes scarce context and reasoning capacity.
The key challenge is to estimate memory worth—not merely retrieve relevant experiences.
TokenWorth is a lightweight online framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback.
It uses the learned worth signal for both memory retrieval and bounded memory management.
Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and local/API deployments, it achieved the highest task success with the fewest output tokens among evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: We study whether geometric relationships between conversation turns, memory texts, and queries can predict answer correctness before generation. We evaluate four memory implementations with dense or hybrid retrieval and one observation-summary comparator. We embed these texts in a shared space. A logistic classifier uses 25 features describing query proximity, memory-conversation correspondence, and conversation structure. On LongMemEval-small, pooled AUROC is 0.640 over 2,367 question-system pairs, below a question-difficulty baseline of 0.655. Performance varies by question type: geometry reaches 0.841 on single-session-assistant questions, but system identity alone reaches 0.826. After controlling for difficulty and identity, geometry adds no statistically established pooled improvement (delta = +0.002, 95% CI [-0.010, 0.014]). A fixed-store context-selection experiment finds higher accuracy with proximity-ranked memories than with random subsets, consistent with ordinary retrieval relevance. On LoCoMo, nearest-turn similarity has modest predictive value for single-hop questions and near-chance estimates for several other categories. Training uses correctness labels; prediction uses pre-answer features and no additional LLM generation call. The results characterize associations between memory representations and correctness, rather than establish a reliable deployment diagnostic. In particular, embedding proximity does not verify fact coverage or distinguish memory-construction, retrieval, and generation errors.
authors: Iliya Zhechev, Radoslav Ralev, Chris Coleman, Srijith Rajamohan, Jen Agarwal, Tyler Hutcherson, Simba Khadder

papers.abstract: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.
authors: Adri\'an S\'anchez-Freire, Gonzalo P\'erez-G\'omez, Aitziber Atutxa, Ander Barrena
bullets: Expanding retrieval collections can change performance patterns observed on small or controlled corpora.
Abstract retrieval works best for abstract-aligned evidence, while full-text is preferable when richer evidence is needed.
Hierarchical full-text retrieval usually matches or exceeds flat full-text performance while using 67% fewer indexed units and 44–56% less storage.
RAG improved most external benchmark configurations and all held-out test configurations, with gains of up to 9.6 and 30.3 percentage points, respectively.
Reranking benefits depend on the corpus and retrieval setting; design choices should reflect evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can ground LLM outputs in domain-specific knowledge, but legal documents are hard: standard chunking fragments hierarchical argument structure, and generic embeddings struggle with both precise citation matching and semantic understanding. We propose StrucChunk (Structure Aware Chunking) with hybrid dense-sparse retrieval for hierarchically structured legal documents. It treats documents as directed acyclic graphs of provisions, preserves clause boundaries, resolves cross-references before embedding, and combines BM25 with BGE-M3 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. We evaluate on five corpora, three legal traditions and two languages. StrucChunk reaches 100% boundary precision (vs. 7.7% for recursive splitting on CrPC), preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references (vs. 0%), and matches section coverage with 40.3% fewer chunks on GDPR. On LegalBench-RAG (6,858 query-passage pairs), it achieves Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% vs. 23.59% for the best baseline (+104%), surpassing the published state of the art by +83%. On 501 queries each for CrPC and CPC (Indian law), Recall@5 improves from 0.557 to 0.804 (+44.4%) and from 0.158 to 0.259 (+64.6%); chunking accounts for 88% and 73% of the gain. On 501 GDPR queries, Recall@5 is 0.868 with R@1 improving +59%. On NitiBench-CCL (3,730 Thai financial law queries), HR@5 is 0.856 vs. 0.594 for naive chunking (+44.1%), showing that section-boundary alignment is the dominant factor across languages, and cross-reference augmentation adds +2.3% on cross-reference queries. We release the implementation, 5,256 evaluation queries across five legal corpora, annotation methodology and chunking quality metrics. Code: github.com/SinghSuryaDeep/legal-rag-strucchunk-1
authors: Surya Deep Singh, Ashutosh Tripathi, Gaurav Deep Singh
bullets: Represents legal documents as provision graphs, preserves clause boundaries, and resolves cross-references before embedding.

Achieves perfect boundary precision, preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references, and uses 40.3% fewer chunks while maintaining section coverage on GDPR.
Improves retrieval substantially across benchmarks, including Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% on LegalBench-RAG and higher Recall@5/HR@5 on Indian, European, and Thai legal queries.
Releases implementation, evaluation queries, annotation methodology, and chunking-quality metrics.

papers.abstract: Voice-based public services have evolved from manual switchboards to intelligent platforms to meet modern user needs. However, current systems remain constrained by rigid menu-driven interaction, fragmented vertical services, and limited extensibility. To address these issues, we present VISAGENT, an agent-based end-to-end voice interaction system for large-scale public services that integrates end-to-end speech interaction, hierarchical agent routing, a scalable voice-agent marketplace, and user memory support. The system replaces menu-driven workflows with natural speech and dynamically dispatches user requests to either a general conversational model or specialized domain agents via a two-level routing paradigm that achieves sub-second intent-to-agent selection over hundreds of agents. User memory informs preference-aware agent selection and supplies relevant preferences and context to selected agents, supporting personalized task execution and reducing the need for users to repeat previously provided information. A voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational entities, enabling dynamic onboarding and ecosystem-level extensibility. We validate VISAGENT through a real-world deployment in China's 114 hotline across multiple service domains. Experimental results demonstrate low-latency full-duplex interaction, robust routing scalability, and competitive speech naturalness. More broadly, this work advocates a shift from isolated voice assistants toward agent-centric conversational infrastructures, providing a general blueprint for building extensible voice-agent systems in public services and beyond.
authors: Xiang Wang, Zhaoxiang Liu, Xiang Chen, Liqiang He, Kai Wang, Shiguo Lian
bullets: Targets rigid menu systems, fragmented services, and limited extensibility in public-service voice platforms.
Combines end-to-end speech interaction, two-level hierarchical routing, a voice-agent marketplace, and user memory.
Routes requests to general or specialized agents and uses stored preferences and context for personalized task execution.
Supports dynamic onboarding of task agents as conversational entities, enabling ecosystem-level extensibility.
Validated in China’s 114 hotline, demonstrating low-latency full-duplex interaction, scalable routing, and competitive speech naturalness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of VISAGENT. The framework comprises a full-duplex user interaction layer, a two-level hierarchical routing layer, and an extensible voice-agent marketplace. The user memory service provides shared context for agent selection and task execution, while the voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational agents and onboards them into the marketplace.

Figure 3: Request-processing workflow of VISAGENT. Spoken input is routed either to the end-to-end conversational model or to a domain-specific agent selected according to the request, dialogue context, and relevant user memory. During agent execution, failures return to the first-level router with the available context and failure feedback, while additional service requests explicitly introduced by the user are redispatched within the same session. After successful task completion, the system asks whether the user has another request. An affirmative response initiates a new request cycle, whereas a negative response triggers interaction summarization, memory update, and session termination.

Figure 4: Architecture of the speech interaction component used in VISAGENT. The primary speech-to-speech path integrates an audio encoder, an input adapter, an LLM, a streaming audio decoder, and a vocoder. An auxiliary CTC transcription branch supplies textual representations to the hierarchical routing layer and downstream service agents.

Figure 5: Three-phase training procedure for the speech interaction model. papers.abstract: Large language models remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks requiring procedural reasoning. We argue that a key cause is the absence of explicit procedural memory: accessible, modifiable knowledge of how tasks are accomplished, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. Goal-Oriented Graphs offer such a representation, encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable symbolic structure. We examine their construction, the challenges they pose, and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning.
authors: Jonathan Leung, Zhiqi Shen, Deheng Ye
bullets: Long-horizon procedural reasoning remains unreliable in large language models.
Procedural memory is proposed as distinct from semantic and episodic memory.
Goal-Oriented Graphs encode goals and prerequisite dependencies in inspectable symbolic structures.
The paper examines graph construction challenges and principles for integrating symbolic structure with neural reasoning.

Table 2: Expected tradeoffs among procedural memory representations for LLM agents. A “∼” indicates partial or moderate support. These ratings are conceptual expectations based on representational properties rather than a quantitative benchmark comparison.

papers.title: Procedural Memory for Language Agents: A Neurosymbolic Perspective on Explicit Goal Structure

papers.abstract: Generator--critic trading systems pair an LLM-based trader that makes trading decisions with a red team agent that evaluates these decisions and provides feedback for revision. However, improving individual trading decisions does not ensure that both agents learn from experience and improve together over time. This raises an important question: how can the trader and red-Team select useful experience and learn from each other's evolving behavior? On one hand, experience that benefits decisions under one market condition may become ineffective or harmful under another. On the other hand, trading outcomes reflect both agents' actions, making it difficult to derive appropriate experience for each role. In this work, we propose ACE-Trader, an adversarial co-evolution trading framework. Specifically, we first develop separate context-dependent memory selectors that learn to identify useful experience for the current trading decision. Both selectors receive shared feedback from net-return differences between complete memory-assisted and memory-free trading pipelines, with online updates emphasizing recent outcomes. We further design a co-evolution mechanism that links role-specific memories through shared trading records. We use these records to evaluate the Red-Team's risk assessments and the effects of the Trader's revisions against realized market outcomes, then derive experience for their respective memories. By linking this experience to the corresponding records, we enable the Trader to improve its proposals based on prior critiques and the Red-Team to adjust its review focus as the Trader's behavior changes. Experiments on U.S. stock trading show that ACE-Trader outperforms all 22 active baselines in cumulative return and achieves the highest Sharpe ratio and lowest maximum drawdown across both active methods and passive benchmarks.
authors: Chang Zhou, Jiarun Zhou, Xingtong Yu, Hong Cheng, Hui Zhang, Xinming Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that improving isolated trading decisions does not ensure long-term co-learning between trader and critic.
Uses separate, context-dependent memory selectors for each role, updated from net-return differences between memory-assisted and memory-free trading.
Links role-specific memories through shared trading records to evaluate critiques, revisions, and realized market outcomes.
Experiments on U.S. stock trading report higher cumulative return, the highest Sharpe ratio, and the lowest maximum drawdown among evaluated baselines and passive benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.
authors: Guanqun Jiang, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Introduces procedural hallucination: producing retrieval-supported answers that violate a governing skill or procedure.
Presents SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains.
Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% with conflicting retrieval, versus 78.2% and 72.8% with supportive retrieval.
Mechanistic analysis finds the largest answer-preference divergence shortly after generation begins, with repair primarily attributed to value vectors.
Intervening in the identified value pathway improves final answer validity.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates how language models handle conflicts between retrieved context and stored skills, framing skills as a form of memory. Relevant to LLM memory mechanisms and retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models often follow useful but skill-violating retrieval cues, causing procedural hallucinations that can be traced to early value-pathway dynamics.

papers.abstract: Reflection lets LLM agents improve from their own attempts, but the memory it builds is local to a single task, so an agent reflecting on its own tends to revisit the same explanation for failure. Cross-task reflective memory addresses this in two forms: retrieved memory keeps past experience explicit and looks up related cases, which is specific but bounded by the bank, and parametric memory internalizes experience into parameters, which generalizes but is grounded in nothing beyond the task description. When both are used, existing agents combine them additively, feeding their outputs to the solver side by side, so retrieved experience never changes what the learned memory produces. We introduce CoMem (Compounding Memory), which makes retrieved experience an input to the learned memory itself, at training and at inference. The agent builds a bank of its own successful and failed reflections, learns from retrieved cases to write failure hypotheses, candidate explanations of how an attempt is likely to go wrong, and at test time reasons from newly retrieved cases to guide each attempt. Varying the retrieved cases gives the memory different perspectives, yielding reflective diversity that is not merely sampled but also grounded in retrieved experience. Across two backbones and five benchmarks in math, code, and multi-hop QA, CoMem achieves strong overall performance. Additional evaluations show that it generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and enables smaller models to provide effective guidance to stronger solvers.
authors: Yun Shen, Ming Shen, Tianjun Yao
bullets: Addresses repetitive, task-local self-reflection and the grounding–generalization trade-off between retrieved and parametric memory.
Builds a bank of successful and failed reflections, then uses retrieved cases to generate failure hypotheses during training and inference.
Different retrieved cases provide grounded reflective diversity to guide future attempts.
Shows strong overall performance across two backbones and five math, code, and multi-hop QA benchmarks.
Also generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and helps smaller models guide stronger solvers.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces compounding memory for LLM agents, using retrieved experience to anticipate failures, relevant to LLM memory and agent adaptation.
papers.title: CoMem: Learning to Anticipate Failures from Retrieved Experience
papers.tldr: CoMem improves LLM agents’ failure anticipation by conditioning learned reflective memory on retrieved past experiences rather than using retrieval and learning separately.

papers.abstract: Recovering from failures in long-horizon, stateful language agents is challenging because the action introducing a defect, the symptom exposing it, and the persistent state requiring repair frequently diverge. Existing methods largely focus on retrospective failure attribution, leaving sequential diagnosis and state repair poorly integrated under constrained budgets. We introduce TRACE-FIX, a unified recovery framework centered on versioned residual task state. Trace transforms execution logs into a structured dependency-linked ledger, prioritizing unresolved task requirements rather than salient surface errors. Fix formulates recovery as budgeted planning over admissible actions, incorporating outcome forecasting and explicit repair-reserve constraints to prevent premature budget exhaustion. To rigorously decouple localization accuracy from downstream repair capability, we present LongH-Debug, evaluating root-cause attribution, verified-fault recovery, and end-to-end closed-loop execution independently. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that structured residual tracking substantially improves causal localization over raw-trace baselines, while budget-aware sequential planning converts verified fault signals into more reliable task recovery without destructive trial-and-error. Code is available at https://github.com/toffeecat/tracedp.
bullets: Targets failures where the triggering action, observed symptom, and state needing repair occur at different points in execution.
Trace converts execution logs into a dependency-linked ledger focused on unresolved task requirements.
Fix plans admissible recovery actions using outcome forecasts and repair-reserve constraints to avoid exhausting the budget prematurely.
LongH-Debug separately evaluates root-cause attribution, verified-fault recovery, and end-to-end execution.
The framework improves causal localization over raw-trace baselines and enables more reliable recovery without destructive trial-and-error.

(b) The planned 1,500-trajectory corpus allocates quotas across seven environments grouped into search/retrieval, symbolic/embodied, transactional/social, and persistent artifact/system state. Hypothetical planning outcomes are kept separate from observed execution receipts throughout.
