papers.selection_reason: Implements a persistent per-user relationship memory layer over an LLM; relevant to agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Love for Believable AI: Artificial Partiality and Relationship Persistence as an Engineerable Stance
papers.tldr: A persistence-layer mechanism operationalizes artificial partiality through bounded caring and relationship-specific state, but current results support only a protocol-defined behavioral signature—not perceived love or attachment.

papers.abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further. We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.
authors: Shangyin Tan, Ben Zhou, Lakshya A Agrawal, Jialin Zhang, Yilin Chen, Qiuyang Mang, Donghyun Lee, Dennis Jacob, Koushik Sen, Alex Dimakis, Matei Zaharia
bullets: Parallelism, longer iteration, and agent communication eventually plateau as accumulated history anchors agents to small edits.
The proposed strategy periodically discards agent sessions and candidate history, then restarts from the best candidate found.
Implemented in a communicating multi-agent system and evaluated across four tasks in programming, kernel optimization, and model training.
Forgetting improved results by up to 15% over parallel agents and up to 39% over a single agent.
The findings suggest memory management is as important as compute for open-ended automated discovery.

figures.caption: Figure 3: The harness. The reducer reads the agent’s search state and its sessions and decides what the agent sees and which session it continues. The agent then edits a candidate and the judge scores it. The harness records the new candidate with its score in the search state and the turn in the agent sessions. A team runs four such loops at once, each with its own state, and the candidates of an agent’s peers come from the other three loops.

Figure 5: Every session narrows, and forgetting resets it. Inside the AtCoder Heuristic Contest 014 runs of Table 1, three replicates per configuration, pooled. Each point is the median over the proposals that finished within one dollar of a replicate’s spend; the team’s line breaks at each forget, where its sessions are discarded and it restarts from the best candidate.

Figure 4: Continue or forget, from the same plateaued state. Best score so far on AHC014 against total money spent. The black line shows the first 30 proposals prefix for all runs. At the forget line, the next 30 proposals per agent either continue the same sessions or forget. Left to right, a single agent, four parallel agents and a team of four. Forgetting climbs higher on average and spends less than continuing the same sessions overall due to shorter context.

Figure 2: The core idea. Top, autoresearch, where one agent proposes candidates iteratively inside a single continuous session with the whole history in context. Running several such agents in parallel or letting them read one another’s candidates through peer communication still keeps every session, and all of these configurations plateau. Bottom, a team of four agents with communication and forgetting. At each forget line every session and search state are discarded, and only the best candidate so far is remembered, so all four agents of the next round start fresh from that single candidate.

Table 1: Final best score of each configuration, over three runs per task, with the same total token cost. Bold marks the best configuration on each task; percentages are the change relative to the single agent baseline.

Table 3: Continuing versus forgetting from the same plateaued state on AHC014. Gain is the best new candidate over the state’s best, as mean and standard deviation over three replicates. Spend is per replicate.

Table 2: Mean best score of the team with forgetting at the end of each round, over its three runs per task, with the change from the previous round. Most of the gain comes from the first forget. As the candidate solution approaches the optimum, progress slows down.

papers.selection_reason: Shows forgetting search state improves LLM agent discovery; directly relevant to agent memory and adaptation.
papers.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
papers.tldr: Periodic forgetting lets LLM-agent research systems escape history-induced plateaus and discover better solutions with the same compute budget.

papers.abstract: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. However, existing methods train embeddings from scratch, which needs expensive GPU memory for fast reading and writing. Meanwhile, the ordinary memory of the host system is cheap and underutilized by these training methods. To scale on host memory, we introduce COUNT (Counting Offline Unlocks N-gram Transformers), which builds n-gram embeddings without adding learned parameters by storing precomputed n-gram counts on host. We use the corpus frequencies to weight together the LM's own unembeddings of the next tokens most often following the current n-gram history. At a fixed compute budget, COUNT can be added as an additional input embedding for pretraining 1B-parameter LMs to improve validation loss as much as an LM with 57% more compute. If GPU memory is limited, using COUNT to let backbone parameters fill GPU memory gives better performance than splitting memory with additional learned n-gram embeddings. Beyond efficiency, COUNT allows switching in a different table of n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time to adapt to a new task without any training.
authors: Ian Magnusson, Noah A. Smith, Pang Wei Koh
bullets: Addresses the GPU-memory and training cost of learned n-gram embeddings.
Builds n-gram embeddings from corpus frequencies and the LM’s next-token unembeddings, without adding learned parameters.
Stores count tables in inexpensive host memory while accessing only relevant embedding rows during inference or training.
For 1B-parameter LMs at fixed compute, COUNT improves validation loss by as much as 57% more compute.
Supports training-free adaptation by swapping in n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time.

papers.selection_reason: N-gram embedding memory that scales LM memory on host and enables training-free adaptation; fits LLM memory and architecture topics.
papers.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
papers.tldr: COUNT uses offline n-gram counts stored in host memory to provide training-free, domain-adaptable embeddings that improve language-model efficiency and validation loss.

papers.abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. We introduce a five-task-family testbed measuring consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. We propose Cortex, which generates prospective queries to anticipate uses of context and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. Across 4B--120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, including both text-only and multimodal models, Cortex lies on the empirical consolidation--retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of original non-target performance.
authors: Jintian Zhang, Feng He, Xinnian Liang, Ziwen Xu, Haoming Xu, Haojing Huang, Shuangzhi Wu, Ningyu Zhang
bullets: Frames memory consolidation as retaining context-induced gains after the context is removed.
Uses prospective queries and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward updates.
Evaluates consolidation and retention across five task families with single, batch, and sequential updates.
Tested on 4B–120B dense and mixture-of-experts text-only and multimodal models.
After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovered 88.9% of the context-induced gain and retained 99.8% of original non-target performance.

papers.tldr: Cortex consolidates temporary context-driven improvements into compact model updates while preserving non-target capabilities.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses drafter degradation on long inputs without costly long-context training.
Preserves exact positions for recent tokens while assigning distant entries a shared far-memory position.
Sharpens attention over distant memory and controls its total influence to reduce attention dilution.
Evaluated across six target–drafter pairs and benchmarks up to 256K tokens.
Predominantly achieved the highest speedups; the best case improved from 2.08× to 4.22× over autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: A ReAct-style agent accumulates observations, intermediate results, and failed attempts in a single context. As this context grows, stale and off-path information consumes its limited capacity and obscures relevant evidence, making focused reasoning increasingly difficult. We introduce TreeFlex, a framework in which the agent's own policy decides where to search. The agent records each intermediate state, with a short summary, as a node in a search tree maintained by the harness. The policy is a single language model that acts in two roles. In the Reflection role, it has a global view of the tree through these summaries and picks a node to resume, together with an instruction. In the Execution role, the harness restores the path that led to that node, and the model carries out the instruction with the usual task tools until it saves a new node or proposes a solution, which Reflection then approves or sends back to another node. Through these choices, the policy decides whether to deepen the current line, branch from or revisit an earlier state, verify a proposal, or stop, without a fixed traversal order or a score for each node. We train navigation, task actions, checkpointing, and proposal review jointly with a tree-aware adaptation of GRPO, using task-level outcome rewards augmented by process rewards. After small-scale RL of a 4B model, with the same active-context limit for all methods, TreeFlex reaches 48.8% accuracy on a challenging deep-research benchmark, versus 41.5% for flat ReAct and 42.8% for FoldAgent, and its Pass@8 is about ten points higher than either. On SWE-bench Verified, with all three systems trained with RL from the same 9B model, TreeFlex resolves 54.9% of tasks, versus 43.3% for FoldAgent and 45.2% for its step-wise variant.
authors: Dongzhuo Li, Fangzhou Cheng, Weiwei Li, Kevin Han, Haixu Ma, Zhongchang Sun, Ruiyi Li, Serena Li, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang, Yuandong Tian

papers.abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.
authors: Jiangcheng Song, Haodong Jing, Yulin Mu, Lesong Tao, Jixin Wang, Jin Cui, Tianjing Ren, Runxuan Xie, Yongqiang Ma, Nanning Zheng
bullets: Addresses the accuracy–inference-efficiency trade-off in reasoning over very long documents.
Uses a small language model for parallel evidence selection and a large language model for ordered memory verification and updates.
Trains the two systems through supervised evidence-selection tuning, GRPO-based memory optimization, and joint coordination.
Evaluated on RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA, achieving a 9.74× end-to-end speedup and 73.91% fewer output tokens than RL-MemAgent.
The abstract scopes results to the reported long-context benchmarks and evaluation settings.

papers.abstract: Enterprise group chats record project progress, decisions, task ownership, and other organizational information valuable to enterprise agents. Reliable retrieval is challenging because evidence spans interleaved threads, channels, and time, with meaning and authority conditioned on the speaker. Neither RAG's independent chunk retrieval nor memory systems' summary-based consolidation can reliably recover such distributed evidence. We present EGCForest, a novel multi-view hierarchical memory framework for enterprise group chats. EGCForest organizes an immutable message log into three complementary forests: a Channel forest for temporal workflows, an Actor forest for speaker-conditioned context, and an Artifact forest for deliverable lifecycles. Cross-view connections are enabled by a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges. Built on this memory backbone, EGCForest retrieves and assembles evidence by jointly leveraging message-level relevance, hierarchical context from forest summaries, and cross-view links, recovering distributed evidence. Experiments on three enterprise-chat benchmarks show that EGCForest consistently outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines, improving answer accuracy by up to 20.85 points over MemOS while supporting efficient online retrieval.

bullets: Addresses retrieval challenges caused by interleaved threads, channels, time, and speaker-dependent authority.

papers.abstract: The lasting gains in AI have come from methods that absorb more computation, and language models already scale computation within a call. Useful work, though, happens across calls: over hours or days, through tools and external systems, among many agents and the humans they work for, and increasingly through code the agents write themselves. Whether that work compounds is enabled by the harness around it, and the harness faces a constraint the model does not: of the three participants in such a computation, the human, the model and code, only the human's attention does not scale, so the computation can grow only if the human is not in every loop. L3M is a runtime built on that premise, written in Lean 4 so that one language implements the harness, states its invariants, and is the language agents extend it in. One computation spans humans, agents, models and code, and all of its state lives in Git: a rich state trajectory -- rather than a chat conversation -- is an object the runtime can resume, rewind, fork, compare and merge. Waiting, communication, delegation and undo are primitives, not patterns the model reasons through each time. When an agent works out a procedure, it can write it once as a sealed Lean program whose type is its permission request, and the harness offers it back as a tool -- machinery for the model to use. To take the human out of the loop, L3M uses reversibility to decide where that is safe: a tool's review tier follows from how far its effects can be undone, so agents act freely where the runtime can recover. Because the machinery can change, the properties that make this safe are stated as kernel-checked theorems about the code that runs. On Terminal-Bench, an untuned L3M reaches about two thirds of its (unsafe) shell-equipped pass rate using only safe (not needing human review) tools.
authors: Carson Eisenach, Robert Joseph George, Vincent Quenneville-Belair, Kate Gwimm, Dean Foster
bullets: Targets multi-call agent work involving tools, external systems, other agents, humans, and self-written code.
Stores the full computation state in Git, enabling resume, rewind, fork, comparison, and merge instead of relying on chat history.
Provides primitives for waiting, communication, delegation, and undo; agents can turn procedures into sealed Lean tools whose types specify permissions.
Uses reversibility to assign tool review tiers, allowing autonomous execution where effects can be safely undone.
An untuned system achieves roughly two-thirds of its unsafe shell-equipped pass rate on Terminal-Bench using only safe tools.

figures.caption: Figure 3: How an agent is defined. (a) The system prompt is assembled at boot from layers owned by the persona and by L3M, and each request adds a suffix for the model it is sent to. (b) Hooks decide what the agent does with each event, and each decision is journaled.

Figure 11: Two ways to collect the TODOs in a tree. Left: the agent is the loop, and every file costs model calls and context. Right: the agent writes the scan as a sealed program that runs under the tokens it already holds; each file is read and matched with no model call, and the model reasons once, over the summary.

Figure 7: From grant to system call, for a child with one project worktree and no network. The grant decides which tokens exist, the tokens decide which tools the model is offered, and each call carries its token to the provider, which checks its scope again.

Figure 12: L3M on one host. One daemon serves every hub on the host, and a hub is a folder: a bare repository, a forest of ACRs, its settings and a cache. Sessions are processes that the daemon starts and that call the model themselves. The human’s own settings name the hubs, the models and the credentials.

Figure 2: The body of an agent. Its write roots are worktrees on its own branches; the harness’s checkouts are denied to it; the rest of the agent is refs the harness writes and the agent reaches only through tools.

Figure 4: What the model sees is a pure function of the Log. Record 6 is retracted by the rewind at 7; the machine record at 3 lowers to nothing; the budget note at 5 becomes a delta that the dialect folds into the next user turn.

Figure 9: How a ceiling is known. An undo is a Reversible instance, which carries its proof; each class’s evidence is typed by the ceiling it supports; and the file class cites the round trip of one anchored write. The law that reversing twice is the identity is omitted.

Figure 20: One instance of improving agents inside L3M. Every arrow is an L3M primitive: a persona branch forks and syncs, a parent reads its children’s Logs, a program summarizes them and the model proposes edits, and a human publishes the result.

Figure 13: A tree of agents at spawn time. Each child’s grant lies within its parent’s, and its fuel is lent from the parent’s. A request that exceeds either is refused. The private child keeps the project’s refs but not the right to push them. The two children are the peers of Section 5.2.

Figure 15: Mail between hubs. The sender’s authority ends at its own outbox; carrying mail across machines is the postmaster’s duty, and only the human’s settings name the offices. Read marks travel back the same way, as receipts.

Figure 14: A letter, and its address. The host writes every field that says who sent a letter and when; the model writes the rest. An address names five parties, the persona being the agent’s name, and stars one. A letter for another hub adds the office and the recipient.

Figure 6: An effect class, its token, and a tool body written over them. The body’s type is its permission: it names NetEffects and nothing else, so it cannot reach IO, and the hosts it may fetch from are the ones its token carries.
Figure 8: A grant is a record of axes, a child’s grant is a meet with its parent’s, and the bound is a theorem.

Figure 10: A sealed program’s type is its permission request. The body is polymorphic in the host monad, so it can reach the world only through the eleven classes it is given, and Confined admits only the classes the program lists in footprint. ProgramCaps holds the tokens the agent’s grant minted, including the child-lifecycle door when the grant may spawn.

Figure 17: A staged build across two agents. Fetch sees only public lockfiles and warms a cache; build and run have no network. The builder cannot run what it built, though its build recipes execute inside the build sandbox; the runner receives the artifact by digest, cannot change it, and writes only a fresh output directory.

Figure 21: The bottleneck. A private parent P holds the secrets and has no network; its child C has the network and no secrets. Every message across the boundary is a metered edge, and the charged direction is private to public (orange). P seeds C with k bytes (1); C works publicly and returns a menu of N options (2); P answers with a selection (3), so at most log2 N bits leave the private side however much P read. In L3M this is a spawn pattern over the grants of Section 5.2.

Figure 5: The event loop. Signal sources and activities only post signals, and the sequencer alone appends to the Log. Each pass accepts what is consistent with the Log, journals the hooks’ decisions, folds the Log to decide what is owed, stores it, and only then starts the activities it names, so a kill at any point is repaired by the next pass.

Figure 18: Why the split bounds leakage. (a) An agent whose grant holds both the source and the network can leak through every byte it sends. (b) Split into peers with different grants that talk only by mail, the private side’s contribution to anything leaving is the seed, however much traffic the researcher does, under the channel model of the text. Arrow width stands for volume; orange marks bytes that may carry the source.

Figure 19: A quarantined reader. The program hands the page to a fresh subagent Q whose grant is empty, and parses its reply into one of three words fixed in advance. A page that hijacks Q gains a model that holds nothing, and can change only which word reaches A. Arrow width stands for volume; orange marks bytes that may carry an injected instruction.

Figure 16: Write, gate, execute: W⊕X for authority. No party both writes bytes and runs them, and the gate’s approval names the exact bytes. The staged build of Figure 17 is the same shape with two agents.

papers.title: L3M: A Verifiable Harness and Runtime for Self-Extending and Self-Improving Agents

papers.abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM's parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett--Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.
authors: Shijun Li, Yang Liu, Najmeh Sadoughi, Dongmei Wang, Xinjie Li, Zhu Liu, Rohith Mysore Vijaya Kumar, Yuzong Liu

The approach treats retrieval as a learnable translation action, with benefits shown under both offline and online retrieval.

papers.abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory. We combine zeroing with separately trained models that cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document. Across nine systems, some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the trained alternative. For example, in experiments that predict states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens a model's prediction loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original model with intact memory. On TriviaQA, giving xRAG memory from another question's passage raises F1, which measures word overlap with accepted answers, from 19.38 without a document to 24.78. Its effect on how often outputs contain an accepted answer is statistically uncertain. The question's retrieved passage scores higher still (29.88 F1). Thus a gain over no document alone does not establish that the gain requires the question's passage. Evaluations must therefore specify the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.
authors: Minsu Oh, Seunghui Jwa, Chanjun Park, Yeo-Chan Yoon
bullets: Zeroing memory can hurt performance without proving memory improves over a model trained without memory.
Across nine systems, some depend on memory yet perform worse than memory-free trained alternatives.
In story-state prediction, intact memory underperformed a separately trained no-memory model despite zeroing worsening loss.
On TriviaQA, unrelated passage memory increased xRAG F1 from 19.38 to 24.78, while the question’s passage reached 29.88; accepted-answer rates were statistically uncertain.
Evaluations should report comparison models, absolute performance, and generation/scoring conditions.

papers.abstract: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main}{GitHub}
bullets: Addresses the tension between precise information retention and efficient long-context inference.
Uses hierarchical neural memory modules, blockwise attention, and full attention over recent tokens while compressing older context into fixed-size memory.
Replaces attention layers post-training, avoiding training a new language model from scratch.
On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, improves QuALITY and LongHealth accuracy over segmented attention windows and reports faster prefill/decode with lower steady-state decode memory.
Evaluated configurations show benefits at medium context lengths; broader scope beyond the reported model and tasks is not established by the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Titan-Llama architecture at a glance. Left: The inner loss generates gradients at test-time w.r.t. MLP weights, teaching it to memorize historical attention key-value bindings. Right: The query associated with a local hidden state is used to retrieve a value from the NMM. This value, approximating the historical attention output, is then used as a residual and injected into the lambdagated output stream.

Figure 2: Long-context language modeling and decode latency. Left. Change in per-token negative log-likelihood relative to full attention, measured on Pile. Titan-Llama with 1024-token segments beats full attention from 16K through 128K. Right. Median single-token decode latency on an A100 at batch size one, after prefill and warmup (lower is better). Titan-Llama’s CUDA-graph-enabled decode is faster than the measured full-attention, Mamba-2, Gated DeltaNet, and In-Place TTT implementations across the reported lengths (Dao & Gu, 2024; Yang et al., 2025).

Figure 3: The effects of scaling chunk size on downstream performance and efficiency. Left. Scaling chunk size improves performance on long-context reasoning tasks like QuALITY and LongHealth. Middle. RULER trends are mixed. Longer chunks help at intermediate lengths but do not consistently improve associative recall. Detailed RULER results can be found in Table 5 in the Appendix. Right. Larger chunks increase prefill latency as memory bandwidth saturates.

Figure 4: Increasing the proportion of Llama 3.2 1B layers retrofitted with NMMs increases token decode throughput, decreases prefill latency, and also decreases memory footprint during token decoding. Peak memory footprint during prefill for partial Titan-Llama hybrids exceeds full-attention Llama while retrofitting all layers leads to lower peak memory footprint. Benchmarking was performed on a single 80GB NVIDIA A100 GPU.

Figure 5: Inference cost when later attention layers are restricted to local windows. The plot shows a 512-token window. Restricting more layers limits the growth of the KV cache and makes decode throughput less sensitive to prefill length.

Table 1: RULER S-NIAH accuracy (%) across context lengths. Titan-Llama matches full attention on 32K pass-key retrieval and achieves the strongest non-full-attention UUID scores at 8K–32K. Relative decode time (↓) averages next-token latency divided by full-attention latency at 8K, 16K, and 32K on A100. † marks timings of publicly available code that may not utilize caching.

Table 2: RULER accuracy by task family and context length. Titan-Llama recovers much of the accuracy lost to attention segmentation, although the gap to full attention widens on some tasks at longer contexts. Multi-key and FWE/CWE results exceed the full attention baseline.

Table 4: RULER accuracy by task family and context length when later attention layers are restricted to local windows. Results use cached autoregressive decoding. Accuracy remains low on most tasks, indicating that the NMM does not recover the information available through the later full-attention layers in the main configuration.
Table 5: RULER accuracy by task family, context length, and chunk size. Bold marks the best result among the three chunk sizes for each task and length.

Table 3: Multiple-choice accuracy when the later attention layers are also restricted to local windows. Neural memory improves both tasks relative to segmented attention alone, but does not recover the full-attention baseline.

papers.abstract: Personal-agent memory has largely focused on learning what users know, prefer, and want. However, knowing the user does not necessarily mean knowing what the user and the agent have established together. An assistant's proposal should not become an authorized instruction merely because it is remembered. We introduce Grounding Awareness, the ability to distinguish accepted, unacknowledged, revised, and scoped arrangements when selecting actions. We develop a controlled benchmark to test whether agents can tell the difference between proposals users have accepted and those they have not, and whether they apply accepted arrangements only where appropriate. Across multiple agents and memory systems, we find that strong memory performance does not ensure Grounding Awareness. More surprisingly, providing more complete user information can increase execution of unacknowledged proposals, while persistent memory can cause agents to treat these proposals as if they were user instructions. We trace these failures through memory writing, retrieval, and action selection. Finally, we introduce Grounding Layer, a lightweight, training-free extension that explicitly tracks grounding status and checks consequential actions, substantially improving agent behavior without modifying models or memory systems.
authors: Jiajun Chen, Xinyue Chen, Yicheng Jiang, Hua Shen
bullets: Introduces Grounding Awareness: distinguishing accepted, unacknowledged, revised, and scope-limited arrangements.
Presents a controlled benchmark for testing whether agents apply only accepted arrangements in appropriate contexts.
Finds that strong memory can still lead agents to execute unacknowledged proposals, especially when more user information is available.
Traces failures to memory writing, retrieval, and action selection.
Grounding Layer, a lightweight training-free extension, improves behavior by tracking grounding status and checking consequential actions.

papers.abstract: Evolutionary approaches to LLM-driven discovery often generate new programs from a small set of selected ancestors. This keeps contexts manageable but can omit useful evidence from other experiments, whereas including the full experimental history produces long, redundant contexts. We introduce a simple, single-agent discovery harness built around LabBook, an agent-maintained memory that serves two complementary roles: guiding retrieval of relevant evidence from a complete experimental log and informing the generation of new solutions. At each iteration, the same agent combines its memory with retrieved evidence and jointly produces the next program and an updated LabBook. This separates complete history retention from selective context construction, without requiring an explicit population or branching search structure. On 49 Frontier-CS problems, LabBook improves the observed quality-cost trade-off over the evaluated evolutionary baselines with two backbones, while remaining competitive across nine additional mathematical, systems, and heuristic-design tasks. Code will be released at https://github.com/BoYuanVisionary/LabBook.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between losing useful past evidence and using overly long experimental contexts.
Maintains an agent-updated LabBook alongside a complete experimental log.
Retrieves relevant evidence and jointly generates the next program and updated memory with a single agent.
Improves the observed quality–cost trade-off over evaluated evolutionary baselines on 49 Frontier-CS problems.
Remains competitive on nine additional mathematical, systems, and heuristic-design tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the LabBook harness. At each iteration, a single agent combines the task, the latest evaluated attempt, and the compact LabBook state; it may retrieve exact evidence from the append-only experimental log before jointly producing the next program and a rewritten LabBook. Evaluation appends a new record to the log, closing the discovery loop.

Figure 2: Cost–performance on Frontier-CS with DeepSeek V4 Flash (left) and Qwen 3.6 Flash (right), averaged over three independent runs. Each point averages the best-so-far score and cumulative cost across the 49 problems. LabBook is shown after 5 iterations and every 10 iterations thereafter; the baselines are shown every 10 iterations.

Figure 3: Memory and retrieval ablation over 30 iterations with DeepSeek V4 Flash. Full LabBook is shown as a solid line; component ablations, Best-of-N, Top-score Retrieval, and Full History use distinct dashed styles. Markers denote iterations 5, 10, 20, and 30.

Figure 4: Iteration–performance trajectory for the Heilbronn Convex case study. The vertical axis begins at 0.85 to emphasize improvements beyond the initial naive-sampling regime. LabBook records and repairs an early implementation failure, preserves iteration 33 as a reliable backbone, and retrieves that program 44 iterations later to produce a new best at iteration 77.

Higher scores are better for the first six tasks. For the final three tasks, E-Graph Extraction reports total extraction cost, Operator Scheduling reports total latency, and Pedigree reports total genotype changes; lower is better for all three. Bold denotes the best score for each task and backbone, and underlining denotes the second-best distinct score. All methods use 50 iterations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an agent-maintained memory system (LabBook) for LLM-driven discovery, relevant to LLM memory and online learning.
papers.title: LabBook: Harnessing Experimental History for Efficient LLM-Driven Discovery
papers.tldr: LabBook helps LLM agents use complete experimental histories without overwhelming context, improving discovery efficiency across diverse tasks.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory agents increasingly rely on it- erative search and reusable experience to answer questions over large personal, factual, or narrative histories. However, current experience-memory systems largely optimize relevance: they re- trieve past search lessons that appear similar to the current state and inject them into the prompt. A relevant experience can still be harmful when the memory substrate, question intent, answer granularity, or evidence boundary changes. We propose CAVE- Mem, a training-free framework that represents experience as a typed intervention operator with applicability, boundary, and utility conditions. CAVE-Mem first obtains a base memory-search answer, then allows an operator to change it only if the oper- ator matches the current substrate, answer contract, evidence boundary, and cross-fitted utility; otherwise the system abstains. Experiments across long-term conversational memory, multi-hop question answering, and long-document narrative reasoning show consistent gains over relevance-only experience reuse.
bullets: Addresses harmful reuse of seemingly relevant experiences when the memory source, question intent, answer granularity, or evidence boundary differs.
Represents experiences as typed intervention operators with applicability, boundary, and utility conditions.
Generates a base memory-search answer, then applies an experience only when its conditions match; otherwise abstains.
Evaluated on conversational memory, multi-hop QA, and long-document narrative reasoning, with consistent gains over relevance-only reuse.

papers.abstract: Automated post-training transforms pre-trained large language models (LLMs) into models capable of handling diverse domains by automatically constructing and optimizing a recipe of coupled decisions over data sources, data processing, cross-domain composition, and training configuration under a limited experimental budget. Existing automation either searches predefined recipe spaces that enable systematic optimization but remain fixed rather than adapting their available choices to the target tasks, or uses open-ended agents that discover task-specific choices but leave them implicit in trial-level edits, limiting their systematic reuse and recombination across trials. To fill this gap, we introduce optimization over a task-adapted recipe space, a novel paradigm that can adapt the recipe space itself to the target tasks while representing its choices explicitly for systematic reuse, recombination, and joint optimization. We instantiate this paradigm with Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO), comprising an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer that constructs the task-adapted recipe space and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer that uses structured trial evidence to guide LLM candidate construction and multi-objective Bayesian trial selection. Extensive experiments show that SRO achieves the highest average score in all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations. In joint post-training across three capability domains and six benchmarks, SRO reaches 41.1 versus 15.4 for the strongest baseline on Qwen3-1.7B with GPT-5.4, and 53.8 versus 40.8 on Qwen3-4B with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Our code is available at https://github.com/RuohLiuq/SRO.
authors: Ruohong Liu, Bohan Tang, Lekang Jiang, Jack Umenberger, Yiwen Guo
bullets: Addresses the rigidity of predefined recipe spaces and the implicit, hard-to-reuse edits of open-ended agents.
Introduces task-adapted recipe-space optimization, with explicit choices that support reuse, recombination, and joint optimization.
Uses an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer guided by structured trial evidence and multi-objective Bayesian selection.
Reports the highest average score across all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations.
In joint post-training across three domains and six benchmarks, scores 41.1 vs. 15.4 and 53.8 vs. 40.8 for the strongest baselines in two evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: Persistent textual memory lets language-model agents reuse lessons from past tasks to improve on future multi-step tasks without retraining. Systems such as ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet keep it as a playbook: lessons the agent writes after each task and reads in its prompt. A key challenge is to decide which lessons improve later tasks. Current systems leave the decision to the agent itself, which makes performance unstable: the same procedure can write a playbook that helps or one that falls up to 69.6 points below no playbook. These findings motivate valuing lessons by their measured effect on task success rather than by the agent's judgment. We propose Randomized Block Curation (RBC), which measures this effect with a randomized experiment on practice tasks. It groups related lessons into blocks large enough to move success measurably and, on each practice task, includes or leaves out every block at random. Random inclusion makes tasks with and without a block comparable, so the gap in their success estimates the block's effect. RBC keeps the blocks that help and, since the same procedure can write a helpful or a harmful playbook, grows several and serves whichever curated, whole or no playbook scores best on fresh practice episodes. Across two memory systems, three models and three benchmarks, RBC raises average success to 66.9, against 55.5 with the whole playbook, 54.1 with no playbook and 53.8 when the agent's own judgment picks the lessons to keep.
authors: Hoang Pham, Cong-Duy Nguyen, Dong Le, Ponhvoan Srey, Anh Tuan Luu
bullets: Persistent playbooks can help future multi-step tasks but may also substantially hurt performance when agents judge their own lessons.

The system grows multiple candidate playbooks and selects the best curated, complete, or empty playbook on fresh practice episodes.
Across two memory systems, three models, and three benchmarks, RBC achieved 66.9 average success versus 55.5 with the whole playbook, 54.1 with none, and 53.8 with agent-selected lessons.

papers.abstract: Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the moment it is made; the action it commits to is latent, carried out later, in a changing world. We therefore introduce a timestamp theory of decision validity and a decision ledger that realises it. Six timestamps define a decision; a freshness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence guarantees at action time, placing the remaining risk in information published afterwards. Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities: routing, which delivers that information to affected decisions before their revision deadlines, and temporal judgment, which reads it for the time of action. The ledger is persistent state holding each decision's times, evidence and background knowledge, indexed by watch conditions written at decision time. Controlled decision streams with exact labels confirm four predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to frontier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on decisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows routing; the ledger's index sets what routing reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect dependencies at low exposure; and the remaining errors concern when a change takes effect. Freshness makes a decision right when it is made; routing and temporal judgment keep it right when it is carried out.
authors: Ayoub Merimi, Souhail Bakkali, Abdeljalil Sakat
bullets: The paper distinguishes decision freshness at creation from validity at later execution in a changing world.
A six-timestamp theory defines decision validity and a freshness ceiling for evidence available at action time.
The ledger persistently stores decision times, evidence, background knowledge, and watch conditions for targeted updates.
Accuracy decomposes into routing new information to affected decisions and temporal judgment about when changes take effect.
Controlled streams across five LLMs support the theory: watch conditions can capture indirect dependencies, while remaining errors involve temporal effects.

papers.abstract: Scaling recursive self-improvement requires additional computation to produce useful research progress in reaching persistent objectives. Intuitively, more researcher agents can explore more hypotheses, but early evaluation scores might misrepresent their promise, shared findings could lose their applicability conditions, and useful procedures could remain confined to completed investigations. In this paper, we present AReaL-RSI, a framework for organizing a persistent research team of agents without updating backbone LLM weights. We formulate the scaling problem in terms of evaluated outcomes and whole-system resource expenditure. Concretely, a leader agent selects task-appropriate research orientations and guides ongoing investigations; conditional memory sharing distinguishes unresolved problems from supported findings and enables recipient adaptation. During recursive evolution, after each campaign, evidence-based review revises researcher orientation, knowledge, and skills for later campaigns. Experiments compare AReaL-RSI with Codex-Goal on downstream harness optimization, GPU kernel optimization, and AI research tasks using two backbones. Under the reported resource allocations, AReaL-RSI improves Terminal Bench performance by 2.2 percentage points for each backbone and increases mean KernelBench speedup by 32.2-36.8%; further scalability comparisons favor the design of AReaL-RSI over native scaling: combining experience sharing with specialized researcher roles yields 1.9-27.5% lower kernel latency than independent exploration and 1.3-33.9% lower latency than sharing alone across all seven comparable task-backbone pairs.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have substantially improved the capabilities of GUI agents, while memory augmentation has emerged as a promising approach for reusing knowledge from past interactions. However, existing memory augmented GUI agents typically adopt a fixed representation strategy, providing retrieved experience as a static modality. It remains unclear whether a single memory modality is consistently optimal, or how modality preference changes across interaction steps. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of memory modality in VLM based GUI agents. Across GUI benchmarks, we find that the preferred memory representation is strongly step dependent. Motivated by the finding, we introduce \textbf{SwitchMem}, a routing framework that dynamically selects between textual and visual memory representations at each step. Across three GUI benchmarks, SwitchMem outperforms memory augmented baselines that rely on static memory representations. Our findings validate our claim that memory modality is a step dependent decision rather than a fixed design choice. Code and project resources are available at https://txxnrd.github.io/switchmem
authors: Taeyun Roh, Suhyeong Park, Gijin Kim, Wonjune Jang, Jaewoo Kang
bullets: Existing memory-augmented GUI agents typically use one fixed memory representation.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. To address this phenomenon, we introduce the Family--Provenance--Authority framework (FPA). Specifically, FPA selects one representative per source family, conditions the eligibility of old records for the answer context on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with DeepSeek V4 Flash and from 0.782 to 0.916 with Kimi K2.6; mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from 0.106 to 0.030 and from 0.109 to 0.038, respectively. These results show that agent memory can preserve traceable history without allowing repeated historical information to govern current decisions. The code is available at https://github.com/OrcasSam/memory-echo-benchmark.
authors: Yufeng Li, Sheng Yao, Peng Zeng, Dezhang Kong, Shi Lin, Changting Lin, Xun Wang, Meng Han
bullets: Defines Memory Echo as excess retrieval exposure for historical information repeated from the same source without new independent evidence.
Introduces MEchoBench to evaluate emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and answer impact across memory lifecycles.
FPA selects one representative per source family, filters outdated records after verified corrections, and prioritizes authoritative evidence.
In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA improves reported accuracy and lowers Decision Contamination Effect for both evaluated models.
Scope: the evaluation focuses on same-source accumulation, post-correction persistence, and provenance-guided mitigation.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates and mitigates memory echo in single-agent long-term memory with provenance-guided framework, directly relevant to LLM memory.
papers.title: Memory Echo in Single-Agent Long-Term Memory: Lifecycle Evaluation and Provenance-Guided Mitigation
papers.tldr: Memory Echo causes repeated same-source memories to unduly influence agent answers, while the provenance-guided FPA framework substantially reduces this effect and improves accuracy.

papers.abstract: Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF
authors: Yutong Chen, Zhichao Xu, Rui Liu, Kunpeng Liu
bullets: Targets inefficient independent sampling in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
Stores recent responses, rewards, and verifier feedback in an evolving per-problem context memory.
Separates rollouts from policy updates and uses self-distillation for learning.
Across four benchmarks and two open models, it accelerates exploration by about 4× versus random sampling.
Improves unseen-test accuracy by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points while using less compute than RL baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of LEAF. Rollout: each problem keeps a memory of its last response, reward and feedback, which forms the context of the next attempt. papers.selection_reason: In-context memory for exploration in LLM reasoning; fits LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Explore with Memory, Learn without It: In-Context Exploration and Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: LEAF improves RLVR exploration by giving each rollout dynamic problem-specific memory and training the policy via self-distillation.

papers.abstract: Agents build knowledge graphs as memory, and building them has become easy. Maintaining them has not. When a source is retracted, overruled, or erased, everything built on top of it (entity merges, entailed edges, community summaries) must be re-examined, and the maintainer must choose between deleting too much and too little. Deployed pipelines delete only the directly extracted facts: on our corpus that reduces contaminated queries from 32.2% to 28.0% under a real retraction and changes nothing under predicate revocation. Rebuilding is no repair for a constructor that samples: two builds of the same 300-document corpus differ in 29,475 artifacts, five times the 6,248 that removing the 61 retracted documents changes. PolyGraph instead asks the constructor for receipts: for every artifact, alternative bundles of source evidence, each claimed sufficient on its own, emitted in the call that creates it. Cleanup is then set arithmetic over the receipts, with no model calls. Because receipts are the model's own self-report, a re-derivation audit checks them by deleting the cited evidence and testing whether the constructor still produces the artifact. The audit finds that a receipt is trustworthy when it is shaped like the claim it backs. Merge receipts, each backing one narrow claim, agree with re-derivation 68% and 85% of the time. Summary receipts, elicited per sentence but stored as one flat list for the whole text, are wrong about two thirds of the time, almost always by keeping dead content. One receipt per sentence instead is 100% and 88% faithful and lets cleanup keep 33 of 35 touched summaries. The result holds under a second oracle model, a claim-blind prompt, ten further deletions, a second domain and a second constructor. Distrusting the summary layer cuts contaminated queries to 0.4% and 0.8% at 99.8 to 100% of the recall a perfect maintainer would return.
bullets: Retractions or predicate revocations can invalidate merges, inferred edges, and summaries, while deleting only directly extracted facts leaves substantial contamination.
PolyGraph captures alternative sufficient evidence bundles when each artifact is created, enabling cleanup through set arithmetic without additional model calls.
A re-derivation audit tests whether receipts actually support their artifacts; narrow merge receipts were faithful 68%–85% of the time.
Per-sentence summary receipts were substantially more reliable than one flat receipt list, achieving 100% and 88% faithfulness across reported settings.
Distrusting unreliable summary evidence reduced contaminated queries to 0.4%–0.8% while retaining 99.8%–100% of perfect-maintainer recall across robustness tests.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two real chains from the corpus. Deployed deletion removes only the extracted claims (dashed). The entity merge keeps one evidence source from a paper that still stands, so it is correctly retained (green); five of five re-derivations agree. The entailed edge and the summary rest only on retracted evidence, mention no retracted paper, and keep reaching the retriever (red). Support labels delete the edge with one disjointness test. The summary’s label wrongly claims it still stands, the failure Section 6 measures; the layered policy of Section 6.4 removes it.

Figure 2: The audit as a classroom exercise, and its protocol translation (italics). A report claims wolves live in Duisburg on the strength of two books, each sufficient alone. When book A is retracted, the audit does not argue with that receipt: it removes book A and has the passage rewritten five times from book B only. Whether the wolves come back decides whether the sentence stays; the receipt does not.

Table 2: Self-reported labels graded against re-derivation (R = 5, τ = 0.2). Every model-authored artifact touched by the deletion was adjudicated, so rows are populations; n counts touched artifacts and undecided ones are listed separately. Leaky: label says alive, re-derivation says dead. Entailed edges are re-derived symbolically, agree by construction, and are excluded. Summary rows use the pipeline’s original summary prompt, which asks for support per sentence but stores one flat label for the whole summary; Table 3 varies that format.

Table 4: Retrieval-level consequence of the verification verdict. BM25, k=10, 300 MeSH-descriptor queries; truth is the re-derivation oracle. “Deployed” deletes only claims whose every asserting source is withdrawn, which is what current pipelines do. “Distrust the failing layer” applies the Table 2 verdict: summary labels are ignored and touched summaries are removed outright.
Table 1: Symmetric difference in artifacts. The floor is |G1△G2| for two independent builds of the same unchanged corpus; the effect is |G1△G3|, where G3 omits the 61 retracted documents.

Flat is the original prompt of Table 2: support asked per sentence, one flat list of alternatives stored for the whole summary. Whole summary asks only for sets that each support the entire summary; under it 10 of 59 summaries list more than one support set, against 46 of 59. papers.selection_reason: Addresses trustworthy maintenance of agent-built knowledge graph memory via provenance receipts, directly relevant to LLM memory.
papers.title: Keep Your Receipts: Trustworthy Cleanup of Agent-Built Knowledge Graphs
papers.tldr: PolyGraph makes agent-built knowledge graphs safely maintainable by recording and auditing source-evidence receipts for every derived artifact.

papers.abstract: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.
authors: Yue Wang, Qizhou Wang, Feng Liu, Gang Niu, Masashi Sugiyama, Bo Han
bullets: Long-context inference is costly, motivating test-time encoding of context into model weights.
Weight-encoded information can be confused with the model’s pre-existing knowledge and ignored as context.
The method associates each encoded context with an identifier, enabling the LLM to recite it later.
A prompting framework further guides the model to use the recalled information for subsequent inference.
It outperformed a baseline across controlled tasks and practical benchmarks using off-the-shelf LLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of (a) full-context inference, (b) encoded-context inference with meta-trained TCE, and (c) encoded-context inference with ACE. Full-context inference jointly processes c1:T and x, becoming infeasible when their combined length exceeds the input context window. TCE and ACE instead encode the chunks c1:T into LLM weights, illustrated here as FFN weights. Prior TCE methods often rely on additional meta-training-based fine-tuning, whereas ACE operates directly on off-the-shelf LLMs without such fine-tuning.

papers.title: Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?
papers.tldr: The paper makes context encoded into temporary LLM weight updates usable by assigning it an identifier and prompting the model to apply the recalled information as context.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon coding requires agents to maintain an evolving view of the project they are changing: what problem is currently being solved, what has already been learned or modified, which other artifacts may be affected, and what work remains unresolved. When this information is scattered across a growing interaction history, local edits can become disconnected from their later consequences and progress can be difficult to carry forward. We introduce StateHarness, a runtime framework that maintains evolving project state without updating model parameters. The working agent records its current problem and hypothesis, important findings and decisions, discovered repository relationships, and unfinished work. Runtime support prompts record updates, searches for callers, tests, and documentation that may be affected by a change, and maintains a compact working brief for subsequent decisions. When behavioral signals accumulate, a separate diagnostic session revisits the recorded history and surfaces overlooked evidence. Across three repository-level evaluations, StateHarness improves task completion and several measures of change consistency. On RefactorBench, full-chain completion increases from 29.4% to 35.3% and cleanup-check accuracy from 87.0% to 95.4%. On five LHTB software-engineering tasks, mean reward improves from 0.427 to 0.576, exceeding LongHorizon-Harness at substantially lower recorded execution cost. On ChainSWE, bug-fix rate increases from 35.1% to 39.5% and residual debt decreases from 60 to 43 items, although pass-to-pass regressions increase. These results show that maintaining project state can improve long-horizon coding while introducing measurable execution and regression trade-offs.
authors: Chuan Zou, Yujun Zhou, Xiaonan Luo, Xiangliang Zhang
bullets: Addresses project knowledge scattered across long interaction histories and disconnected local edits.
Maintains hypotheses, findings, decisions, repository relationships, and unresolved work without changing model parameters.
Uses runtime prompts for updates, impact searches, tests, documentation checks, and a compact working brief; diagnostic sessions revisit history for overlooked evidence.
Across three repository-level evaluations, it improves completion, change consistency, and bug-fix outcomes, while reducing residual debt in one evaluation.
Scope limitation: pass-to-pass regressions increase, showing a trade-off between stronger state maintenance and execution consistency.

papers.abstract: Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories and caches turn many reasoning steps into one. We call this reasoning contraction. A contracted memory saves reasoning steps and errors until its facts change, then quietly answers wrong. Most systems trust memories by counting successes and failures. We prove that such counters are badly tuned change detectors: a symmetric counter notices a partial change only after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped one may never notice it. On five LLMs answering multi-hop questions over edited facts, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters serve 7.0-13.5x more stale answers than certified memories given the same information, and on code tasks with an exact verifier 35-73x more. Safety also has a price. When facts change and each memory is judged only by its own verified outcomes, one number, the certification load, sets how much reasoning any safe memory can skip, and under Zipf demand it yields a scaling law. Our recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies its utility against live reasoning, and restarts the certificate when facts change, with the likelihood-ratio detector as the safety net for unannounced changes; for large edits it also invalidates the memory.
authors: Jianghong Zhou, Hao Rong, Chen Lin, Daoan Zhang
bullets: Reasoning contraction compresses many reasoning steps into reusable templates, skills, memories, or caches, but becomes unsafe when underlying facts change.
The paper shows symmetric and unclipped counters can detect partial changes extremely slowly or not at all.
Across five LLMs, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters produced 7.0–13.5× more stale answers than certified memories; on verified code tasks, the gap was 35–73×.
The proposed approach weights failures by likelihood ratios, certifies memory utility against live reasoning, restarts certification after changes, and invalidates memories after large edits.
Certification load determines how much reasoning a safe memory can skip; under Zipf demand, the paper derives a corresponding scaling law.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses safe memory reuse, certification, and change detection for LLM agents, fitting LLM memory.
papers.title: Many Steps into One: Reasoning Contraction and the Limits of Safe Memory Reuse for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Safe reuse of compressed reasoning memories requires principled change detection and certification, because common success/failure counters can silently preserve stale answers after facts change.

papers.abstract: As LLM agents take on more autonomous roles, they may interact with multiple clients and counterparties whose goals and incentives conflict. If an agent maintains shared inference state across these interactions, information associated with one relationship may influence decisions made for another. We test OLMo-3-7B-Instruct in a controlled two-client environment with 20 market scenarios, where each client is assigned an opposing objective. With shared conversational memory, the model deviates from the current client's objective in 22% of eligible decisions. We then investigate how these goals are represented in the KV cache. Linear probes show that client-goal ownership becomes highly recoverable in middle layers and is concentrated in particular attention heads. We use these results to identify where to intervene in the cache and test whether these representations affect the model's decisions. Ablating the competitor's cached goal representations at these locations shifts the model toward the current client. The effect is larger for heads identified by probing than for randomly selected heads, and larger when ablating goal tokens than matched non-goal tokens from the same client. Our results show that client-specific goal representations persist in the KV cache and can causally influence decisions made for other clients, highlighting the importance of relationship-specific state isolation in persistent LLM agents.
authors: Saloni Gupta, S\'ebastien Krier, Glenn Matlin
bullets: In a controlled two-client setting with opposing objectives, shared conversational memory led to deviations from the current client’s goal in 22% of eligible decisions.
Client-goal ownership was highly recoverable from middle-layer KV-cache representations and concentrated in specific attention heads.
Ablating a competing client’s cached goal representations shifted decisions toward the current client.
Interventions were stronger for probe-identified heads and goal tokens than for random heads or matched non-goal tokens.
The findings motivate relationship-specific state isolation for persistent multi-client agents.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Study overview. Conflicting client goals coexist in a shared persistent KV cache. We localize relationship-conditioned goal state and selectively ablate it to test its effect on later decisions.

Ablating the current client’s own state reverses the direction. Results shown for K (blue) and V (vermilion). Error bars are 95% family-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates persistent goal representations in the KV cache of LLM agents, relevant to LLM memory and state isolation.
papers.title: When Goals Leak Across Relationships: How Cached Goal Representations Shape Cross-Client Decisions
papers.tldr: Shared KV-cache state can cause an LLM agent to carry one client’s goals into another client’s decisions, but targeted cache ablation reduces this leakage.

papers.abstract: Although users may express different personalization needs across tasks, these task-specific behaviors can reflect shared underlying preference mechanisms. Existing LLM personalization methods often focus on surface-level interactions or undifferentiated histories, overlooking the shared mechanisms underlying these behaviors. We introduce PersonaFactors, a framework that distills reusable and interpretable personalization factors from heterogeneous user interactions. We construct a library of thirteen PersonaFactors by extracting evidence-grounded rationales and clustering recurring patterns across tasks, and develop a dynamic factor-guided generation framework that selects factors relevant to each user's history and current request. Across four personalization benchmarks and four backbone models, Dynamic PersonaFactor achieves the best score on every reported metric. Representation analyses further show that PersonaFactors and user history induce partially overlapping low-dimensional representations, and that their joint use yields complementary shifts. Taken together, these findings suggest that factor-based and history-based personalization can mutually reinforce each other.
authors: Hang Su, Zequn Liu, Jianghan Chao, Qiuyu Tian, Xuesong Lu, Yingce Xia
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between task-specific personalization behaviors and shared underlying user preferences.
Builds a library of 13 reusable PersonaFactors from evidence-grounded rationales and recurring cross-task patterns.
Dynamically selects factors relevant to the user’s history and current request during generation.
Achieves the best score on every reported metric across four personalization benchmarks and four backbone models.
Representation analyses suggest factors and history provide partially overlapping but complementary personalization signals.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reduce hallucination by abstaining from questions they would likely get wrong. Abstention can be implemented outside the model (selective answering) using a confidence threshold that controls the answer rate (coverage), or learned inside it (abstention training), which can perform better but fixes coverage once trained. To compare the two, we match their coverage and decompose risk (error rate) into answering ability and distinguishing ability, i.e., how well the model answers and how accurately it abstains, respectively. The decomposition shows that abstention training performs better mainly by answering better: with strong confidence estimators, the two have nearly equal distinguishing ability. This motivates Train for Accuracy, then Post-hoc Select (TAPS), a modular approach that keeps coverage controllable, needs only standard post-training and an off-the-shelf confidence estimator, and benefits from advances in either component. Across three LLMs and three factual QA benchmarks, TAPS with a probing-based confidence estimator attains 1.5--9.4 percentage points lower mean risk than three representative abstention training methods at matched coverage. Within TAPS, accuracy training often weakens the model's own confidence signals, yet refitting the estimator largely preserves distinguishing ability. Together, these results establish TAPS as a strong yet controllable baseline and raise the bar for future abstention training: sacrificing control over coverage should yield gains beyond what can be achieved by optimizing answering and abstaining separately.
authors: Junwei Zhang, Yifei Wang, Wanli Yang, Hexiang Tan, Rui Tang, Xin Chen, Jingang Wang, Du Su, Fei Sun
bullets: Abstention reduces hallucinations by skipping questions the model is likely to answer incorrectly, but learned abstention fixes coverage after training.
At matched coverage, abstention training’s advantage mainly comes from better answering, while strong confidence estimators provide similar distinguishing ability.
TAPS combines standard post-training with an off-the-shelf, probing-based confidence estimator, preserving controllable coverage.
Across three LLMs and three factual QA benchmarks, TAPS reduces mean risk by 1.5–9.4 percentage points versus three abstention-training methods.
Accuracy training can weaken the model’s native confidence signals, but refitting the estimator largely preserves abstention quality.

papers.abstract: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update fast-weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient-based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction-derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot-product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction-error residual and establish conditions under which inner-loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective used by TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero-epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per-token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8-2.9% on TTT-Linear-760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2-4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta-rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction-derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test-time memory.
bullets: Analyzes prediction-derived updates in released test-time-training (TTT) implementations.
For dot-product objectives, finds no explicit prediction-error residual and shows ascent/descent equivalence under reparameterization in certain conditions.
For LayerNorm-based TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP objectives, derives the inner gradient and identifies a component that cancels at initialization in the zero-epsilon limit.
Removing the component reduces gradient norms to 0.25–0.32 of the original and modestly increases perplexity, while freezing all fast-weight updates causes much larger degradation.
Synthetic tests show that plain delta-rule overwriting depends on step size.
